sources.text:
Decoding America: are the Democrats having their own Maga moment?
Full Story
Today
29 min
In this episode of Guardian Australia’s weekly US politics podcast, co-hosts Jonathan Yerushalmy and Reged Ahmad take a look at how the Michigan Senate primaries could decide the future of the Democrats. This is a race that has revealed the civil war raging inside the party, as some seek to take it further to the left, with candidates such as Abdul El-Sayed. But will this schism be the Democrats’ Maga moment, or will it leave the party open to a Republican communist ‘red scare’ campaign that could cost them the midterms? They also look at why the Senate unanimously passed a resolution declaring its opposition to any presidential pardon for Ghislaine Maxwell, the longtime associate of Jeffrey Epstein, as well as the next chapter in the reflecting pool saga and why Donald Trump said US attorney and Maga faithful Jeanine Pirro had ‘folded like an umbrella’

sources.news_title: After losing to Whitmer by 21 points, El-Sayed triumphs in Michigan and shocks Democratic Party
sources.text:
Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official who harnessed Democratic frustration with the party establishment, narrowly defeated Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan’s U.S. Senate primary, setting up a crucial test for progressives in a key battleground state.
El-Sayed will face Republican Mike Rogers, a former congressman, in November in a race that will help determine control of the Senate. His first challenge will be unifying Democratic factions after a bitter primary that offered divergent visions for a party desperate for a path back to power.
Stevens, who pledged her support for El-Sayed after conceding defeat, was backed by the Democratic establishment, including outgoing Sen. Gary Peters, whose retirement spurred a scramble to fill his seat. El-Sayed promised a more aggressive approach for confronting entrenched corporate interests and President Donald Trump, and declared his victory was nothing short of a political earthquake despite only scraping by Stevens.
“In the words of Muhammad Ali, we shook up the world,” he said.
Progressives have been gaining strength this year
The Associated Press declared El-Sayed the winner having confirmed that — after Wednesday morning updates in election returns in Wayne and Oakland counties, two of the state’s largest in the Detroit area — there were simply not enough votes left to count that would allow Stevens to catch up and overtake him as the leader.
El-Sayed’s victory was ultimately so narrow that it wasn’t assured until almost all ballots cast statewide were counted. At the time the AP declared him the winner, El-Sayed led Stevens by 14,893 votes — a margin of just under 1 percentage point — out of more than 1.5 million ballots counted.
His win, however slim, represents a significant shift for the Democratic Party; in 2018 he lost the gubernatorial primary to now-Gov. Gretchen Whitmer by 21 percentage points.
The former health official campaigned on “Medicare for All,” halting military aid to Israel and campaign finance reform. He had support from progressive leaders including Sen. Bernie Sanders and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who framed the race as a grassroots-focused movement and a broader fight against the establishment and big-money spending.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, another progressive leader, said El-Sayed’s victory “should be a wake-up call to the Washington Democratic establishment.”
Now comes the more difficult challenge for Democrats: uniting the party to defeat Rogers, for whom Republicans have already reserved large sums of money ahead of the general election.
“We have got to work together to take this country back,” Curtis Hertel, the chair of Michigan Democratic Party, said.
Michigan is a must-win Senate race for Democrats
The race will help decide which party controls the chamber in the last two years of Trump’s term. Those stakes added heat to the rivalry, with moderates arguing that El-Sayed would have a harder time than Stevens against a Republican in the general election.
Stevens, a four-term congresswoman, won election to Congress in 2018 after serving as chief of staff to President Barack Obama’s auto task force, which helped oversee the federal rescue of General Motors and Chrysler. Her campaign focused on manufacturing and the economy, and she stressed her past victories in tough races as proof she would be best positioned to beat Rogers.
El-Sayed cast himself as the anti-establishment candidate and argued that Democrats need to reject corporate influence and embrace a more progressive agenda.
While the candidate has said he is not a democratic socialist, he found support from some of the group’s members. That included Melat Kiros, who recently beat a longtime incumbent in a Democratic primary for a Denver-based House seat and was at El-Sayed’s watch party. Also there was Hasan Piker, a progressive and controversial influencer online.
The candidates’ differences were clear to some voters.
Kenneth Woodside, 87, of West Bloomfield, said he voted for El-Sayed because “the nation is ready for someone who wants to take some more action rather than on the road we are now, which is on the road to an oligarchy and authoritarianism.”
Nessa Fuller, 51, of Birmingham, said she voted for Stevens because she will “fight to get the right things done, and she’ll work with other people, which is really important to me.”
Outside influences spent millions on the Senate race
National groups poured unprecedented sums into the race, making it one of the country’s biggest tests of outside spending.
Outside groups backing Stevens spent more than $50 million, including more than $30 million from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, amounting to the largest investment ever from the organization that supports pro-Israel candidates.
“We took on a machine,” El-Sayed said.
Support for Israel is contentious within the Democratic Party and the Michigan primary reflected that divide: El-Sayed called for ending military aid to Israel, while Stevens maintained strong support for the relationship.
AIPAC issued a statement Wednesday saying it would oppose El-Sayed and “his radical anti-Israel agenda” in November’s election.
McKinney wins Detroit US House primary
In a heavily Democratic district representing Detroit, the 13th, state Rep. Donavan McKinney defeated Rep. Shri Thanedar. McKinney argued that the city should once again have a Black representative in Congress.
After Thanedar won election in 2022, Detroit had no Black representation in Congress for the first time since the early 1950s.
___
Associated Press reporters Nathan Ellgren in Washington and Jesse Bedayn in Detroit contributed.

sources.news_title: Sen. Fetterman warns El-Sayed faces tough general election after primary win in Michigan
sources.text:
Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan Democratic Senate primary
Abdul El-Sayed has emerged as the projected winner of Michigan's closely watched Democratic primary for U.S. Senate, defeating Congresswoman Haley Stevens and securing the party's nomination.
"We all knew they were going to spend their money. We didn't know they were going to spend $70 million of their money," El-Sayed said. "America can do glorious things, but to love America isn't just to dress up in some colors and pretend that everything's fine. To love America is to will America to do the hard work of being better."
Pennsylvania Sen. John Fetterman weighed in on the race, saying El-Sayed faces significant challenges in the general election.
"Without a doubt. I mean, the polling seems to indicate that it is in danger," Fetterman said. "And now he was really arrogant in that race, and now he has just found out that less than a majority of Democrats want him. And he has a serious responsibility between now and November to hold that seat."
El-Sayed will face Republican Mike Rogers in November for Michigan's U.S. Senate seat.

Stevens, a four-term congresswoman, was first elected to Congress in 2018 after serving as chief of staff to President Barack Obama's auto task force, which helped oversee the federal rescue of General Motors and Chrysler. In another key Michigan race, state Representative Donavan McKinney defeated Representative Shri Thanedar in the Democratic primary for the heavily Democratic 13th district in Detroit. McKinney had argued that the city should once again have a Black representative in Congress. After Thanedar's 2022 win, Detroit had no Black representation in Congress for the first time since the early 1950s.
El-Sayed's narrow win now sets up a high-stakes November contest against Rogers, while Democrats in Michigan face the task of closing ranks after a divisive primary that highlighted the party's ideological split.

sources.news_title: The Average Man Rejected Socialism. Liberals Chose It For Him
sources.text:
Socialist Abdul El-Sayed narrowly defeated Rep. Haley Stevens by roughly a point with nearly all votes counted in Michigan’s Democrat primary for U.S. Senate.
El-Sayed campaigned on things like Medicare for All, investing in “affordable” housing, and abolishing ICE. He previously called for defunding the police. His campaign website says he believes “in an economy built by and for working people.”
But the coalition that helped El-Sayed cinch the Democrat nomination is not the constituency his rhetoric implies he cares about. His victory was not the result of support from the low-income or rural voters or groups traditionally thought to constitute working-class communities (which his policies claim to focus on). Instead, younger, wealthier, and “educated” voters in college towns spurred his campaign to victory.
The New York Times’ Reid J. Epstein wrote Wednesday that El-Sayed “was strongest in communities with young voters, college students and educated and wealthy white voters. That coalition carried him through the primary.”
USA Today wrote that El-Sayed won “the most liberal voters and White voters with college degrees” and “swamped Stevens among younger voters and in college towns like Ann Arbor and East Lansing” while also leading in Arab neighborhoods.
In contrast Stevens “showed strength among Black voters in Detroit and Flint and carried most of the state’s interior rural counties, aside from a few with college towns and resort communities,” according to Epstein, while USA Today wrote Stevens’ support came “from Black voters in Detroit and from seniors. She did well in working-class communities in the suburbs, and she carried many of the more conservative and predominantly White rural counties.”
In other words, El Sayed won over voters who are more insulated from the consequences of his socialist policies. And none of this is unique to El-Sayed’s win.
Socialist Darializa Avila Chevalier narrowly beat incumbent Adriano Espaillat, D-N.Y., after performing best with younger voters, college-educated precincts, and higher-income areas. Espaillat won low-income areas and majority-Hispanic precincts.
Brad Lander (a Mamdani-backed candidate) unseated Rep. Dan Goldman, D-N.Y., after winning high-income areas and college-educated areas while Goldman performed better in low-income areas.
All of these candidates campaign as though they are for the working people and the poor, and yet they get most of their support from affluent leftists and wealthy people, while being rejected at the ballot box by those they claim to represent.
Affluent voters can champion candidates who support defunding the police, for example, because when things become dangerous, they can pack up and leave. But low-income residents don’t have that same luxury and are instead left to deal with unsafe streets and communities. Or take government-run grocery stores: Affluent voters can champion the idea because if local businesses fail to compete with a subsidized food store, the affluent voters can just go shop at Whole Foods or somewhere else. But locals without cars or disposable income may be left with nowhere to shop.
Affluent voters can throw their support behind open-border globalists who want to abolish borders, ICE, and immigration enforcement because it won’t be their housing supply that is squeezed by tens of millions of illegal aliens pining for the limited apartments. It’s not their communities that are transformed into Third World hellscapes. It’s the low-income communities most affected.
As with every form of socialism ever, the socialism of the Democrat Party is authoritarian slavery dictated by self-appointed elites.

sources.news_title: Michigan Senate primary shows Democratic establishment has lost its grip
Progressive Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan primary in jolt to Democrats
sources.text:
Progressive Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan primary in jolt to Democrats
He defeated moderate Haley Stevens, who was backed by the Democratic establishment, in a vote seen as a test of the party’s direction
The Democratic Party’s progressive wing scored a high-profile victory on Wednesday when Abdul El-Sayed won the party’s US Senate nomination in Michigan, giving its anti-establishment message a boost ahead of November’s midterm elections.
El-Sayed, a doctor whose campaign focused on healthcare, the economy and an end to unconditional military aid to Israel, was the first progressive to win a statewide primary in a state that US President Donald Trump carried in 2024.
He will face Republican former congressman Mike Rogers in November.
The vote, billed as a defining test of the party’s direction, became an election-night cliffhanger between El-Sayed and US congresswoman Haley Stevens, a moderate supported by Democratic leaders and pro-Israel groups.
With 99 per cent of the estimated votes counted on Wednesday, El-Sayed led Stevens 48.5 per cent to 47.5 per cent, according to Associated Press.
“My hope is that our democracy will never be the same,” El-Sayed said at a press conference on Wednesday. “From here on out, we can always point and say, ‘No, this is the people’s democracy, and we will always own it.’”

sources.text:
US: Abdul El-Sayed wins contentious Michigan Senate primary
August 5, 2026
US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed scored an important victory against incumbent House Representative Haley Stevens in Michigan's Democratic primary, a closely watched contest that pitted progressives against moderates of the US party.
El-Sayed, who represents the leftwing progressives, narrowly defeated the moderate leaning Stevens 48.5% to 47.5%.
He will go on to face Republican incumbent Senator Mike Rogers in a seat that Democratic party must win if they hope to take control of the US Senate this November in the midterm elections.
Trump insults El-Sayed after primary race
The race between El-Sayed, who was endorsed by the likes of Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, and Stevens, who had the backing of the Democratic party establishment was seen as a proxy war for the future ideological direction of the party.
Stevens was also backed with a big fundraising effort of the pro-Israel lobby AIPAC.
Democrats "have to come together to make sure that we never let Mike Rogers see the inside of the US Senate," El-Sayed said after winning the primary.
Stevens conceded to El-Sayed, saying she would "offer him my full support as we work to defeat Mike Rogers."
Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump reacted to the news by calling El-Sayed "a Communist loser who hates Jews and Israel."

Even Donald Trump’s harshest critics would find it hard to deny he carries his own unique set of political skills.
The fact he was written off after the attacks on the US Capitol on 6 January 2021 and able to secure a second term with a populist campaign that made a billionaire sound more in touch with the needs of working people than Joe Biden, is evidence alone.
What Trump doesn’t do well is variety or variation. Confronted with evidence that his policy of tariffs is hurting the people he claims to be helping, he simply doubles down on their purported success.
Making certain life choices in middle age increased your chances of keeping dementia at bay later in life, according to a new study.
What did the study find?
Those who do not smoke, have no diabetes and have normal blood pressure in middle age can stave off dementia for nearly 13 years.
The study, published in the journal Neurology, looked at 12,500 people who were free of dementia when they were aged 55.
People were assessed for high blood pressure, diabetes and smoking and followed for an average of 26 years.
People with no diabetes, no high blood pressure and who did not smoke had an average of 30 more years free of dementia.
Meanwhile, those with one risk factor had an extra 26 years, those with two had 21 years, and those with three had just over 17 years.
Preserving healthy years
Rather than focusing only on the chances of developing dementia, this study asks a question that matters to people: how long can we expect to live free from dementia?
Dr Jacqui Hanley, head of research funding at Alzheimer’s Research UK
What does this mean?
The study authors explained: “These factors often emerge in midlife and exert lasting effects on neurodegenerative pathology, underscoring the critical importance of early identification and management.”
It also found that regardless of risk factors, women lived longer without dementia than men and white people had more dementia-free years than black people.
Thomas Newdick, an aviation specialist at military news outlet The War Zone, said: “Ukraine is being increasingly innovative in the way it’s moving air defence assets around the country, and the way it’s operating jets from highway strips and secondary airfields.”
Mykola Bielieskov, a military analyst at the National Institute for Strategic Studies think-tank in Kyiv, said it is hoped Ukrainian attacks can “impose a dilemma on Russia”, forcing it to choose between offence or defence.
CRIME
Murder suspect appears in court in Athens
A man accused of killing a Scottish woman and disposing of her body in a suitcase has appeared in court in Athens.
The 26-year-old is accused of killing Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, who was discovered by a homeless man in a derelict building in the Kypseli area of the Greek capital on 18 July.
What you need to know
The suspect is understood to be Sharif Ahmadzai, 26, an Afghan boxer who was orphaned as a teenager.
He is facing a charge of homicide with intent, as well as allegations that he stole more than £8,500 from the victim’s bank accounts.
Greek officials said he admitted moving the body but denied the homicide allegations.
A closer look at the case
After allegedly killing Ross, Ahmadzai is accused of sending a series of messages from her phone to her friends and family before switching off the device.
He is then said to have bought another phone and texted her friends in Athens, including his wife, impersonating an unnamed jihadist saying he had killed the Scot because of her religion, Greek newspapers Proto Thema and Ta Nea reported.
Victim identified through fingerprints
His wife, US citizen Alaina Hall, reportedly told the police she suspected her husband’s involvement when she woke up to find he was gone, and tracked his phone to where Ross was staying.
Ross is believed to have died between five and seven days before she was found, during which time temperatures reached 36°C.
The Hellenic Police, Greece’s national force, were able to identify her using fingerprints.
Tributes paid
Lisa’s life was all about mission. She had been to many places and served people. She was a very precious girl and it is a tragic loss.
Peter Anderson, pastor from City on a Hill church in Edinburgh
entertainment
Star Wars dubbed into Welsh for first time
Dialogue from the original 1977 film has been rerecorded in collaboration with Welsh language TV channel S4C and the Welsh Government to celebrate its 50th anniversary next year. Boed i’r Grym fod gyda chi!
Everything we know so far
Voices will be provided by Welsh actors Matthew Rhys (Han Solo), Rhys Ifans (Obi-Wan Kenobi) and Aimee-Ffion Edwards (Princess Leia).
Later renamed Star Wars: A New Hope, George Lucas’s film was the first released in the series but the fourth in the saga’s chronology.
Star Wars: Gobaith Newydd will be broadcast on S4C and across its platforms from Christmas Day.
A new hope for Welsh film
It is the first time a Star Wars film has been translated into Welsh, with Lucasfilm co-president Lynwen Brennan celebrating “speakers will finally be able to enjoy the film in our native language”.
Welsh First Minister Rhun Ap Iorwerth added: “To see a Welsh language version of this iconic film, using the talents of some of our best actors, is fantastic.”
New single-sex space guidance comes into force – what we know
The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) said the use of single-sex spaces like public toilets and changing rooms should be based on biological sex.
What does the guidance say?
The new code says trans people should either use gender-neutral facilities or ones that match their biological sex.
The EHRC’s guidance comes after the UK Supreme Court ruled “sex” in equality law means “biological sex”.
The code also states that forcing a trans person to use facilities corresponding to their biological sex only could constitute discrimination.
Trans rights groups have strongly criticised the Supreme Court decision and the subsequent code.
Alexandra Parmar-Yee, director at Trans+ Solidarity Alliance, said: “Trans people will be shut out of the services they need, made to feel unwelcome and unsafe in public spaces. Our lives will feel smaller and more precarious.”
But gender critical campaigners like the charity Sex Matters welcomed the guidance. Maya Forstater, the charity’s CEO, said: “The law is clear and the code is practical, giving many examples that apply to everyday services.”
artificial intelligence
How trial AI bots went on rogue hacking spree
Advanced artificial intelligence agents ran riot during Government testing, attempting 19 different hacks.
One of the models researched the project’s human maintainers to try to trick them into unknowingly approving malicious code.
What actually happened?
The incident happened when the Government was testing Anthropic’s Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6-Sol.
The AI Security Institute (AISA) flagged “unusual data transfers” during the testing on 28 July.
An investigation found the Mythos model had tried 17 hacks, while GPT-5.6-Sol attempted them twice.
The AI programmes were targeting GitHub, a software platform owned by Microsoft.
AISI acknowledged it had purposefully set the AI models the task and connected it to the wider internet.
But it added: “The activity undertaken by the agent shows signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.”
AI experts expressed concerns about the models being connected to the internet during testing.
Alan Woodward, professor of cybersecurity at Surrey University, told The Times: “Why did AISI connect the agent to the internet, and did the agent know it was no longer in a test environment? If the latter, why did AISI do that? “
He added: “It’s raised more questions than the report answers.”
Ollie Whitehouse, chief technology officer for the National Cyber Security Centre, said: “Relying on detection alone after the fact of an incident will not be enough.”

Family pays tribute to ‘beloved’ nine-year-old girl as man in court over death
The family of nine-year-old Minnie Merriman, who died after she was found seriously injured on an industrial estate in Arbroath, have described her as “beloved, absolutely incredible and beautiful”.
What happened?
Minnie, from West Yorkshire, was found just after midnight on Monday at the Elliot industrial estate in the Angus town while her family were camping in the area.
She was taken to Ninewells Hospital in Dundee, where she later died.
A 35-year-old man has been charged in connection with her death and appeared in court on Wednesday.
We are devastated with the loss of our beloved, absolutely incredible, beautiful and brave Minnie Moo. Our family asks that our privacy is respected at this extremely difficult time.
What else do we know?
Police have said Minnie and the 35-year-old man were known to each other and they are not looking for anyone else in connection with her death.
Minnie is believed to have been camping in the area with her family, who police say are being supported by specialist officers.
When polls suggest he’s the most unpopular president in history he looks away or does not let it enter his consciousness. When it was suggested he had a closer relationship with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein he doubled down again on that denial and threatened to sue anyone who claimed otherwise.
And so it was with Abdul El-Sayed, the former Democratic health care administrator who won a hard-fought primary Senate contest against Congresswoman Haley Stevens in the battleground state of Michigan on Tuesday.
“Great news for the Republican Party. El-Sayed, a Communist loser who hates Jews and Israel, is the projected winner in his race with the Socialist,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
“She was not expected to do nearly as well as she did. Now, the Dumocrats crazy policies will only get worse.”
With more than 95 per cent of the votes counted, El-Sayed had led Stevens by just 48.5-47-5 and was declared the winner by the Associated Press.
While El-Sayed is not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), he did receive the backing and support of high-profile members including Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
He supports universal health care, has called the Israel war in Gaza a “genocide” and wants to get big money out of politics. It was no surprise then that Trump would try to smear him as a “communist loser”, even though he had won and was one step closer to making history as America’s first Muslim senator.
Indeed, the clue about how Trump and the Republicans will fight the general election contest in November, where their candidate is Mike Rogers, was not in the words he used to describe El-Sayed.
Rather it was in the language he used for Stevens, the centrist, mainstream candidate supported by the Democratic establishment and backed by $60m in campaign spending, a hefty chunk of it from an Israel-aligned super pac group.
In his social media post he called Stevens, who worked in the Obama administration to help bail out the car industry after the economic collapse of 2007 and 2008, a “socialist”.
It is pretty easy to imagine that had she won rather than El-Sayed, the president and other Republicans would have started calling her a “communist loser”. It is not as the president feels any obligation to tell the truth.
Tuesday was a big night for the Democrats. Many were looking to see if the contest would determine once and for all whether the progressive wing of the party had the upper hand. It appears that the divide is still there.
Michigan is a genuinely purple state. Trump won the presidential contest there in 2016 and 2024. If Democrats are to have any chance of taking control of the Senate later this year, it is critical El-Sayed can beat Rogers, especially after the party’s hope of flipping the state of Maine appear to have self-imploded.
Ahead of Tuesday’s race, some polls suggested Stevens had a better chance than El-Sayed against the Republicans in November, a reason – presumably – more people voted for her than the polls had predicted.
A lot will depend on whether Democrats in Michigan can unite around El-Sayed after this often ugly civil war, and whether he can reach out to those who voted for Stevens. One thing he will not have to contend with is the $60m of attack ads leveled at him by his own party.
On Wednesday, Stevens called El-Sayed to concede the race and said she would back him. She said: “I am proud to offer my support as he takes on Mike Rogers in the general election.” El-Sayed also struck an inclusive tone in a speech praising Stevens as “one of the most committed public servants”.
He added: “Whatever differences that we might have had in the primary, they pale in comparison to what unifies us.”

sources.news_title: Election results show mass movements can beat corporate cash and lobbyists
sources.text:
DETROIT—Primary election results Aug. 4 showed corporate donors—as well as pro-Israeli government lobbyists—that it’s not going to be easy for them to buy voters anymore. In many areas across the nation, and not just in deep-blue districts and states, mass movements beat corporate cash and manipulation by Democratic Party leaders determined to maintain a status quo that makes tweaks around the edges rather than institute the sweeping changes needed by the people.
Dr. Abdul El-Sayed’s win in the Michigan Democratic Senate primary was the biggest example of what a mass movement can produce. Record turnout propelled him to victory over the party establishment’s choice, “moderate” Rep. Haley Stevens—despite the fact that he was outspent 10-to-1.
El-Sayed benefited from a strong ground game, as his volunteers were energized by his progressive stands on Medicare for All, against U.S. military aid to Israel, against the Trump-Israeli war on Gaza and Iran, and for battling climate change and for aid to education. On the stump, El-Sayed fiercely and passionately denounced MAGA’s attacks on workers, immigrants, and democracy.
“Dark money” donations, including $60 million funneled through the right-wing American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), backed Stevens, who had support from the U.S. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and outgoing Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, among others.
AIPAC acts as a voice for Israeli foreign policy in U.S. politics, including the genocide in Gaza. It dumped more funds into the campaign against El-Sayed than it has spent in any other single election in history. AIPAC was so prominent in the primary that the vote became, in part, a referendum on its role in elections.
Michigan has a large and growing Muslim-American population centered, among other places, in Hamtramck, which is surrounded on all sides by the city of Detroit. It has long been a major center in the auto industry and went heavily for El-Sayed. Metro Detroit’s notable Jewish population split. Older voters went for Stevens, with aid to Israel a major concern. Younger ones, opposing the Israeli government’s war on Gaza—and the Israeli government’s close ties to President Donald Trump—went for El-Sayed.
After Stevens’ loss, AIPAC pivoted to essentially declaring it now backs the Republican nominee for the seat, former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers. Trump endorsed Rogers, who has repeated the president’s false claims about election theft in 2020. AIPAC issued a statement saying that it remained “determined to ensure voters reject” El-Sayed “and his radical anti-Israel agenda.”
Despite the big money spent to block the progressive candidate, though, AIPAC came up short, and plenty of forces are determined to repeat that outcome in November. Volunteers on the ground and pro-worker organizations—including National Nurses United and the United Auto Workers—along with progressive leaders such as Reps. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass., and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Sen. Bernie Sanders, Ind-Vt., produced 735,625 votes (48.6%) for El-Sayed to 716,222 (47.3%) for Stevens.
Progressives gain steam
El-Sayed’s triumph wasn’t the sole people-powered win on Tuesday. Another was the victory in a congressional primary in Michigan by the young William Lawrence, a founder of the Sunrise Movement, an organization of young people determined to protect the environment.
In Michigan’s 13th U.S. House district Democratic primary in Detroit and suburbs, 34-year-old Donavan McKinney, a Democratic Socialist, defeated second-term incumbent and multimillionaire Shri Thanedar 52%-48%.
The seat is safely Democratic, and it also means Detroit, which is 75% African-American, 11% white, and 8% Hispanic, will have one African-American member of Congress, instead of none. The city’s other lawmaker, Tlaib, a Palestinian-American, scored an easy win in her race. She, along with Sanders and Ocasio-Cortez, aided McKinney’s drive.
These developments follow a pattern, apparent in Zohran Mamdani’s victory in the New York City mayor’s race last year: Take a progressive stand, defend it, stand up strongly against Trump and MAGA, and you can emerge triumphant.
That trend was also evident in a special U.S. House election in Arizona last year, where progressive Adelita Grijalva won, and in New York when former City Comptroller Brad Lander ousted millionaire pro-AIPAC Rep. Dan Goldman in the party primary, while progressive Darializa Avila Chevalier beat insider Rep. Adriano Espaillat.
Virginia featured two notable U.S. House primaries on Tuesday, both won by progressive Democrats. In the 2nd District anchored by Newport News and Hampton Roads, former Rep. Elaine Luria, a Trump impeachment manager and a military veteran, will face the pro-Trump Republican who narrowly unseated her four years ago, Jen Kiggans. The Steelworkers union is strong in the district.
In the 5th District, where deep-red territory surrounds the blue college town Charlottesville, former Rep. Tom Perriello, who represented the area for one two-year term, will face Republican Rep. John McGuire. The GOPer is a Trump backer, and the district tilts Republican.
Missouri’s mixed picture
Bucking the trend, the most prominent progressive loss came in Missouri’s St. Louis-based 1st U.S. House district. Rep. Wesley Bell, a “moderate” former prosecutor and a favorite of AIPAC, faced a rematch with the former incumbent, Cori Bush.
Bell beat Bush with AIPAC’s help two years ago. Their 2024 race was close, but this one wasn’t. Bell prevailed over Bush—a nurse and social worker, a member of “The Squad,” and a strong critic of U.S. military aid to Israel—59% to 37%.
Other outcomes in the state were positive, though. The Republican majority in the heavily gerrymandered state legislature pushed two favorite right-wing brainstorms to ballot referenda, but both lost.
One referendum was a constitutional amendment to gradually eliminate the state income tax and other taxes that hit the rich and shift the Show Me State’s chief revenue source to sales taxes, which disproportionately hurt lower- and middle-income voters. It was sunk, earning only 17% support.
The other constitutional amendment would have made it difficult for citizen-initiated referenda to pass, by requiring them to win majority support in every individual Missouri congressional district, not just statewide. The practical impact of that would be to give the most-right-wing district, in southwest Missouri, a veto over the rest of the state.
Had it been in effect already, Missouri voters could not override the right-wingers in the legislature and raise the state’s minimum wage, enact paid family and medical leave, support workers’ rights, and vote to keep abortion—as they’ve done in recent years. This outcome means voters can still exercise their will statewide, as this GOP brainstorm lost by a 4-1 ratio.
Unrelated to the primary or the two referenda but coming on the same day, Missouri’s Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins refused to certify a separate referendum initiated by citizens seeking to reverse the state’s new GOP-drawn congressional map, arguing that the effort was unconstitutional. Calling it a “desperate move to silence the people’s voice,” the key group opposing the Republican gerrymandering, People Not Politicians, said it plans to sue Hoskins.
Prairie progress
After the U.S. Supreme Court stripped women nationwide of their reproductive rights, the Kansas legislature’s GOP majority enacted an almost-total ban on abortions. Citizens groups and unions petitioned it to a referendum and decisively overthrew the ban.
Angered, Republicans reacted this year with a referendum to change how state Supreme Court justices are chosen—moving to a popular vote rather than having them be appointed by the governor with consent of the legislature. The voters saw through the scheme and defeated it, 61% to 39%.
Kansas Democrats nominated the pastor of the largest Methodist Church in the U.S., Adam Hamilton, to face off against incumbent GOP Sen. Roger Marshall in a race that GOP leaders in D.C. are suddenly worried about.
The party has a slim hold—53 seats out of 100 total—in the U.S. Senate, and the GOP has reserved more ad time on Kansas media this fall than it has in much-larger, and vastly more-expensive, Texas.
Other state races
Kansas and Michigan voters nominated potential successors to term-limited Democratic Govs. Laura Kelly and Gretchen Whitmer. In Michigan, the nominee is incumbent Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, a progressive menaced by Trump supporters two years ago. Whitmer was also a target of a kidnapping plot.
Benson will face U.S. Rep. John James, a Trump supporter. His swing seat is open and former prosecutor Christina Hines won a three-way race for the Democratic nomination, garnering 46% of the vote.
In Kansas, GOP State Senate Majority Leader Ty Masterson will face Democratic State Sen. Cindy Holscher, who favors a ban on water-guzzling, power-guzzling data centers.
Years of work paying off
In many cases, Our Revolution said in a statement, the victories Aug. 4 followed years of community organizing by progressive labor and other organizations.
“Workers have learned that the elections are the way billionaires buy power to benefit themselves at their expense. The results last night show this clearly,” the group said.
“They want elected officials to take care of the crisis facing the nation, not just to manage our decline.”

sources.news_title: CBS Barely Challenges ‘Progressive’ Abdul el-Sayed on Hate for Jews, Israel
sources.text:
Beating out ABC and NBC, Wednesday’s CBS Mornings secured a live interview with Michigan Democratic senatorial nominee and “progressive” Abdul el-Sayed that, at nearly six minutes long, largely let the socialist filibuster on his campaign talking points with only one probing question and a brief follow-up about his demands the U.S. cease all foreign aid to Israel, but wasn’t framed as anti-Semitic or anti-Jews.
The rest of the questions were inviting him to explain how he will “sway Haley Stevens supporters,” “[w]hat is your message to” “members of the Democratic establishment,” and if he’d support Chuck Schumer as Senate Majority Leader.
Featured co-host Vladimir Duthiers set it up by calling el-Sayed “a progressive” whose “win would be a very big deal for the party’s left” and then wondering if he had spoken to his opponent, Congresswoman Haley Stevens.
WATCH: CBS actually had a live interview on Wednesday’s ‘CBS Mornings’ with Michigan socialist Abdul el-Sayed, referring to him as a “progressive,” and inviting him to explain how he will “sway Haley Stevens supporters,” “[w]hat is your message to” “members of the Democratic… pic.twitter.com/AJhzigpLZT
— Curtis Houck (@CurtisHouck) August 5, 2026
Once el-Sayed said he had yet to do so, but was “grateful for the hard-fought race that we had,” Duthiers lobbed a softball: “So, let’s talk about that unity. What do you think you need to do to sway Haley Stevens supporters over to your side?”
El-Sayed promptly delivered another stump speech (click “expand”):
Well, Vlad, I’ll tell you this, and we set out 13 months ago, 15 months ago now to build a movement, to get money out of politics, put money in your pocket, pass Medicare for All. Mike Rogers is a guy who wants to put more money in politics. He is dead set on taking money out of your pockets by colluding with some of the worst folks and the worst corporations who’ve taken money out. And, if he had his way, he would have Medicare for none. So, I think the things that bring us together are so much bigger, and the focus that we need to have to take on my garage and the Trumpism that he’s chosen to represent are the things that are gonna bring us together. There’s a lot of healing to do after a hard-fought primary like this, but I have said that this is a big, open movement. We welcome anybody and everybody who understands that we need a government of the people, by the people, and for the people to it, and I’m looking forward to welcoming our new friends to this coalition to beat Mike Rogers in the fall.
This went into the only challenging question, which Duthiers framed as concerning the fact that Stevens “was obviously pro-Israel” whereas he was “very clear about pulling back the spending for countries like the state of Israel.”
Duthiers then asked him to address what “many people see...as a false choice” in foreign aid being a few million dollars when “[t]he federal budget is nearly $7 trillion”:
But what would you say to some of her supporters who see Israel as a key ally of the United States, and that they deserve our financial support? I know that you’ve gone on the record to say that you think that that money that we spend should be spent and invested here in the United States. But many people see that as a false choice. The federal budget is nearly $7 trillion. Many voters would say that the United States can invest at home while also supporting allies whose security interests advance America’s own. How do you address that?
While a perfectly legitimate and arguably shrewd way of framing the issue, el-Sayed ducked by asserting Detroit schools do not appear as they “did 50 years ago,” and thus fixing them has somehow fallen by the wayside in favor of funding...Jews?
El-Sayed tried to have it both ways, invoking foreign aid to other arab countries such as Egypt, Pakistan, Qatar, and Saudi Arabia.
Duthiers offered a brief follow-up: “But what kind of message does that send, doctor — what kind of message does that send to our allies, and our adversaries that the United States would not be willing to support a key ally in global strategy?”
El-Sayed ducked with another filibustering answer about the “principle” of not giving money for others “to do apartheid and genocide” while America’s in the midst of “an affordability crisis” (click “expand”):
Well, I think it would send that we’re about principle. If you’re gonna use the money that we send you to do apartheid and genocide, then you should think twice about getting our funding, and also think about the message that that sends to families who are in need in our own communities. It says that we see you, you have been contributing to our tax base for a very long time, and you haven’t been getting the deal that you deserve. It says that we really are about trying to make your life more affordable, trying to make sure that you have the resources you need, and it says that we believe you have the right to your tax dollars, and so, I think too often we’re too worried about what something says to someone else we’re not as worried about what we say to people who are struggling for the ability to afford the basic things that they need for a dignified life. We are in an affordability crisis right now. It is high past time for us to prioritize spending on the things that make people whole, guaranteeing their health care, making sure that they have housing and good schools, making sure they can breathe, clean air and drink, clean water, standing up to the corporations and special interests who have corrupted our politics for far too long.
Fill-in co-host and Entertainment Tonight co-host Nischelle Turner jumped in with a question from the left: “[M]embers of the Democratic establishment seemingly pulled together to try and defeat you — Chuck Schumer, Gretchen Whitmer, Jim Clyburn, all of those folks. What is your message to them today after seeing the race that you have run?”
El-Sayed resorted to reiterating past lines about the “historically corrupted President...who made $2.2 billion on his office in just the first year alone” and party seeking “to squash democracy itself,” both of which will have been “[held]...accountable for the next several years.”
Of course, Turner didn’t push back on this.
Duthiers had the last question about whom he’d support for Senate Democratic leader: “[D]o you think that it’s time for Chuck Schumer to step aside? Do you think that Chuck Schumer is — has the pulse of the Democratic Party?”
El-Sayed said he knew Schumer was “united” in the shared “goal” of him winning the seat, but only after emphasizing “I’ve said very clearly that I think Senator Chris Van Hollen would be an amazing Senate majority leader.”
Nothing about his views about the ayatollah, the attack on a Michigan synagogue, his ties to pro-9/11 podcaster Hasan Piker, his wife’s psychiatry practice refusing to accept health insurance, or links to radical imams, to name a few.
Reminder: CBS News is not MAGA TV.

sources.news_title: Kamala Harris Backs Abdul El-Sayed After Razor-Thin Michigan Senate Primary Win
sources.text:
Kamala Harris is moving quickly to help unify Michigan Democrats behind Abdul El-Sayed.
Following El-Sayed’s narrow victory in the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate, Harris officially endorsed the progressive candidate through a joint fundraising email designed to turn primary momentum into general election support.
The endorsement arrives after one of the most closely watched races of the 2026 midterm cycle. El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and longtime progressive advocate, edged out Rep. Haley Stevens and state lawmaker Mallory McMorrow in an August 4 primary decided by less than one percentage point.
Harris acknowledged the “hard-fought Democratic primary” before directing the party’s attention toward November, where El-Sayed will face Republican nominee Mike Rogers. The race will determine who succeeds retiring Senator Gary Peters and could play a major role in deciding control of the Senate.
El-Sayed’s victory also came after a bruising and expensive campaign. More than $60 million in opposition advertising poured into the race, including spending connected to corporate political action committees and pro-Israel groups such as AIPAC. His campaign survived the financial pressure and delivered one of the cycle’s biggest progressive upsets.
The fast release of Harris’ fundraising appeal signals a broader Democratic effort to close ranks, rebuild support across primary factions, and prepare for what is expected to be a highly competitive general election.
For El-Sayed, the stakes reach beyond party control. A victory in November would make him the first Muslim elected to the United States Senate.
Michigan now heads into the fall with a matchup that will command national money, attention, and political firepower.

sources.text:
Michigan Senate Democratic primary race ends with Abdul El-Sayed winning
DETROIT, Mich. (KLKN) — After a tight, competitive race, Progressive Dr. Abdul El-Sayed won the Michigan Senate Democratic primary. Moderate Rep. Haley Stevens called El-Sayed to concede the race, according to ABC.
El-Sayed now faces Republican Rep. Mike Rogers for Michigan Senate. According to ABC, the winner of the election in November could decide which party controls the Senate.
El-Sayed said the odds were stacked against them in a speech after winning.
“We took on a machine. You’re not supposed to be able to beat $70 million of outside spending,” El-Sayed said. “That’s a record amount of money spent in a campaign against a Democrat in a primary in any campaign. You’re not supposed to be able to beat that. What we showed is that the power of our many is greater than the power of their money.”
Stevens offered support for El-Sayed.
“This was a thorough and rigorous campaign that brought out the full span of views within the Democratic Party — and that is why we have primaries,” Stevens said. “I am proud to have put up my hand to serve, and prouder to continue to work together to make sure this Senate seat remains blue, that we flip the United States Senate and continue the work for Michigan.”
President Donald Trump posted to socials after El-Sayed’s win. Trump said El-Sayed is a “communist loser”, saying the polls were off in this primary election.

sources.news_title: Who is Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat who could become the first Muslim US senator
El-Sayed decried AIPAC. Now he hopes to win over pro-Israel Democrats.
sources.text:
In the first 90 seconds of his victory speech in Detroit Wednesday, Abdul El-Sayed both lambasted the influence of AIPAC and appealed to his rival Haley Stevens, who had benefited from the pro-Israel lobby’s massive resources, to campaign with him.
The jarring and almost immediate transition in the freshly elected Michigan Senate nominee’s remarks illustrates the daunting bridge-building that Democrats face between the party’s pro- and anti-Israel wings ahead of a midterm election the party sees as crucial to wresting control of the Senate from the GOP.
Later, El-Sayed devoted a chunk of his speech to ensuring the safety of Michigan’s Jews, still rattled by his equivocal reaction to an attack on a suburban Detroit synagogue earlier this year.
At the outset of his speech, the newly minted nominee lauded Mallory McMorrow, another contender for the Democratic nomination who dropped out early, and who had introduced him Wednesday, stating, ”You took on the power of AIPAC.” He continued, “You were willing to speak truth to a level of power that sometimes is unbeatable.” Like El-Sayed, McMorrow attacked Stevens for accepting the backing of funders affiliated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee.
Three sentences later, El-Sayed appealed to Stevens, who was backed by upwards of $30 million in pro-Israel money, to join him in defeating Mike Rogers, a former congressman who is the Republican nominee to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters.
“Whatever differences that we might have had in the primary,” he told his “colleague and friend” Stevens, “they pale in comparison to what unifies us – a recognition that so long as we want to keep our democracy, that democracy better be working for people, and that all of us have to come together to make sure that we never let Mike Rogers see the inside of the U.S. Senate.”
Stevens lost by less than 1 percentage point, a stunning rebuke to multiple pollsters who said she would lose by double digits. The more than $60 million spent on the race on her behalf helps make it the most expensive in Senate primary history.
Despite the close margin, Stevens quickly endorsed El-Sayed Wednesday, as did Democratic Sen. Chuck Schumer, the Jewish New York Senate minority leader who pushed hard for her to win.
“I spoke with Abdul a few moments ago to offer him my full support as we work to defeat Mike Rogers this November,” Stevens said on X.
The close call means El-Sayed now has to pivot to the voters Stevens won. Many of them are Black and working-class moderates who live in the Detroit area, as well as Jews who were unsettled by his attacks on Israel and his seeming insensitivity to Jewish security.
Republicans immediately signaled that El-Sayed’s animus toward Israel and its supporters – a dynamic that came to dominate the primary race – would be a focus of their general election campaign.
“Great news for the Republican Party,” President Donald Trump said Wednesday on the social media platform he owns, Truth Social. “El-Sayed, a Communist loser who hates Jews and Israel, is the projected winner in his race with the Socialist.” El-Sayed, a physician who is a former county health official, is not a communist and Stevens, a congresswoman who built her reputation as a champion of the state’s auto industry after its late 2000s crisis, is not a socialist.
El-Sayed in his victory speech acknowledged a primary race that was at times intensely bitter, with mutual accusations of anti-Arab racism, misogyny and antisemitism.
“As bitter and as divisive and as cynical as the campaign against us might have been, I want us to realize that there is so much more that unites us now, because the campaign that Mike Rogers and Donald Trump and their GOP MAGA allies are launching is already more bitter,” he said.
El-Sayed also appeared to recognize the aspects of his campaign that unsettled the approximately 130,000 Jews in the state, including his claim that “hurt people do hurt people,” after a man plowed a truck into a synagogue during pre-school hours. The assailant had relatives who were killed in an Israeli strike on Lebanon and El-Sayed’s remarks were interpreted by many as explaining away the attack.
“I want you to know that my commitment to your safety, my commitment to Jewish safety, is the same commitment that I have to the safety of my own daughters,” he said.
He also appeared to acknowledge the Jewish right to self-determination, something he has largely resisted. He thanked “Jewish American brothers and sisters” who backed his campaign, who he said “understand that self-determination for one people does not require the quenching of self-determination for another people.”
Notwithstanding that the comment came in the context of upholding the Palestinian right to self-determination, El-Sayed has until now declined to affirm Israel’s right to exist as a Jewish state.
The speech was nonetheless laced with references to his criticism of Israel, which he has accused of a genocide in its conduct of the Gaza war sparked by the Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023. . He repeated his pledge to reallocate the funds the United States spends on defense assistance to Israel to domestic priorities.
“I kept running up against one thing: the kind of politics that tell us that we cannot invest in those children because we should be sending their money to deny rights to other children abroad,” he said.

Progressive Democrats propel El-Sayed to Michigan Senate primary win
sources.text:
Progressive Democrats propel El-Sayed to Michigan Senate primary win
Loading...
A narrow victory in Michigan’s Democratic primary for Abdul El-Sayed, a quick-talking former health official, over Rep. Haley Stevens, his establishment-backed rival, has put a left-wing candidate for the U.S. Senate on the ballot in a crucial swing state that has long sent moderates to Congress.
The closeness of Tuesday’s result – Dr. El-Sayed is projected to win by less than a percentage point – might give progressives a reality check in the limits of left-wing populism in statewide races. Ms. Stevens’ allies had argued that she had a better chance of beating Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee, in November, because of both her track record in Congress and her appeal to independent voters. They can cite the close margin as proof that a significant number of Democrats, particularly in Detroit, a majority-Black city, were hesitant about Dr. El-Sayed and his ambitious plans for government intervention in the economy.
But his victory over an opponent who massively outspent him provides more ballast for the party’s progressive wing after a string of primary wins in New York, Colorado, and other states. To Dr. El-Sayed’s allies, his grassroots campaign showed that a focus on working-class stresses and on affordable healthcare, in particular, was a winning strategy that met the moment.
Why We Wrote This
Abdul El-Sayed’s close primary victory in Michigan notches another win for the progressive wing of the Democratic Party. Now, Democrats must unite to face Republican Mike Rogers in November.
Now, Democrats in Michigan must come together after a bitter contest. One of the sharpest divides between the two candidates was over U.S.-Israeli policy: Dr. El-Sayed is a fierce critic of Israel and defender of Palestinian rights; Ms. Stevens is pro-Israel and was the beneficiary of massive campaign spending by pro-Israel groups.
In a statement, Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin called for party unity. “Michigan voters chose a candidate who will fight to lower costs, strengthen communities, stand up for working Americans, and build an economy that works for everyone. Democrats are united in working together to keep this seat blue and send El-Sayed to the U.S. Senate,” he said.
Ms. Stevens also announced her support for her opponent in November to “make sure this Senate seat remains blue.” The seat is open because Sen. Gary Peters, a Democrat, is retiring. He endorsed Ms. Stevens in the primary, as did the state’s governor, Gretchen Whitmer.
Michigan’s primary comes a week before neighboring Wisconsin holds a gubernatorial primary in which left-wing state lawmaker Francesca Hong appears to have a commanding lead in polls over a moderate rival backed by outgoing Democratic Gov. Tony Evers. Both primaries, held in battleground Midwestern states that President Donald Trump won in 2024, are being scrutinized to gauge the strength of progressives within the Democratic coalition.
In recent weeks, Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign had trumpeted partisan polls showing him comfortably ahead of Ms. Stevens. That might have raised expectations of a decisive victory among left-leaning national Democrats who have donated to his campaign. And it will be seized upon by skeptics who argue that progressives can turn out younger, college-educated voters but aren’t reaching the party’s less ideological core, including older Democrats in cities like Detroit.
Pro-Israel donors did better in Missouri: Rep. Wesley Bell defeated former Rep. Cori Bush, a progressive critic of Israel. Mr. Bell won the deep-blue seat with support from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the same organization that spent heavily on Ms. Stevens.

"I'm all in for Abdul," said US Sen. Chris Murphy.
Democrats from across the ideological spectrum lined up behind Abdul El-Sayed on Wednesday after he clinched the party's nomination for a US Senate seat in Michigan.
Shortly after The Associated Press projected El-Sayed as the victor in the closely watched primary, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) released a joint statement supporting the newly minted nominee.
"Abdul El-Sayed has run an energetic campaign that inspired thousands of Michiganders across the state, with a clear focus on lowering costs and standing up for working families," they said. "Democrats are united by a common purpose: putting a check on [President] Donald Trump by defeating his Republican enablers and taking back the Senate."
Schumer and Gillibrand also took a shot at El-Sayed's Republican rival, Mike Rogers, whom they described as "a rubber stamp for Donald Trump, backing the same reckless agenda that has driven up costs for working families, imposed chaotic tariffs that have hurt Michigan's auto industry, and put special interests ahead of the people of Michigan."
Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), El-Sayed's top rival for the Democratic nomination, conceded the race on Wednesday morning and offered "my full support as we work to defeat Mike Rogers this November."
Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, who had endorsed Stevens, also threw her support behind El-Sayed and all other Michigan Democratic candidates.
"They’ve got my support as we fight like hell together to win in November," said Whitmer. "Together, let’s stop MAGA Republicans so we can get to work and deliver results for the people of Michigan."
Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) said he was "excited" to see El-Sayed win the primary.
"Voters will have a clear choice in Michigan now," said Murphy. "A corporate-owned Trump loyalist or a doctor who will stand up for the little guy and will hold Trump and the corporations to account. I'm all in for Abdul."
Beth Miller, political director at Jewish Voice for Peace Action, hailed El-Sayed's victory as a "political earthquake," given that it came after the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) spent an estimated $30 million trying to defeat him.
"Voters in one of the most consequential states for the 2028 Presidential race have just sent a clear message," said Miller. "They want candidates who will fight for working families at home while unapologetically speaking out for Palestinian freedom. This cycle, AIPAC is being relegated to the dustbin of history."
According to a Wednesday report from Semafor, Michigan Democrats have already begun pivoting toward the general election campaign by planning negative attacks on GOP rival Rogers as a tool of moneyed interests and labeling him "the biggest name in corruption."
During a Wednesday morning victory speech, El-Sayed accused Rogers of spending 14 years in Congress with the sole goal of "figuring out how to cash out the day he left."

sources.news_title: AOC-Backed Progressive Wins Michigan: What Do Prediction Markets Say About Her 2028 Chances?
sources.text:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) scored one of her highest-profile wins of the midterm cycle as Abdul El-Sayed, the progressive she backed in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, narrowly defeated establishment-backed Rep. Haley Stevens.
The Associated Press called the race Wednesday morning, capping an upset in which he overcame more than $50 million in outside spending behind Stevens, the candidate supported by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer.
Stevens conceded and urged Democrats to rally behind El-Sayed for the general election.
Ocasio-Cortez endorsed El-Sayed in early July, her first contested Senate primary endorsement of the cycle, then joined Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) for a three-city Michigan rally swing two weeks before the election.
Traders Already Have AOC Near the Top for 2028
Polymarket traders currently give Ocasio-Cortez a roughly 14% chance of winning the 2028 Democratic nomination, behind Governor Gavin Newsom at 19% and just below Senator Jon Ossoff (D-GA) at 15%.
Her odds have risen from around 8% in May, with much of the gain coming in early July, when Vice President JD Vance predicted she would lead the Democratic field.
A July University of New Hampshire poll offered another sign of strength, putting Ocasio-Cortez first at 22%, one point ahead of Pete Buttigieg.
Nate Silver Sees a Warning for Traders
Polling analyst Nate Silver argued in his Silver Bulletin newsletter that the result was less decisive than the headline suggested.
The last seven surveys tracked by The New York Times had El-Sayed ahead by 10 to 19 points, yet he won by about one.
That gap matters, Silver wrote, because a larger victory would have delivered a stronger boost to the progressive wing.
A one-point squeaker instead lands in what he called the establishment’s "second-guessing zone," where moderates can ask whether Stevens might have won with additional support or a different campaign.
The night was mixed for progressives elsewhere, with former Rep. Cori Bush losing a Missouri comeback bid by 22 points.
November Is the Bigger Test
El-Sayed now faces Republican Mike Rogers, who narrowly lost Michigan’s 2024 Senate contest. Polymarket traders give the Democrats a 60% chance of holding the seat, but this is down from 68% before the result was announced.
President Donald Trump weighed in Wednesday morning on Truth Social, writing that “The Radical Left Socialist has a real shot” and urging supporters to “VOTE FOR MIKE ROGERS, and make Michigan TOO BIG TO RIG.”
The president also repeated unsupported claims about election fraud in Wayne County, asserting that more ballots are cast there than there are voters.
The real test of the progressive bet, for El-Sayed and for Ocasio-Cortez, is whether El-Sayed can beat Rogers in November.

sources.news_title: Abdul El-Sayed Won: Revisiting the Democratic Establishment’s Medicare for All Problem
sources.text:
From Gavin Newsom in California to Gretchen Whitmer in Michigan, the debate over Medicare for All continues to expose the tension between campaign promises, corporate influence, and the political power of the health insurance industry.
Editor’s note: We are republishing this article following Abdul El-Sayed’s victory over establishment-backed Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary. Despite being dramatically outspent and opposed by powerful party leaders and corporate interests, El-Sayed prevailed on a platform centered on Medicare for All, economic justice and an end to unconditional U.S. military aid to Israel. His victory reinforces the argument made below: Democratic voters are not rejecting bold progressive policies—they are rejecting a party establishment determined to contain them.
Joshua Scheer
Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary is increasingly becoming a referendum on who really shapes the party’s agenda: voters or the powerful corporate interests that finance modern campaigns. With David Sirota reporting examines why Whitmer’s endorsement cannot be viewed as just another political calculation. Instead, he places it within the broader struggle over Medicare for All and the political influence of the health insurance industry in Michigan.
As Sirota argues, Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign represents something far more consequential than another Democratic primary challenge. His candidacy is built around Medicare for All—a proposal that would fundamentally reshape the private insurance industry. That reality, Sirota contends, helps explain why so much of the Democratic establishment has rallied behind Haley Stevens, whose positions pose no comparable threat to the existing health care system.
For years, Abdul El-Sayed has made Medicare for All the centerpiece of his public life and political career. He has written extensively on the subject and is now campaigning for the U.S. Senate on a promise to replace the private insurance system with universal coverage. That makes him a direct political challenge to an industry that has spent decades protecting its place at the center of American health care. His opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens, does not support Medicare for All, making her a far less disruptive prospect for the insurance industry.
Against that backdrop, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s endorsement of Stevens carries significance beyond a routine political endorsement. Critics argue it reflects the interests of an established Democratic network with longstanding ties to Michigan’s health insurance industry.
Whitmer’s connections to Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan have long drawn scrutiny. Her father served as the company’s chief executive for many years, and Blue Cross donors were among the largest financial supporters of her gubernatorial campaign. Reporting at the time also highlighted the company’s close relationship with her campaign, and after taking office Whitmer selected Blue Cross’s CEO to serve as an honorary co-chair of her transition team. Those relationships have fueled renewed questions about whether Michigan’s political establishment is closing ranks against a candidate whose signature proposal would fundamentally reshape—or potentially eliminate—the private insurance model on which companies like Blue Cross depend.
Once again, I find myself writing about Gavin Newsom—his ties to the billionaire class, his failure to deliver Medicare for All in California, and his recent claim that such reform can only happen at the national level. It is an argument that conveniently ignores the opportunities he had to lead when he had the chance.
Now, Michigan offers a strikingly similar example. As David Sirota’s reporting makes clear, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s endorsement in the Senate primary raises broader questions about the Democratic Party’s relationship with corporate power, particularly the health insurance industry. Whitmer, widely viewed as a potential future presidential candidate, is once again illustrating the limits of a party establishment that often promises transformational change while remaining closely aligned with the interests most threatened by it.
The result is a growing sense of frustration among many voters. If even Democratic primaries appear structured to protect establishment candidates over reformers, it becomes increasingly difficult to believe that meaningful change can emerge from national elections. The familiar argument of choosing the “evil of two lessers” no longer seems confined to the general election—it has become embedded in the primary process itself.
Like Newsom before her, Whitmer represents a wing of the Democratic Party that speaks the language of reform while remaining deeply intertwined with the corporate interests that benefit from the status quo. Whether the issue is California or Michigan, the pattern is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore: transformative policies are welcomed as campaign rhetoric but resisted when they threaten entrenched political and economic power.
For more context, read my previous article on how the Democratic establishment’s approach to Medicare for All has become a national pattern—not just a Michigan or California issue. California Democrats Keep Selling “Medicare for All” — While Protecting the System That Profits From Sickness
Now back to Michigan.
If my previous article explored how California Democrats repeatedly promised Medicare for All while protecting the interests of the healthcare industry, David Sirota’s interview with Abdul El-Sayed asks whether Michigan Democrats are following the same path. Their conversation goes far beyond one Senate race. It examines why Medicare for All remains such a threat to corporate power, how AIPAC and big-money politics are shaping Democratic primaries, and why El-Sayed believes the party can only win again by breaking with the corporate model that has alienated so many working-class voters. Whether you agree with him or not, it is one of the clearest discussions of the forces shaping today’s Democratic Party—and where it may be headed next.
Editor’s Note: At a moment when the once vaunted model of responsible journalism is overwhelmingly the play thing of self-serving billionaires and their corporate scribes, alternatives of integrity are desperately needed, and ScheerPost is one of them. sources.news_title: A Progressive Victory in a Nail-Biter Primary
Trump Hails El-Sayed Win as ‘Great News’ for GOP
sources.text:
by Ben Whedon
President Donald Trump on Wednesday celebrated progressive Abdul El-Sayed’s win in the Michigan Democratic Senate primary, hailing it as a boon to Republicans.
El-Sayed narrowly defeated Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., in the Democratic primary. What had been expected to be a clear win for him, however, ended up being a close contest that the Associated Press did not call until Wednesday morning. He will face former Rep. Mike Rogers, R-Mich., in the general election.
Trump, for his part, suggested that El-Sayed’s win was a benefit to Rogers.
“Great news for the Republican Party. El-Sayed, a Communist loser who hates Jews and Israel, is the projected winner in his race with the Socialist,” he posted on Truth Social. “As usual, the Polls were way off on this one. She was not expected to do nearly as well as she did. Now, the Dumocrats crazy policies will only get worse!”
Rogers, for his part, has seized on El-Sayed’s win, saying it made the race a choice between “common sense” and “complete insanity.”
The race is expected to be one of the most hotly contested in the battle for the Senate in November.
New York Senators Chuck Schumer and Kirsten Gillibrand issued a statement to journalist Andrew Desiderio after El-Sayed won, saying they are backing him.
“Abdul El-Sayed has run an energetic campaign that inspired thousands of Michiganders across the state, with a clear focus on lowering costs and standing up for working families,” they said.
“Democrats are united by a common purpose: putting a check on Donald Trump by defeating his Republican enablers and taking back the Senate. We look forward to working with Abdul and Democrats across Michigan to win this seat in November,” the senators added.
– – –
Ben Whedon is a reporter for Just the News. Zachery Schmidt is the digital editor of The Star News Network and contributed to this story.
