sources.news_title: Abdul El-Sayed overcomes massive AIPAC spending to win Michigan primary
sources.text:
Former public health official Abdul El-Sayed has won the Democratic Senate nomination in Michigan, defeating Rep. Haley Stevens in the primary.
In the general election, El-Sayed will face GOP nominee Mike Rogers, who ran unopposed in the Republican primary.
The primary race was viewed by many as a referendum on the political influence of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), which spent over $30 million backing the centrist Stevens. Stevens has been a staunch supporter of Israel throughout her four terms in the House, once claiming that the country appeared in her dreams. In contrast, El-Sayed highlighted Palestinian human rights on the campaign trail and called for an arms embargo on Israel.
Overall, Stevens was the beneficiary of roughly $62 million in ad spending from six outside groups, resulting in a 9-to-1 spending advantage according to the ad-tracking service AdImpact.
In a Responsible Statecraft article last month, Quincy Institute’s Eli Clifton showed that money spent on Stevens by AIPAC’s Super PAC, the United Democracy Project (UDP), was disproportionately donated from Republicans and individuals from outside the state.
“AIPAC can try dumping millions of dollars into propaganda, but at the end of the day, American voters don’t want our tax dollars to go toward bombing families abroad,” said US Campaign for Palestinian Rights Action Political Director Iman Abid. “We want to fund healthcare, not warfare. Dr. Abdul El-Sayed led his campaign to victory on that powerful vision, and USCPR Action is proud to endorse him.”
“The victory in Michigan is a political earthquake,” said Beth Miller, Political Director at Jewish Voice for Peace Action. “Voters in one of the most consequential states for the 2028 Presidential race have just sent a clear message: they want candidates who will fight for working families at home while unapologetically speaking out for Palestinian freedom. This cycle, AIPAC is being relegated to the dustbin of history.”
“AIPAC spent over $30 million to stop Dr. Abdul El-Sayed in this race, and that record-high sum wasn’t enough because Democratic voters have had it with the fringe and extremist view that our tax dollars should pay for Israel’s bombs, wars, and genocidal ambitions,” said IMEU Policy Project’s executive director Margaret DeReus in a statement.
At a rally in support of El-Sayed, Senator Bernie Sanders (I-VT) declared that the race would “show the nation whether AIPAC and other billionaire-funded Super PACs can buy a U.S. Senate seat or whether the people of Michigan can prevail.”
“I’ve never seen one single issue external to candidates’ platform and campaign become so central,” Omid Memarian, a Michigan political analyst and director of communications at Democracy for the Arab World Now, recently told Haaretz. “Even voters unfamiliar with El-Sayed came to see rejecting AIPAC as proof he was ‘clean.’”
The pro-Stevens ads bankrolled by UDP predictably omitted any mention of the country, as Israel has become deeply unpopular among the Democratic base. An April Pew poll found that 80% of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents now have an unfavorable view of the country, up from 69% last year and 53% in 2022.
El-Sayed victory follows a wave of progressive electoral wins across the country, in races where AIPAC spending became a focal point, including contests Pennsylvania, New York, and Colorado.
That wave continued throughout Michigan this week, as pro-Palestine candidate and AIPAC targets Donavan McKinney and Rep. Rashida Tlaib won their primaries, and Uncommitted co-founder Abbas Alawieh was elected to the Michigan State Senate.
However, Tuesday night wasn’t a total wash for the Israel Lobby.
In Missouri, AIPAC-backed incumbent Wesley Bell defeated a challenge from activist Cori Bush, who was fighting to reclaim the 1st district seat that he won from her in 2024. The United Democracy Project spent just $3.1 million on that race, which is a small sum compared to its Michigan effort, but according to AdImpact, Bell’s campaign and outside groups outspent Bush by a margin of 27-to-1.
“What we’ve seen over and over is talking about an issue that is not impacting folks right here in St. Louis, and while we take those issues seriously, you know, the M in Missouri doesn’t stand for Middle East. It stands for Missouri,” said Bell on Election Day.
The debate over Israel and Palestine will undoubtedly carry over to the November race between El-Sayed and Rogers, where lobbying groups are expected to spend heavily yet again. “Our members remain determined to ensure that voters reject Dr. El-Sayed and his radical anti-Israel agenda in November,” said AIPAC in a statement.
Whereas other progressive primary winners face an easy path to victory in their solid blue districts, the polling in Michigan suggests the Senate race will be narrow.
Speaking to POLITICO, El-Sayed predicted he would beat Rogers solidly and explained why his left-wing platform was generating broad appeal among voters.
“I don’t know what a normie Democrat is,” said El-Sayed. “I think most Democrats want to see money out of politics, money in your pocket, and Medicare for all. I think this factional thing that we’re talking about just is not consistent with what I’ve been hearing on the ground for the better part of 15 months where I’ve traveled. People are sick and tired of not being able to afford their groceries or pay their rent or believe they could ever own a home. I think that’s true of all Democrats.”
Michael Arria
Michael Arria is Mondoweiss’ U.S. correspondent. He is the author of Medium Blue: The Politics of MSNBC. Follow him on X at @michaelarria.
The Forward has some commentary on El-Sayed:
El-Sayed’s most articulate statement of his views came midway through an interview with New Yorker editor-in-chief David Remnick published the day before the primary….Remnick asked: [I]t seems that you get very prickly when you’re asked the question: Does Israel have a right to exist? You come from a country that, in the late seventies, made its accommodation, a kind of rough peace, between Egypt and Israel…. But what is your hope for a resolution in the Middle East? Is it two states? Is it one state? What underlies your sense of the situation there?….El Sayed concluded: So here’s what I believe. I believe we have a responsibility to uphold international law. I believe we have a responsibility to treat every single state the same way, around international law. I believe in a process that offers a free Palestinian people the equal rights to peace, dignity and self-determination that a free Jewish Israeli people ought to have. And then I will support whatever the outcome is that a free Palestinian people and a free Jewish Israeli people decide is the right outcome. …[ his views are ] roughly, the view of non-anti-Zionist progressive organizations like the New Israel Fund, J Street, T’ruah, and others: there should be a negotiated solution between Israelis and Palestinians, whatever form that takes, but that the current government in Israel is squarely opposed to finding one, as they have been since the 1990s when it was still a realistic possibility. Traitor, they called Yitzhak Rabin at the time.
Abdul El-Sayed is right about the future of Israel and Palestinians – The Forward
This is the New Yorker interview with El-Sayed:
Abdul El-Sayed’s Argument for America—and Against His Own Party | The New Yorker

sources.news_title: Dr. Abdul El-Sayed wife, kids and net worth: All we know about winner of Michigan's Democratic Senate primary
sources.text:
Dr. Abdul El-Sayed wife, kids and net worth: All we know about winner of Michigan's Democratic Senate primary
Dr. Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan's Democratic Senate primary, set to challenge Republican Mike Rogers in November.
Dr. Abdul El-Sayed emerged victorious in Michigan's highly competitive Democratic US Senate primary on Wednesday, overcoming an establishment favorite to challenge Republican Mike Rogers in the upcoming November election.
El-Sayed, a progressive former public health official from Wayne County, has not previously held an elected position. However, he is familiar with the political landscape, having run for governor in 2018, where he secured second place in the primary behind Gretchen Whitmer.
Abdul El-Sayed's campaign
During the primary, El-Sayed was targeted by multiple attack advertisements, and it is anticipated that he will encounter further opposition in the general election. But who is he, beside from being a proponent of Medicare for All backed by Bernie Sanders and the owner of a podcast company?
El-Sayed was born in Rochester Hills on October 31, 1984. He is currently 41 years old.
As a Muslim, his complete name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, which he has humorously remarked includes "sounds that come out of parts of people’s throats they don’t know they got.”
He was raised in the Detroit region alongside his father, Mohamed, an Egyptian immigrant who arrived in the United States to pursue his studies at Wayne State University, and his stepmother, Jacqueline, who hails from Wayne County. Both of them are engineers. His biological mother, Fatten Elkomy, works as a psychiatric nurse practitioner in Missouri.
Abdul El-Sayed's education
Describing himself as "as Michigan as you get," El-Sayed completed his education at Bloomfield Hills High School in 2003, located less than 15 minutes from Seaholm High School, where his main rival, Haley Stevens, graduated two years prior. During his time in school, he served as the captain of the lacrosse, wrestling, and football teams.
He enrolled at the University of Michigan, where he pursued a double major in biology and political science, in addition to participating in the university’s lacrosse team. El-Sayed graduated from UM in 2007 with a bachelor’s degree with the highest distinction, and he had the honor of delivering the commencement address for that year’s graduating class.
He met his spouse, psychiatrist Sarah Jukaku, during his time at the University of Michigan.
Abdul El-Sayed's wife and kids: Here's all we know
Abdul and Sarah are the parents of two daughters, Emmalee and Serene. El-Sayed frequently identifies himself as a "girl dad," sharing experiences of tea parties and the daily activities involved in raising young children.
His wife, Sarah, is characterized by her husband as a "mama bear," who passionately safeguards and prioritizes their family.
Sarah has appeared in various campaign materials for El-Sayed, including a video where she discusses the support she received from her union during her medical complications following childbirth. At that time, she was a medical resident. She mentioned that she and El-Sayed have positive discussions regarding unions.
Abdul El-Sayed's net worth
The filings for 2025 and 2026 estimate El-Sayed's net worth to be between $870,000 and $2.1 million, as per Fox News.
In his last previous political campaign, El-Sayed secured the second position behind Gov. Gretchen Whitmer in the 2018 gubernatorial primary. He surpassed Shri Thanedar, who subsequently won a seat in the state Legislature and later in the US House.
Out of approximately 1.1 million votes cast in that year's Democratic primary, El-Sayed garnered 342,179 votes compared to Whitmer’s 588,436.
Although Whitmer achieved victories in all 83 counties of Michigan that year, El-Sayed managed to present a strong challenge in the progressive bastion of Washtenaw County — where he currently resides — narrowly losing to the now two-term governor by a mere two-tenths of a percentage point.

sources.news_title: Abdul El-Sayed's COVID radicalism is a callback to a more united party
sources.text:
Abdul El-Sayed's COVID Radicalism Is a Callback to a More United Party
The pandemic provided a glue that held the Democratic Party together. Without it, they don't know what they believe.
Most of the votes are in, and it looks like former public health official Abdul El-Sayed is going to win the Michigan Democratic Party's much-watched Senate primary.
Coverage of the race has treated it as the latest battle in Democrats' civil war; the progressive (but not officially socialist) El-Sayed was going up against the more moderate Rep. Haley Stevens (D–Mich.). El-Sayed's likely victory would seem to confirm that Democrats' left flank is ascendent in this intra-party struggle.
The well-covered fissures between El-Sayed and Stevens include their stances on Israel (El-Sayed calls Israel's war in Gaza a genocide, Stevens wants military aid to the country to continue) and healthcare (the former wants Medicare for All, the latter merely supports a public option).
Interestingly, one criticism that Stevens did not levy against El-Sayed was his extreme progressivism during COVID.
As right-wing websites have extensively covered in the final days of the primary, during the summer of 2020, El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and former director of Wayne County's health department, expressed simultaneous support for lockdowns and mass demonstrations in the wake of George Floyd's death.
"There is no fair pitting of the protests for Black lives against public health," El-Sayed said to liberal podcaster Brian Tyler Cohen, per Breitbart. "Unless you devalue the lives that we're fighting for, which are Black lives, by saying that they're somehow less important to focus on than the lives that are lost to COVID-19, which, by the way, are disproportionately Black lives as well, then there is no coherent approach to pitting these protests against public health."
He was backing renewed lockdowns well into 2021.
One would think that this peak wokism might be a fruitful avenue of attack for Stevens as she tried to paint her opponent as excessively left-wing.
A possible reason that she demurred is that El-Sayed's pro-lockdown unless it's a left-wing protest position is the one that effectively everyone in the Democratic Party adopted during the summer of 2020.
For all the talk of a Democratic civil war, the pandemic shows how recently the left and liberal wings of the party were in lockstep on the issue of the day.
Stevens herself gave less explicit support for Black Lives Matter protests than El-Sayed, but she did express the requisite "love" for George Floyd at the time while signing on to Democrats' criminal justice legislation.
On COVID specifically, she urged people to "listen to Dr. Fauci" while she voted for trillions in pandemic stimulus funds and criticized efforts to target those stimulus funds to the truly needy.
During the primary, Stevens' moderate campaign bid received the support of Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, who issued lockdown orders that closed schools and banned people from buying seeds at the hardware store while also offering full-throated support for George Floyd protests.
The governor's support for demonstrations did come with the weak request that mass demonstrations follow "social distancing guidelines."
Support for COVID mandates, trillions in federal COVID spending, and anti-racist criminal justice reform was the glue that held the Democratic Party together during the presidency of Joe Biden.
Arguably, one of the reasons that no one in the party was able to launch a successful challenge to Biden's bid for a second term until long after it became undeniable he was not physically up for the job was that no one within the party (progressive or moderate) had a real policy critique to level at this COVID-era three-legged stool.
But COVID is far enough in the rearview mirror that it can't serve as a unifying force for the party anymore. It doesn't help that voters found extreme public health and fiscal interventions to counter the pandemic, and all the inflation and crime spikes that came with it, unpalatable enough to elect Donald Trump again.
Democrats are still united in their opposition to Trump. Yet the current president's unpopular wars, trade policies, and corruption haven't proven enough of a crisis to get all of the party on the same page.
Instead, issues like the Israel-Palestine conflict and socializing healthcare rule the day. They're divisive enough that while El-Sayed was expected to win, the primary was not a blowout by any means.
For Democrats to be united again, they'll need another pandemic. Until then, expect the intra-party civil war to continue.

sources.news_title: Abdul El-Sayed defeats AIPAC-backed rival in Michigan Democratic Senate primary
sources.text:
Abdul El-Sayed defeats AIPAC-backed rival in Michigan Democratic Senate primary
Progressive advocate Abdul El-Sayed won the Democratic nomination for the US Senate in Michigan on Wednesday, defeating Congresswoman Haley Stevens in a race that became one of the most expensive and closely watched primaries in US history.
NBC News projected El-Sayed's victory late on Tuesday after a bruising campaign in which more than $60m was spent, much of it by outside groups seeking to block his path to the Senate.
As of 15:30 BST, NBC reported that El-Sayed had received 48.5 percent of the votes to Stevens' 47.5 percent, with 98.7 percent of expected votes tallied.
Mallory McMorrow, a state legislator who was in the US Senate race but dropped out weeks before the elections, endorsed El-Sayed shortly after NBC made the announcement.
The result is being viewed as a major setback for pro-Israel lobbying groups, particularly the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), which spent more than $30m backing Stevens in an effort to unseat one of the Democratic Party's most outspoken pro-Palestinian candidates.
El-Sayed touted his narrow lead as results started to trickle in early on Wednesday, but said there was still a big fight to come.
"I wish I could tell you that I was declaring victory right about now," he told his supporters at a watch party in Detroit, Middle East Eye reported.
If declared the winner, the 41-year-old doctor will face former Republican congressman Mike Rogers in November in what is expected to be one of the country's most competitive Senate races.
The contest could help determine control of the Senate during the final two years of President Donald Trump's term.
"I know you’re listening, Mike. Mike, we are coming for you," El-Sayed added.
The projected victory marks a watershed moment for progressive Democrats and Arab American voters, who rallied behind El-Sayed after months of organizing around opposition to Israel's genocidal war on Gaza and frustration with the Democratic Party's traditional alignment with pro-Israel advocacy groups.
Throughout the campaign, El-Sayed accused AIPAC and affiliated political action committees of attempting to "buy" the election with unprecedented outside spending.
Stevens rejected suggestions that she was beholden to outside interests, arguing that she had a strong record of delivering for Michigan.
El-Sayed also described Israel's military campaign in Gaza as a genocide, echoing language used by many human rights organizations and Palestinian advocates but rejected by Israel and successive US administrations.
He also argued that billions of dollars in US military assistance to Israel should instead be invested in healthcare, affordable housing, education and infrastructure at home.
His position resonated strongly with many voters in Michigan who played a crucial role in organizing against former President Joe Biden during the 2024 election over his strong support for the war on Gaza.

“I’m not a socialist. I’m just a capitalist who understands how capitalism works,” El-Sayed said. “I think government ought to be there to regulate monopolies and oligopolies so that everybody can actually participate in the economy without having to be forced to pay more or get paid less.”

sources.news_title: Abdul El-Sayed Edges Haley Stevens in Michigan Democratic Senate Primary
sources.text:
The former public health official overcame heavy establishment and pro-Israel backing for Rep. Haley Stevens, winning the Democratic nomination by a narrow 48.5% to 47.5% margin.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
Abdul El-Sayed narrowly defeated Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary Tuesday, overcoming support for his opponent from senior party figures and millions of dollars in spending tied to the pro-Israel lobby.
El-Sayed received 48.5% of the vote to Stevens’ 47.5%, according to results compiled by The Associated Press. The close outcome followed a campaign that exposed divisions within the Democratic Party over Israel, immigration enforcement, health care and the influence of establishment donors.
The former public health official entered the race with endorsements from independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, Democratic New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Democratic Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren and other prominent members of the party’s left wing.
Stevens, who has represented Michigan in the House since 2019 after flipping a Republican-held seat, was supported by much of the Democratic establishment. Organizations associated with the pro-Israel movement also spent millions of dollars supporting her campaign.
The candidates offered sharply different positions on several major issues. Stevens favored reforming Immigration and Customs Enforcement instead of abolishing the agency, supported adding a public health insurance option rather than adopting Medicare for All and remained an outspoken supporter of Israel.
El-Sayed campaigned on Medicare for All, eliminating ICE, placing abortion protections into federal law and allowing so-called “gender-affirming care,” according to the policy platform published by his campaign.
Although his proposals and political alliances led opponents to characterize him as a socialist, El-Sayed rejected that description.
“I’m not a socialist. I’m just a capitalist who understands how capitalism works,” El-Sayed said. “I think government ought to be there to regulate monopolies and oligopolies so that everybody can actually participate in the economy without having to be forced to pay more or get paid less.”
Sanders cast El-Sayed’s candidacy as part of a broader national campaign by Democratic Socialists of America members, union supporters, younger voters and other left-wing activists to challenge party-backed candidates.
“We are taking on the establishment all over this country. All over the country, ordinary people, unionists, young people, people of color [are] getting involved in the political process and they’re saying wait a minute, maybe the Democratic Party should belong to us and not just wealthy campaign contributors. And then in the midst of this comes Dr. Abdul El-Sayed,” Sanders said in a campaign advertisement.
Stevens’ supporters included Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, Michigan Sen. Gary Peters, South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn and Delaware Sen. Chris Coons.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer also worked privately to build support for Stevens and encouraged Democratic donors to contribute to her campaign, The New York Times reported. Schumer told Punchbowl News in June that Stevens had the “best chance of winning.”
The general election is expected to feature El-Sayed against former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers, the presumptive GOP nominee.
A Michigan Education survey conducted July 28 showed Rogers leading El-Sayed by 10 percentage points in a hypothetical matchup, according to the poll results. The same survey showed a much closer contest between Rogers and Stevens, with Stevens holding a 46% to 45% advantage.
Spending in the Michigan Senate contest had reached approximately $80 million, placing it among the country’s most expensive congressional races, CBS News reported. About $60 million was spent in support of Stevens, with a substantial portion connected to pro-Israel interests.
Campaign finance records also showed that approximately 31% of donors who gave at least $200 to Stevens’ Senate campaign had donated to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee since the beginning of 2025, The Detroit News reported in May.
An AIPAC affiliate previously spent more than $5 million through campaign contributions and independent expenditures during Stevens’ 2022 House primary.
The candidates’ opposing positions on Israel became a central issue during a July 28 debate. El-Sayed criticized Stevens for accepting support from pro-Israel donors and groups, while Stevens defended her position, saying she favored a two-state solution and “long-term peace.”
El-Sayed accused Israel of committing “genocide” in Gaza and opposed continued U.S. financial support for the country.
The dispute reflected a growing division among congressional Democrats. A total of 103 Democratic House members voted for an amendment introduced by Republican Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie that would have reduced foreign aid to Israel by $3.3 billion.
Stevens also attracted criticism in mid-July for a campaign speech intended to rally supporters.
“I am gonna be telling the stories on our behalf. And you better believe I’m gonna be doing it with a little bit of joy, a little bit of enthusiasm, a little bit of energy and a little bit of stick it to ‘em. Because that’s the Michigan way,” Stevens said.
Although the final result was decided by approximately 1 percentage point, El-Sayed had held a much larger lead shortly before the election. An Emerson College Polling, WLNS and WOOD-TV survey released the previous Thursday showed him leading Stevens by 15 points.
El-Sayed’s victory followed other recent primary defeats for longtime Democratic incumbents and establishment-supported candidates.
In New York’s 13th Congressional District, Democratic Socialists of America candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier defeated five-term Democratic Rep. Adriano Espaillat in June. In Colorado, socialist Melat Kiros defeated Rep. Diana DeGette, who had served in Congress for 29 years.

sources.text:
Vice President JD Vance floated on Wednesday the possibility that in three years’ time, firebrand Michigan Democratic nominee Abdul el Sayed could be sitting in the White House as commander in chief.
Vance raised the prospect of an el Sayed administration during an anti-fraud event at the Eisenhower Executive Office Building, arguing that Congress needs to codify stricter guidelines to prevent future scams in taxpayer-funded federal programs.

“This effort will fundamentally always have a limitation unless our colleagues in the House and the Senate are working with us,” he said. “We don’t want the next administration, whoever you know, God forbid, you’re going to have President el Sayed in three years. We don’t want him to undo all the incredible work that we’ve been doing when we’ve been taking out the fraudsters and saving the American people money.”
Vance made the comments only hours after el Sayed was declared the victor in Michigan’s hotly contested Democratic primary to replace Sen. Gary Peters (D-MI).
President Donald Trump, who won Michigan in 2024, was quick to praise el Sayed’s victory over Rep. Haley Stevens (D-MI). Trump argued that el Sayed, who has taken positions far outside the Democratic mainstream, would be an easier opponent for GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers.
“Great news for the Republican Party,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “El-Sayed, a Communist loser who hates Jews and Israel, is the projected winner in his race with the Socialist.”
ABDUL EL SAYED DEFEATS HALEY STEVENS IN MICHIGAN SENATE PRIMARY
El Sayed has been criticized by both Democrats and Republicans for his anti-Israel views, which some say border on antisemitism. On the trail, el Sayed has openly embraced and campaigned with controversial internet personality Hasan Piker, who is on record claiming that “America deserved 9/11” and frequently calls Jews and supporters of Israel “Zionist pigs.”
El Sayed, himself, has echoed some of those sentiments, mostly recently on Wednesday, accusing Israel and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of being “blood thirsty.”

sources.text:
Lobbyists Spent $70m to Defeat a Pro-Palestine Candidate. He Still Won
Abdul El-Sayed clinches victory despite record sum dedicated to beating him.
by Joshua Carroll
5 August 2026
A progressive Democrat and fierce opponent of the genocide in Gaza has won a key primary race in the US, even after corporate and pro-Israel lobbying groups spent a record-breaking $70m (£52m) in a bid to defeat him.
Abdul El-Sayed, who in April described the Israeli government as “pretty damn evil”, beat establishment favourite Haley Stevens in the Michigan Senate Democratic primary by a razor-thin margin. He secured 48.5% of the vote while she got 47.5%.
In total, fundraising committees known as super PACs spent almost $70m in a bid to prevent El-Sayed from winning. The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) spent $30m, with the remainder of the money representing interests including oil, tobacco and private healthcare firms, according to figures compiled by Mother Jones.
Meanwhile, El-Sayed’s campaign spent around $6m on the race. “We just fought through the most expensive Democratic Senate primary in history,” his campaign said in an email on Wednesday.
El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and former public health official who was raised by Egyptian immigrant parents in Detroit, campaigned on breaking up the private healthcare industry, getting big money out of politics and ending military aid to Israel.
He supports challenging the US’s exploitative private healthcare insurance system, and championed the policy in a book he authored titled Medicare for All: A Citizen’s Guide.
In April he told CNN: “Killing tens of thousands of people makes you pretty damn evil.’It’s not how evil is this one versus that one – Hamas: evil, Israeli government: evil. We can say both.”
His victory is the latest in a series of progressive wins in the US that suggest Aipac is becoming less able to punish candidates who speak out against Israel’s mass killings and abuses, and US support for them.
Aipac spent more on trying to defeat El-Sayed than it has in any other race in its history.
“The expensive, financed, racist smears didn’t work,” broadcaster Redi Tlhabi wrote on X after his win. “There is hope yet. This is a political earthquake.”
Joshua Carroll is a writer and journalist.

sources.news_title: Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan Senate primary race
sources.text:
Abdul El-Sayed has won Michigan’s Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate, narrowly defeating U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens in a victory for the party’s progressive wing in a battleground state.
The real test of El-Sayed’s and progressives’ strength will now come in a Nov. 3 matchup against Mike Rogers, a former congressman who ran unopposed for the Republican nomination. The seat is pivotal to Democrats’ chances of flipping the Senate and El-Sayed will face the challenge of uniting a divided Democratic base after a bruising primary.
The race remained tight throughout Tuesday night, with a winner not declared until this morning. In his final remarks at a primary night party before the race was called, El-Sayed said ”tomorrow we begin to mend fences.”
Stevens called El-Sayed to concede today, and she issued a statement saying she would back El-Sayed’s candidacy.
”I am proud to offer my support as he takes on Mike Rogers in the general election,” she said.
Stevens added, “This was a thorough and rigorous campaign that brought out the full span of views within the Democratic Party — and that is why we have primaries.”
Progressives have been gaining strength this year
El-Sayed’s win represents a significant shift for the Democratic Party. In 2018, he lost the gubernatorial primary to now-Gov. Gretchen Whitmer by 21 percentage points.
El-Sayed, a former health official in Wayne County, campaigned on ”Medicare for All,” halting military aid to Israel and campaign finance reform. He had support from progressive leaders including U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who framed the race as a grassroots-focused movement and a broader fight against the establishment and big-money spending.
U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen, another progressive leader who endorsed El-Sayed, said the race ”should be a wake-up call to the Washington Democratic establishment.”
”He was running against a lot of Washington insiders as well as parts of the Michigan Democratic establishment. And he won,” Van Hollen said. ”That’s an incredible story.”
In another race that pitted a progressive against a more moderate Democrat, state Rep. Donavan McKinney defeated U.S. Rep. Shri Thanedar in the 13th Congressional District race.
After Thanedar won election in 2022, Detroit had no Black representation in Congress for the first time since the early 1950s. McKinney argued that the city should once again have a Black representative in Congress.
Now comes another challenge for Democrats: uniting the party to defeat Rogers, for whom Republicans have already reserved large sums of money ahead of the general election.
Associated Press reporter Nathan Ellgren in Washington contributed.

Abdul El-Sayed leads anti-war sweep in Michigan; Israel raids Qalandia refugee camp; Russian strikes kill 17 in Kyiv
Drop Site Daily: August 5, 2026
Wednesday, August 5, 2026 – Iran’s talks with Oman about the Strait of Hormuz in final stages, have “nothing to do” with the U.S. Qatari Foreign Minister: Multinational effort underway to reach diplomatic resolution to Iran War. Report: Iran demands say over inbound and outbound Hormuz traffic. Iraq in Hormuz talks with Iran, Iraqi official says. At least 56 executed in Iran since March, UN human rights chief says. Ansarallah claims attack on Saudi tanker. Israel’s assault on Gaza continues. Israel carries on with attacks in the occupied West Bank. Israeli military probe says soldier may have killed settler in Tal attack. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says he has “disagreements” with President Donald Trump over the Gaza plan. Israeli abuse of Palestinian “doctor of the poor.” Israeli Knesset committee approves around 110 million dollars for settlement expansion. Israel orders evacuation, launches strikes after explosion kills soldiers in south Lebanon. Primary results from Michigan, Missouri, and Kansas. ICE arrests hit record 51,000 in July. Trump administration refunds $100 billion in “liberation day” tariffs. Appeals court rules Environmental Protection Agency cannot block $20 billion in climate grants. Rep. Chuck Edwards drops re-election bid after Ethics Committee recommends censure for sexual harassment. Democrat Julian Beaudion withdraws from South Dakota Senate race. Brazil downgrades diplomatic ties with Argentina after President Javier Milei’s latest insults of Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Mass jail break, armed clashes kill three in cities west of Tripoli. Malaysia says it won’t repatriate Rohingya refugees to Myanmar if their lives are at risk. Ceuta seeks transfer of 1,100 unaccompanied minor migrants to mainland Spain.
Iran
- Tehran’s Hormuz talks with Oman in final stages, have “nothing to do” with U.S.: Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said Wednesday that Iran and Oman have agreed on the geographic parameters of a shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz and are in the final stage of preparing a joint announcement, provided “certain third parties” do not interfere. 
  - An agreement on shipping arrangements between Iran and Oman through the Strait of Hormuz would not immediately reopen the waterway, a government source told Iranian state broadcaster IRIB, saying that the ongoing talks have “nothing to do” with the U.S. The source told the broadcaster that the waterway would remain closed as long as “U.S. violations” continue.
  - Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remained severely restricted on Tuesday, with just eight vessels transiting the waterway for a second consecutive day, according to shipping data firm Kpler. Prior to the war, roughly 130–140 ships typically passed through each day.
- Qatar FM: Multinational effort underway to reach diplomatic resolution to Iran War: Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed Al-Ansari said on Tuesday Doha is coordinating with Oman, Pakistan, and GCC states to broker a U.S.-Iran diplomatic resolution and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. 
  - He called mediation efforts “ongoing” and said a draft of a possible agreement was being circulated among the relevant parties, adding that the talks have reached “very progressive stages.”
- Report: Iran demands say over inbound and outbound Hormuz traffic: Iran is demanding control over ships entering the Strait of Hormuz and oversight of outbound traffic, with the power to intervene if necessary, under a temporary reopening plan being discussed with Oman, a senior Iranian source told Reuters on Tuesday. 
  - Outbound vessels would travel between Iran and Oman, with Oman granting exit clearance after notifying Tehran, Reuters reports.
  - The source told the outlet that Iran has already compromised from its initial demand for full control in both directions and is unlikely to shift further.
- Iraq in Hormuz talks with Iran, Iraqi official says: Iraqi Oil Minister Bassem Mohammed Khudair said on Tuesday that the country is in talks with Iran over the “smooth flow of oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz,” expressing hope for a breakthrough in the coming days, according to a statement carried by the Iraqi News Agency. 
  - Iraq exports roughly 95% of its crude through the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, leaving the major OPEC producer heavily exposed to the disruption caused by the waterway’s effective closure.
  - The talks come days after Iraq signed a separate agreement with Turkey to maintain northern crude exports to the Mediterranean through the Ceyhan pipeline, bypassing the Gulf.
- At least 56 executed in Iran since March, UN human rights chief says: Iran has executed at least 56 people on national security-related charges since March 19, including 27 in cases linked to mass anti-government protests in January, according to United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk, with over 100 others at risk of execution on similar charges. “I am alarmed by the rise in executions and death sentences issued in Iran since March, and that capital punishment continues to be used to instill fear among the population and suppress dissent,” Turk said in a statement. He added that executions for drug-related offenses are also continuing “at an alarming rate.”
Yemen
- Ansarallah claims attack on Saudi tanker: Yemen’s Ansarallah movement announced on Tuesday that it had struck the Saudi oil tanker Wafa with ballistic missiles in the northern Red Sea, off Yanbu, claiming a direct hit as part of enforcing its maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia, though neither the Saudis nor major maritime tracking firms confirmed the incident. 
  - Ansarallah said its forces have now targeted eight Saudi oil tankers since the blockade began on July 22, adding that 29 Saudi tankers have been prevented from continuing their voyages and forced to turn back in the Red and Arabian Seas.
Palestine
- Killed and wounded in Gaza: Over the past 24 hours, two Palestinians were killed after succumbing to wounds sustained in earlier attacks, and one was injured in Israeli attacks across Gaza, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health. Two bodies were also recovered from beneath the rubble. 
  - The total recorded death toll since October 7, 2023 has risen to 73,381 killed, with 174,231 injured. Since October 11, the first full day of the so-called ceasefire, Israel has killed at least 1,254 Palestinians in Gaza and wounded 4,121, while 804 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble.
- Israel’s assault on Gaza: 
  - Israel struck and wounded a Palestinian child on Wednesday morning, west of Khan Younis, according to Shehab News.
  - Israeli artillery shelled an area northeast of the Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza on Wednesday, WAFA reported, and also fired on the northern areas of Al-Bureij refugee camp.
  - In the southern Gaza Strip, Israel shelled areas southwest of Khan Younis.
- Israeli attacks in the occupied West Bank: 
  - East Jerusalem: A large force of Israeli soldiers raided Qalandia refugee camp, north of Jerusalem, on Wednesday morning, conducting searches and raids, and detaining several Palestinians. Israeli soldiers distributed leaflets stating that “a large-scale operation” in the camp was underway, according to Quds News Network. The Palestinian Red Crescent said its crews in the camp have so far treated eight people who were assaulted. The army operation comes one week after Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz issued instructions to occupy another Palestinian refugee camp under the model of the army invasions of the Jenin, Tulkarem, and Nur Shams camps in early 2025 that Human Rights Watch said amounted to war crimes and crimes against humanity. In a separate attack in the town of Al-Ram, Israeli soldiers shot a young Palestinian man in the foot, according to the Red Crescent.
  - Bethlehem: Israeli forces raided the town of Beit Fajjar on Tuesday evening, firing tear gas and sound bombs. In Nahalin, west of Bethlehem, Israeli settlers began demolitions on three Palestinian homes.
  - Jenin: Israeli forces detained four Palestinians in several raids on the Jenin governorate on Wednesday, seizing one home in the area and converting it into a military barracks. Settlers bulldozed Palestinian land and uprooted olive trees in nearby Ajja, receiving support from the Israeli military, according to WAFA.
  - Tubas: Israeli settlers attacked a water pipeline in Yerza, East of Tubas, on Wednesday, according to WAFA, the eighth attack on this pipeline since the beginning of July.
  - Galilee: Israeli forces demolished a Palestinian home in Al-Ba’na in Galilee on Wednesday, forcing evacuations from the area, and detaining the home’s owner and his brother when they attempted to resist the operation.
- Israeli military probe says soldier may have killed settler in Tal attack: An Israeli military investigation published Wednesday found that friendly fire may have killed Israeli settler Benayahu Mellet during a deadly settler attack in the occupied West Bank village of Tal last month, The Times of Israel reported. Four Palestinians and two Israelis were killed during the attack after around 20 settlers, some of them armed, stormed the village. The incident sparked a large-scale Israeli military operation across the occupied West Bank. According to the probe, Mellet died shortly after a Palestinian wrestled a rifle from another Israeli, though the military said it could not determine whether he was killed by Palestinian fire or by Israeli troops because his body was buried without an autopsy.
- Netanyahu says he has “disagreements” with Trump over the Gaza plan: After meeting with “Board of Peace” representative Nickolay Mladenov on Tuesday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Israeli media that he had “disagreements with President Trump” concerning “the recent agreement with Hamas.” 
  - Netanyahu maintained, contrary to the roadmap published by the board, that Hamas “must be disarmed and the Gaza Strip [be] demilitarized before moving to the reconstruction phase.”
  - During the meeting, Mladenov reportedly urged Netanyahu to halt Israeli attacks on Gaza, two sources told the AP.
  - Following the meeting, Hamas called for clarifications from the board, the AFP reported, voicing “unease” over Mladenov’s statement after he met with Netanyahu. The statement, a Hamas official said, “focused solely on the issue of weapons and failed to address the occupation’s obligations,” which include an end to all Israeli attacks on Gaza.
- Israeli abuse of Palestinian “doctor of the poor”: Israeli prison guards have beaten a 71-year-old Palestinian doctor, tear-gassed his overcrowded cell, and denied him vital medication, according to testimony published by Haaretz on Tuesday. 
  - Dr. Mazen Al-Rantisi, nicknamed the “doctor of the poor” because of the free and low-charge medical care he provides Ramallah-area residents, was imprisoned by Israeli forces during a raid on June 21, and was indicted for chairing a health nonprofit previously outlawed by Israel.
  - Al-Rantisi told a lawyer from the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel this week that guards force blindfolded prisoners to walk bent over, beat him and other detainees during repeated raids, and fired tear gas into their cells. Younger prisoners surround him during the beatings in an effort to shield him.
  - Israel withheld all of his regular prescriptions for his first 10 days at Ofer Prison and continues to deny him one medication. His requests to see a doctor have been ignored, and his lawyer said he has lost significant weight.
- Drop Site video dispatch from mass funeral in Gaza: 44 children and 37 women were among 112 members of the Al-Hasayna and Abu Sharia families laid to rest at a mass funeral in northern Gaza after Civil Defense crews recently recovered their bodies from beneath the rubble. Drop Site contributor Abdel Qader Sabbah shared footage from the funeral and spoke with attendees. 
  - “The first house was bombed, so they fled to a second house, then to a third, searching for somewhere safe to hide,” family elder Nahed Al-Hasayna told Drop Site. “These were all children and women, peaceful and innocent. For what crime were they killed?”
  - Fares Affana, director of ambulance and emergency services for Civil Defense in northern Gaza, told Drop Site that Israeli attacks had systematically destroyed Gaza’s rescue capacity, leaving crews unable to reach people trapped beneath collapsed buildings. “We could hear the cries and screams of the wounded from beneath the rubble….But because we lacked equipment, we could not reach them,” he said, adding that many remained trapped for days until they died.
  - Watch Sabbah’s full report here.
- Israeli Knesset committee approves around 110 million dollars for settlement expansion: The Israeli Knesset Finance Committee held a special session Tuesday during the election recess to approve 335 million shekels (~$110 million) for settlement expansion, which would raise the Israeli Settlement Ministry’s budget for the year to a record 821 million shekels (not including the 944 million shekels it has committed for future settlements).
Lebanon
- Israel orders evacuation, launches strikes after explosion kills soldiers in south Lebanon: Israel launched a wave of attacks across southern Lebanon on Wednesday after two Israeli soldiers were reportedly killed and others wounded after an explosive device detonated inside a building in Majdal Zoun, a village in southern Lebanon that is partially occupied by the Israeli military, according to Israeli media. 
  - Following the explosion, the Israeli military claimed Hezbollah had violated the ceasefire and ordered residents of Al-Mansouri to evacuate north before carrying out two airstrikes on the Mashaa al-Mansouri area south of Tyre (Sour). Israeli artillery also shelled the outskirts of Majdal Zoun, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency (NNA).
  - An Israeli airstrike struck the rooftop of a prayer room at the Tebnine cemetery, killing one person and wounding 11 others, according to NNA.
  - Israeli forces also dropped illumination flares over the heights of Kfar Reman, which NNA said were intended to ignite fires, while troops set fire to forested areas and fruit orchards in Houla, with the flames spreading to homes in the town’s western neighborhoods.
  - Israel has continued carrying out near-daily attacks in Lebanon despite the U.S.-brokered ceasefire. On Tuesday night, Israeli forces carried out another large-scale demolition in Hadatha in Bint Jbeil district and a drone struck the same location twice in the Roueiss neighborhood of Nabatieh Al-Fawqa, according to NNA.
U.S. News
- Primary results: 
  - Abdul El-Sayed beat Rep. Haley Stevens in Tuesday’s Michigan Democratic Senate primary, overcoming over $60 million in outside funding, mostly from pro-Israel groups, and late endorsements of Stevens from current Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and prominent national Democrats like Rep. James Clyburn. El-Sayed will face Republican Mike Rogers in the November general election. If elected, he will be the first Muslim-American to serve in the U.S. Senate.
  - State Rep. Donavan McKinney prevailed over incumbent Democratic Rep. Shri Thanedar in their Detroit-area primary contest, despite Thanedar’s backing from AIPAC and cryptocurrency interests. McKinney, a 34-year-old endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America, is now the heavy favorite to represent the safely Democratic district.
  - Progressive William Lawrence defeated two moderate candidates in his Democratic primary in the Lansing Area. Lawrence, a climate organizer endorsed by Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rashida Tlaib, will face incumbent Republican Rep. Tom Barrett, rated one of the most vulnerable Republican incumbents in this cycle, in the general election to represent Michigan’s 7th district in the House.
  - Rep. Wesley Bell defeated former Rep. Cori Bush in Missouri’s 1st Congressional District Democratic primary, repeating his 2024 win over Bush, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America. AIPAC spent about $3 million on Bell’s behalf, less than the $8 million he received in 2024, when he was one of the largest beneficiaries of AIPAC spending nationwide.
  - Missouri voters rejected a Republican-backed measure that would have required a majority in each of the state’s eight congressional districts, rather than a simple statewide majority, to pass citizen-sponsored constitutional amendments, preserving a tool voters have used to pass measures including Medicaid expansion, marijuana legalization, and an abortion rights guarantee. Opponents, including a state real estate association and abortion rights groups, noted the measure would have set the highest such threshold among the 18 states allowing citizen-led constitutional amendments and that none of the four amendments Missouri voters passed since 2020 won in all eight districts.
  - Rev. Adam Hamilton, pastor of the largest United Methodist congregation in the country, won Tuesday’s Democratic Senate primary in Kansas, according to The Associated Press, setting up a challenge against Republican Sen. Roger Marshall in a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in nearly 100 years. Though Kansas has not factored into Democrats’ plans to retake the Senate, Hamilton is viewed by some as a talented fundraiser and has some political tailwinds, including the recent re-election of a Democratic governor and an electoral victory for abortion rights in 2022.
  - Kansas voters rejected a Republican-backed ballot measure that would have required state Supreme Court justices to be popularly elected rather than appointed by the governor, dealing another setback to lawmakers seeking to overturn a 2019 court ruling that established a constitutional right to abortion in the state. Kansas Republicans had campaigned for the measure by arguing that the state Supreme Court had failed to represent the “will” of the state’s voters, but told anti-abortion groups that the referendum was aimed at challenging the state’s abortion laws.
  - Abbas Alawieh won his Democratic primary to represent the Dearborn area in the state Senate. Before his work on behalf of the “Uncommitted” movement, which attempted to hold the Democratic Party accountable for its failures on Gaza. Alawieh previously served as a congressional aide to Reps. Andy Levin, Rashida Tlaib, and Cori Bush. If elected, he will be the first Arab-American to serve in Michigan’s state Senate.
- ICE arrests hit record 51,000 in July: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested 51,000 people in July, the largest single-month total in Department of Homeland Security history, according to sources familiar with the data cited by ABC News. 
  - ICE has particularly ramped up its campaign at American airports, with 30 people detained at airports in July, according to the data.
- Trump administration refunds $100 billion in “liberation day” tariffs: The Trump administration has paid out about $100 billion, or 60% of the $165 billion collected, in refunds of “liberation day” tariffs since the Supreme Court struck down the emergency powers used to impose them earlier this year, according to a report U.S. customs officials gave judges at the U.S. Court of International Trade on Tuesday. 
  - Customs and Border Protection said in a Tuesday court filing that more than $128 billion has been “accepted for processing,” indicating that more refunds are imminent.
  - Representative Greg Casar (D-Texas) noted that the refunds go almost exclusively to companies, and are not seen by consumers. “Every single cent of these refunds should go back to American consumers,” he said on X.
- Appeals court rules E.P.A. cannot block $20 billion in climate grants: A divided 10-judge panel on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit upheld an injunction Tuesday barring the Environmental Protection Agency from terminating $20 billion in climate grants under the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund, ruling that recipients should have access to the funds while their case proceeds. If the E.P.A. does not appeal to the Supreme Court within seven days, the ruling will effectively reinstate the Biden-era program, which E.P.A. Administrator Lee Zeldin sought to kill, using as his pretext unsubstantiated allegations of waste and fraud against eight climate groups.
- Rep. Chuck Edwards drops re-election bid after Ethics Committee recommends censure for sexual harassment: Rep. Chuck Edwards, a North Carolina Republican, withdrew from his re-election campaign early Wednesday after the House Ethics Committee recommended censure after finding he sexually harassed two female staffers and created a hostile work environment. 
  - The House is expected to vote on censuring Edwards after the August recess. Edwards said in a post on X that he would complete his current term.
- Democrat Julian Beaudion withdraws from South Dakota Senate race: Julian Beaudion, the Democratic nominee for South Dakota’s Senate seat, withdrew from the race Tuesday after months of vowing to stay in, clearing the way for a one-on-one contest between independent Brian Bengs and Republican incumbent Mike Rounds, The Washington Post reported. 
  - South Dakota becomes the third state where Democrats have opted not to field a Senate candidate, following Nebraska and Idaho, a strategy that gained traction after independent Dan Osborn came within seven percentage points of winning Nebraska’s 2024 race.
  - Beaudion said he would not endorse either Bengs or Rounds and accused Bengs, without naming him, of “intimidating threats to drop out of this race.”
- AP: Trump administration has detained more than 50 relatives of active-duty troops in immigration crackdown: More than 50 parents and spouses of active-duty U.S. service members have been detained under President Donald Trump’s second-term immigration crackdown, with at least six deported, according to an Associated Press investigation published on Wednesday. 
  - The detentions, which experts say reverse decades of bipartisan practice protecting military families and even Trump’s own first-term policy, have disrupted deployments and left troops without childcare, including Army Sgt. Hedar Leonel Turcios Juarez, whose wife was detained outside a Walmart, and Air Force Tech. Sgt. Wendy Gbeve, whose father was deported to Mexico despite a pending legal status application.
  - DHS said in a statement that “military service alone does not automatically grant lawful immigration status,” even as Army and National Guard recruiters continue advertising immigration benefits like “military parole-in-place” to potential enlistees.
📥 Have a tip on Capitol Hill? Email DC Correspondent Julian Andreone at [email protected]
Other International News
- Russian barrage on Kyiv kills at least 17: Russia struck Kyiv and surrounding areas with 24 ballistic missiles, four cruise missiles, and 115 drones early Wednesday, killing at least 17 people, according to Al Jazeera, with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying the strikes hit warehouses, a brewery, and construction supply sites. 
  - Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s supply of air defense missiles is three times lower than in 2025 and that missile interceptors “could have saved the lives of those killed today.” Reuters reported that U.S. officials are discussing options to replenish Ukraine’s depleted Patriot stockpiles, including allowing domestic component manufacturing.
  - Separately, Ukraine struck a Wildberries warehouse in Russia’s Tula region and an oil refinery in Bashkortostan on Wednesday.
- Sheikh Hasina says she plans to return to Bangladesh despite death sentence: Former Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, 78, said in a video address on Wednesday that she plans to return to Bangladesh in December after two years in exile in India, despite a death sentence handed down against her. 
  - Hasina, who was ousted following a violent crackdown on protests in 2024, made the announcement alongside her son, Sajeeb Wazed Joy, and other leaders from her Awami League Party.
  - She said the exact date of her return would be announced “when time comes.”
- U.S. revokes visa of Brazilian ambassador: The United States revoked the visa of Brazilian Ambassador to Washington Maria Luiza Ribeiro Viotti. The move comes after Brasília stalled the approval of the incoming U.S. envoy and refused visas for two U.S. State Department officials over concerns of political meddling. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defended the move by openly accusing the American diplomats of seeking to interfere in the October vote and cast doubt on the integrity of the country’s electoral system. State Department officials indicated the ambassador’s credentials could be reinstated once Brazil accepts Washington’s choice for the post.
- Brazil downgrades diplomatic ties with Argentina after Milei’s latest insults of Lula: Brazil will handle relations with Argentina at the chargé d’affaires level after Argentine President Javier Milei again insulted Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, calling him an “ex-convict,” a “thief,” and “corrupt” in recent interview on Argentine television, a Brazilian government source told Reuters on Tuesday. 
  - Brazil’s ambassador to Argentina, Julio Bitelli, who had already been recalled last month after Milei criticized Lula while campaigning alongside opposition candidate Flavio Bolsonaro, will not return to Buenos Aires.
  - Milei and Lula have not held an official bilateral meeting since Milei took office in December 2023.
- Mass jail break, armed clashes kill three in cities west of Tripoli: Detainees staged a mass escape from a jail in Surman, near Tripoli, on Tuesday as armed clashes between rival groups erupted in the nearby cities of Zawiya and Surman, killing three civilians and injuring several others, Reuters reported. 
  - The origin and cause of the clashes remained unclear. 
Zawiya, located 40 kilometers west of Tripoli, is home to Libya’s largest functioning oil refinery, which urged workers to avoid the areas of fighting.
  - Surman’s Mayor Mohamed Abu Snina described the humanitarian situation as “very bad” but said relative calm had returned to the city after a neutral force was deployed to the area.

sources.news_title: Progressive El-Sayed wins Michigan primary in jolt to Democrats | Honolulu Star-Advertiser
sources.text:
Progressive El-Sayed wins Michigan primary in jolt to Democrats
The Democratic Party’s progressive wing scored a high-profile victory today when Abdul El-Sayed won the party’s U.S. Senate nomination in Michigan, giving its anti-establishment message a boost ahead of November’s midterm elections.
El-Sayed, a doctor whose campaign focused on healthcare, the economy and an end to unconditional military aid to Israel, was the first progressive to win a statewide primary in a state that President Donald Trump carried in 2024. He will face Republican former congressman Mike Rogers in November.
The vote, billed as a defining test of the party’s direction, became an election-night cliffhanger between El-Sayed and U.S. Representative Haley Stevens, a moderate supported by Democratic leaders and pro-Israel groups. With 99% of the estimated votes counted today, El-Sayed led Stevens 48.5% to 47.5%, according to the Associated Press.
“My hope is that our democracy will never be the same,” El-Sayed said at a press conference today. “From here on out, we can always point and say, ‘No, this is the people’s democracy, and we will always own it.’”
El-Sayed’s victory could intensify debate within Democratic ranks over the political appeal of economic populism, anti-establishment campaigning and a tougher approach toward Israel. Leading figures in the party had split their support: progressive Senators Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren backed El-Sayed, while Stevens was endorsed by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer.
Schumer and U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, who chairs the party’s Senate campaign arm, congratulated El-Sayed in a statement.
Don't miss out on what's happening!
Stay in touch with breaking news, as it happens, conveniently in your email inbox. It's FREE!
“Democrats are united by a common purpose: putting a check on Donald Trump by defeating his Republican enablers and taking back the Senate,” they said.
Many Stevens supporters had argued that the centrist Democrat was the more electable candidate in November in a state Trump won twice in the last three presidential elections. But El-Sayed’s backers argued his campaign, which harnessed a groundswell of energy among younger voters, would increase turnout among the liberal base and first-time voters.
The contest to replace retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters had the highest turnout in the history of Michigan’s Democratic primaries, the state party chairman said.
Democrats’ uphill battle to win a Senate majority would be nearly impossible with a Michigan defeat in November. Even if Democrats manage to retain that seat and another competitive Democratic-held seat in Georgia, they would need to flip at least four Republican-held seats, including at least two in states that voted for Trump by double-digit margins.
Stevens congratulated El-Sayed on a “rigorous campaign” and said she would offer her support to help him defeat Rogers in November. At his press conference today, El-Sayed sought to smooth over the sharp divides that characterized the primary contest.
“Whatever differences that we might have had in the primary, they pale in comparison to what unifies us,” he said of Stevens.
Public opinion polls in recent days had suggested El-Sayed held a significant lead, but the results on Tuesday were far closer, a reminder that November’s race is likely to be closely contested.
Republicans wasted little time in attacking El-Sayed as “dangerous” and “radical” in digital advertising from the party’s Senate campaign arm and an allied super PAC.
“Great news for the Republican Party. El-Sayed, a Communist loser who hates Jews and Israel, is the projected winner in his race with the Socialist,” Trump said in a social media post.
In a statement, Rogers wrote, “The choice this November is simple: common sense or complete insanity.”
El-Sayed attacked Rogers as a Trump stooge today and accused Republicans of trying to use his faith and full name — Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed — to scare voters.
“My name is not the reason you can’t afford your groceries,” he said. “You know what is? Their B.S. policies.”
Tuesday’s result is likely to be scrutinized by prospective 2028 presidential contenders searching for a message to reconnect with voters after the party’s loss to Trump in 2024.
The race served as a battleground between progressives and moderates over support for Israel, an issue that has played out in primaries nationwide this year. But unlike contests in liberal bastions, this was a statewide race in a Midwestern swing state for a seat Democrats must win if they have any hopes of securing a Senate majority in November.
Stevens benefited from tens of millions of dollars in spending by a pro-Israel super PAC. But analysts said one significant factor in El-Sayed’s favor was that Michigan is home to some of the country’s largest Arab American communities, where hostility to Israel runs deep. El-Sayed would be the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate if he prevails in November.
During the primary campaign, El-Sayed pointed to the money backing Stevens’ campaign to bolster his grassroots appeal, arguing that he represented the working class against corporate interests.
El-Sayed today specifically reached out to Jewish voters, calling them his “sisters and brothers” and promising that he was committed to their safety.
Tuesday’s results are consistent with broader signs of a leftward shift among Democratic voters. A Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Tuesday found self-described liberal voters now make up 71% of Democrats, up from 55% in 2012.
The poll also found deep Democratic skepticism of U.S. support for Israel. Only 16% of Democrats backed continued military and economic aid to Israel, while 57% opposed it.
Additional reporting by Tim Reid.

sources.news_title: Progressive Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan Senate primary, testing Democrats’ midterm plan
sources.text:
Progressive Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan Senate primary, testing Democrats’ midterm plan
WASHINGTON (TNND) — Progressive Democrats notched another win in a key Midwest primary, as Abdul El-Sayed declared victory Wednesday morning in Michigan’s Democratic U.S. Senate primary after a closely watched contest against moderate Congresswoman Haley Stevens.
El-Sayed’s win came in a closer-than-expected vote count than polls predicted.
“What a race. You know, in the words of Muhammad Ali, we shook up the world," El-Sayed said in his Wednesday news conference.
El-Sayed has been riding a wave of progressive populism. While he is not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, he has likened himself to Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, both of whom endorsed him. But his tight margin has raised questions about whether he will need to move closer to the political center to strengthen his chances in November.
Sen. John Fetterman, D-Penn., has often criticized El-Sayed’s primary campaign and warned about the stakes in the general election on Wednesday.
“He had a very arrogant campaign and now today he just discovered that less than a majority of your state's only Democrats didn't even want you and vote for you. You came in around 48%. So you have a real situation as Democrats now that puts that seat in play," he told CNN.
El-Sayed acknowledged the divisions exposed by the primary but signaled an effort to broaden his coalition.
“Sometimes, you know, intra-family squabbles are the biggest ones,” he said. “We’re going to build a movement that reaches out to everybody.”
Republicans quickly seized on El-Sayed’s nomination. A Senate Leadership Fund ad attacked him as “Dangerously Radical." President Trump also weighed in on Truth Social, writing: “Great news for the Republican Party. El-Sayed, a Communist loser who hates Jews and Israel, is the projected winner in his race.”
Michigan Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers argued El-Sayed’s views are out of step with the state.
“This is really about the heart and soul of our country. I’ve never seen someone so radical, so extreme get nominated by a political party,” Rogers told Fox News Wednesday morning.
The next major test for progressives and democratic socialists is expected in Wisconsin’s race for governor, where the primary is next Tuesday. Democratic socialist candidate Francesca Hong is leading in polls over establishment-backed candidate David Crowley.

sources.news_title: Leftist El-Sayed defeats establishment Democrat in Michigan primary
sources.text:
Abdul El-Sayed's victory in Michigan comes as the Democratic party struggles to define itself in the Trump era.
Progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed won the Democratic party's Senate primary election in the US state of Michigan on Wednesday, highlighting key internal differences over the party's direction.
El-Sayed narrowly defeated moderate congresswoman Haley Stevens - who was backed by many of the party's senior establishment figures such as Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer - in what became an expensive proxy battle over the party's course.
He will now go on to face Republican Mike Rogers in November in a bid to keep the Senate seat with the Democrats. November's elections will determine the makeup of Congress for US President Donald Trump's remaining time in power.
"We won," El-Sayed wrote in a post on X. "I am so proud to be your Democratic nominee for US Senate. Let's win in November".
Both El-Sayed and Stevens - the latter of whom reportedly received tens of millions in backing from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee and affiliated groups - have moved quickly to champion party unity since the result was announced.
"I love Michigan and am so proud to have put up my hand to serve," Stevens wrote in a post on social media, adding that she had spoken with El-Sayed and had vowed to offer her "full support as we work to defeat Mike Rogers this November."
In response, El-Sayed thanked Stevens for running and said he looked forward to "uniting this fall."
"Because what unites us is so much bigger than what divides us," he added.
During his campaign, El-Sayed, who trained as a doctor before working in public health, focused on affordability and healthcare, pledging "Medicare for All" and saying he would work to "get money out of politics" and "put money in your pocket."
His campaign website says he is running for the US Senate as he believes "life in America shouldn’t be this hard."
"As your Senator, Abdul will fight to build a government that works for you, not Elon Musk, Donald Trump, or their billionaire friends," it added.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump called the result "great news for the Republican Party" while labelling El-Sayed as "a communist loser who hates Jews and Israel."

Michigan Democrats Urging Unity After El-Sayed Wins Close And Costly Primary
Abdul El-Sayed narrowly won Michigan’s Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate on Tuesday, defeating Rep. Haley Stevens in a major victory for the party’s progressive faction.
Stevens conceded in a congratulatory call to El-Sayed and immediately endorsed him after a bitter race that featured more than $60 million in spending on her behalf by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC). She joined other Democrats critical of the insurgent candidate’s position on Israel, Gaza, and the Mideast conflict -- including State Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who dropped out of the primary, and Sen. Elissa Slotkin – to call for unity in the general election against Republican nominee, former Rep. Mike Rogers.
“Congratulations to Abdul El-Sayed for winning the Democratic nomination for Senate.,” Slotkin posted on social media. “It’s been a long primary, but now it’s time to gear up to beat Mike Rogers (again) and win up and down the ticket. There is nothing more important than the mission of the next 90 days: uniting, keeping this seat blue, flipping the House and Senate, and providing a real check on President Trump.”
After noting that his upset victory “shook up the world,” El-Sayed reciprocated with an equally conciliatory tone, noting the “great conversation” with Stevens, whom he described as “one of the most committed public servants that you’ll ever meet…whatever differences that we might have had in the primary, they pale in comparison to what unifies us.”
In other Michigan primaries, Sunrise Movement co-founder Will Lawrence defeated former Ambassador Bridget Brink and former Navy Seal Matt Maasam to face GOP Rep. Tom Barrett in the state’s Seventh District, while State Rep. Donovan McKinney, a Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) member, beat incumbent Democratic Rep. Shri Thanedar in the 13th District. Observers regared McKinney’s victory over Thanedar as determined more by ethnic solidarity in a Detroit community – the winner is Black, the loser Asian-American – than ideology.
Aside from the DSA-flavored results in the Great Lakes State, there were few triumphs for the left. In Missouri, Rep. Wesley Bell overwhelmingly defeated former Rep. Cori Bush, a DSA stalwart supported by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) and highly critical of party leadership. Centrist or moderate candidates also won primaries in Virginia, while the more progressive candidate won the Democratic gubernatorial nomination in Kansas.
Missouri voters also rejected a Republican initiative to abolish the state income tax by a margin of four-to-one – a sign that middle America is in no mood to entertain the GOP’s oligarchic platform.

sources.news_title: Progressives score victory as El-Sayed wins Mich. Senate primary
sources.text:
Michigan
Progressives score victory as El-Sayed wins Mich. Senate primary
Democratic newcomer will face Rogers in November
Michigan held its primary on Tuesday, allowing the two major political parties to select their nominees to go head-to-head for the state’s U.S. Senate seat.
NBC News called the Democratic race early, giving the victory to physician Abdul El-Sayed over incumbent U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) in an extremely close primary. El-Sayed won 48.5 percent of the primary vote, with Stevens trailing by just one percentage point at 47.5 percent.
Both candidates have campagined on supporting the LGBTQ community through different avenues— for El-Sayed he focused on his past promoting HIV and PrEP funding and research. Stevens focused on her legislative history working to support transgender rights in the state.
This is a major win for progressive Democrats, who have been bearing the brunt of political attacks from President Donald Trump, the Republican Party, and centrist Democrats.
El-Sayed, a former health director in Detroit, ran his campaign largely on making life in the Great Lakes State more affordable amid rising costs. His policies include promoting “Medicare for All,” pushing health policy that targets the regressive efforts of the Trump-Vance administration that rolls back funding for both Women and LGBTQ people, minimizing the growing amount of money in politics, and he was very vocal in his criticism of Stevens for supporting aid to Israel. He was endorsed by two major progressives — U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio Cortez (D-N.Y.).
Stevens, the four-term congresswoman, is much closer to establishment Democrats on policy than El-Sayed.
During her time in the federal government, she has consistently supported the Equality Act, which would add sexual orientation and gender identity as protected classes under the Civil Rights Act of 1964. She has also emphasized supporting local manufacturing and lowering housing costs in the state.
She was named to Advocates for Trans Equality’s 118th Congressional Champions list for her pro-trans policies and was endorsed by establishment heavy hitters Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.).
The contentious race boiled down not only to Michigan affairs but also extended to international conflicts — namely Palestine. (South Africa has filed a case in the International Court of Justice in The Hague that accuses Israel of committing genocide in the Gaza Strip after Oct. 7.) This primary also acted as one of the first major races that pushed back against AIPAC, a lobbying group that works to promote pro-Israel candidates in U.S. elections. The group has been involved in domestic politics since 1954.
AIPAC devoted a massive amount of money to this race.
The Associated Press reported that the pro-Israel lobbying group spent more than $30 million on ads against El-Sayed because of his vocal denunciation of Israel and his continued criticism of its policies towards Palestine.
Michigan has a large Muslim and Arab American population, which could, in part, explain how El-Sayed was able to win.
The Republican side was far less competitive. Former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) ran unopposed and clinched the GOP nomination. He has consistently held anti-LGBTQ positions, going as far as voting multiple times for a federal constitutional amendment to ban same-sex marriage, voting against repealing the military’s “Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell” policy, and supporting efforts to directly target the attempted expansion of Title IX protections to include trans people.
El-Sayed will face off against Rogers in November for Michigan’s Senate seat — one that could have lasting impacts not only on the state’s politics but also on the Republicans’ narrow Senate majority and Trump’s political agenda.
