FBI thwarts Halloween terror plot targeting Mich. LGBTQ bars
Two suspects arrested with arsenal of weapons and tactical gear
By SARAH BRICKER HUNT | Two men are facing federal terrorism charges after allegedly planning a Halloween attack on LGBTQ+ bars in Ferndale, according to criminal complaints unsealed in federal court Nov. 3.
Momed Ali and Majed Mahmoud were arrested Oct. 31 by the FBI Joint Terrorism Task Force, which seized tactical gear, AR-15-style rifles, ammunition and other evidence from a Dearborn home and an Inkster storage unit. The 72-page complaint says the men, along with other co-conspirators including a minor, were inspired by Islamic State extremism and had scouted LGBTQ+ venues in Ferndale.
According to the New York Post, the suspects discussed copying the November 2015 coordinated ISIS attacks in Paris that killed 130 people. Surveillance footage from gun ranges shows Ali and Mahmoud practicing shooting with firearms, the Post reports.
The Paris attacks involved gunmen and suicide bombers who launched coordinated assaults on multiple locations throughout the French capital, including the Bataclan concert hall, the Stade de France stadium and several restaurants and cafes. The Bataclan attack was the deadliest, with attackers opening fire on concertgoers and taking hostages.
Multiple media outlets are reporting that the suspects discussed doing “the same thing as France” in reference to the Paris attacks, and mentioned potential attacks at clubs or discos similar to the 2016 Pulse nightclub shooting in Orlando that killed 49 people. Investigators discovered the suspects repeatedly referred to “pumpkins” in their conversations, which authorities identified as code for a Halloween-themed attack.
Ali purchased a shotgun, an AR-15-style rifle and a forced reset trigger that increases the rate of fire in semiautomatic weapons, according to federal documents. Mahmoud purchased an AR-15-style rifle and more than 1,600 rounds of ammunition.
In September, Ali, Mahmoud and the minor made multiple trips to Ferndale, traveling to an area on Woodward Avenue near East Nine Mile that includes numerous clubs and bars that attract members of the LGBTQ+ community, according to the FBI.
“Our American heroes prevented a terror attack,” U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi said on X following the arrests.
Both men have been charged with receiving and transferring guns and ammunition for terrorism and appeared in court Nov. 3. One defense attorney declined to comment, while another dismissed the allegations over the weekend as “hysteria” and “fearmongering.”
Popular Ferndale LGBTQ+ bar Soho posted to Facebook following news of the arrests.
“Soho is aware of recent reports concerning a potential threat directed toward businesses in our area. While it appears we were not targeted directly, we commend and deeply appreciate the swift and thorough response of local and federal law enforcement agencies in addressing the matter and ensuring the safety of our community,” the statement read.
The bar emphasized its confidence in local law enforcement. “We have always felt safe in the Ferndale community thanks to our close relationship with local law enforcement and their ongoing diligence and support.”
Soho’s statement also condemned targeting the LGBTQ+ community: “It is abhorrent that the LGBTQ+ community would ever be targeted — a community that stands for tolerance, unity, and peace.”
The bar confirmed its operations continue as normal and expressed gratitude for community support.
Meanwhile, Oakland County Executive Dave Coulter posted to Facebook, “Learning that Ferndale and the LGBTQ+ community were among the potential targets of a terrorist attack is disturbing. The pain of the Pulse Nightclub tragedy in Orlando nine years ago while I was serving as mayor of Ferndale is still deeply felt in the community. I’m grateful for the FBI, Oakland County Sheriff’s Office and other law enforcement for their diligence in seeking out and preventing what could have been another mass tragedy.”

Mich. lawmaker introduces resolution asking SCOTUS to overturn Obergefell
Far-right lawmaker stripped from committee assignments for extreme rhetoric
Republican Michigan state Rep. Josh Schriver introduced a resolution Tuesday asking the U.S. Supreme Court to overturn the 2015 Obergefell v. Hodges ruling, which established the nationwide right to same-sex marriage.
The lawmaker announced the move in a post on X, having previously shared a press release announcing plans to file the resolution, which argues that same-sex marriage is “at odds with the sanctity of marriage, the Michigan constitution, and principles upon which the country was established.”
The Resolution to Restore Marriage
✅ Introduced pic.twitter.com/UrX1zSdmUf
Schriver’s resolution has 12 co-sponsors, and similar measures have been introduced in other states including Idaho, Iowa, Montana, North Dakota, and South Dakota.
Responding to one of his posts advocating for the overturning of Obergefell in December, Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, a Democrat, said “any attempt to strip away gay marriage is wrong.”
Last month, the far-right politician was heard telling colleagues in leaked audio that gender affirming healthcare should be banned for minors as well as adults: “If we are going to stop this for anyone under 18, why not apply it for anyone over 18? It’s harmful across the board and that’s something we need to take into consideration in terms of the endgame.”
Earlier this month, he proposed banning birth control and reposted a message promoting the white nationalist Great Replacement conspiracy theory, the latter leading to Michigan House Minority Leader Matt Hall’s (R) decision to remove Schriver from his committee assignments.
Michigan
Mich. Democrats spar over LGBTQ-inclusive hate crimes law
Lawmakers disagree on just what kind of statute to pass
Michigan could soon become the latest state to pass an LGBTQ-inclusive hate crime law, but the state’s Democratic lawmakers disagree on just what kind of law they should pass.
Currently, Michigan’s Ethnic Intimidation Act only offers limited protections to victims of crime motivated by their “race, color, religion, gender, or national origin.” Bills proposed by Democratic lawmakers expand the list to include “actual or perceived race, color, religion, gender, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, ethnicity, physical or mental disability, age, national origin, or association or affiliation with any such individuals.”
Democratic Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and Attorney General Dana Nessel have both advocated for a hate crime law, but house and senate Democrats have each passed different hate crimes packages, and Nessel has blasted both as being too weak.
Under the house proposal that passed last year (House Bill 4474), a first offense would be punishable with a $2,000 fine, up to two years in prison, or both. Penalties double for a second offense, and if a gun or other dangerous weapons is involved, the maximum penalty is six years in prison and a fine of $7,500.
But that proposal stalled when it reached the senate, after far-right news outlets and Fox News reported misinformation that the bill only protected LGBTQ people and would make misgendering a trans person a crime. State Rep. Noah Arbit, the bill’s sponsor, was also made the subject of a recall effort, which ultimately failed.
Arbit submitted a new version of the bill (House Bill 5288) that added sections clarifying that misgendering a person, “intentionally or unintentionally” is not a hate crime, although the latest version (House Bill 5400) of the bill omits this language.
That bill has since stalled in a house committee, in part because the Democrats lost their house majority last November, when two Democratic representatives resigned after being elected mayors. The Democrats regained their house majority last night by winning two special elections.
Meanwhile, the senate passed a different package of hate crime bills sponsored by state Sen. Sylvia Santana (Senate Bill 600) in March that includes much lighter sentences, as well as a clause ensuring that misgendering a person is not a hate crime.
Under the senate bill, if the first offense is only a threat, it would be a misdemeanor punishable by one year in prison and up to $1,000 fine. A subsequent offense or first violent hate crime, including stalking, would be a felony that attracts double the punishment.
Multiple calls and emails from the Washington Blade to both Arbit and Santana requesting comment on the bills for this story went unanswered.
The attorney general’s office sent a statement to the Blade supporting stronger hate crime legislation.
“As a career prosecutor, [Nessel] has seen firsthand how the state’s weak Ethnic Intimidation Act (not updated since the late 1980’s) does not allow for meaningful law enforcement and court intervention before threats become violent and deadly, nor does it consider significant bases for bias. It is our hope that the legislature will pass robust, much-needed updates to this statute,” the statement says.
But Nessel, who has herself been the victim of racially motivated threats, has also blasted all of the bills presented by Democrats as not going far enough.
“Two years is nothing … Why not just give them a parking ticket?” Nessel told Bridge Michigan.
Nessel blames a bizarre alliance far-right and far-left forces that have doomed tougher laws.
“You have this confluence of forces on the far right … this insistence that the First Amendment protects this language, or that the Second Amendment protects the ability to possess firearms under almost any and all circumstances,” Nessel said. “But then you also have the far left that argues basically no one should go to jail or prison for any offense ever.”
The legislature did manage to pass an “institutional desecration” law last year that penalizes hate-motivated vandalism to churches, schools, museums, and community centers, and is LGBTQ-inclusive.
According to data from the U.S. Department of Justice, reported hate crime incidents have been skyrocketing, with attacks motivated by sexual orientation surging by 70 percent from 2020 to 2022, the last year for which data is available.
Twenty-two states, D.C., Puerto Rico, and the U.S. Virgin Islands have passed LGBTQ-inclusive hate crime laws. Another 11 states have hate crime laws that include protections for “sexual orientation” but not “gender identity.”
Michigan Democrats have advanced several key LGBTQ rights priorities since they took unified control of the legislature in 2023. A long-stalled comprehensive anti-discrimination law was passed last year, as did a conversion therapy ban. Last month the legislature updated family law to make surrogacy easier for all couples, including same-sex couples.
A bill to ban the “gay panic” defense has passed the state house and was due for a Senate committee hearing on Wednesday.

sources.text:
Abdul El-Sayed addresses supporters at his election night event at the Majestic Theatre in Detroit, Michigan, on August 4, 2026. (Photo by JEFF KOWALSKY/AFP via Getty Images)

The left-wing goofball Democrats have nominated as their Senate candidate in Michigan has a bevy of enthusiastic cheerleaders, and it should surprise absolutely no one to learn that a great many of those cheerleaders are wearing stupid red hats.
Republicans ought to be running scared, but Democrats are running Abdul El-Sayed, who has bested normie Democrat Haley Stevens in the Michigan primary.
Kevin D. Williamson is national correspondent at The Dispatch and is based in Virginia. Prior to joining the company in 2022, he spent 15 years as a writer and editor at National Review, worked as the theater critic at the New Criterion, and had a long career in local newspapers. He is also a writer in residence at the Competitive Enterprise Institute. When Kevin is not reporting on the world outside Washington for his Wanderland newsletter, you can find him at the rifle range or reading a book about literally almost anything other than politics.

sources.news_title: Abdul El-Sayed wins U.S. Senate primary in Michigan
sources.text:
Abdul El-Sayed, former Wayne County health director, won the Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate primary Wednesday, Aug. 5, defeating U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Birmingham. With 99% of precincts reporting as of 9:54 a.m. on Aug. 5, El-Sayed earned 48.5% of the vote to Stevens’ 47.5%.
In his victory speech Wednesday morning, El-Sayed told the crowd the tensions they observed during the primary are minor compared to what Democrats will face in the general election.
“I know it was a bitter end to this very long primary,” El-Sayed said. “Whatever differences that we might’ve had in the primary, they pale comparison to what unifies us: a recognition that so long as we want to keep our democracy, that democracy better be working for people and all of us have to come together to make sure that we never let Mike Rogers see the inside of the U.S. Senate.”
Following the campaign suspension of state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, D-Royal Oak, on July 5, El-Sayed and Stevens engaged in a contentious race for the party’s nomination. El-Sayed, a progressive, campaigned on expanding healthcare access through Medicare for All, supporting working-class Michiganders and reducing the influence of money in politics. El-Sayed built his campaign through grassroots donations and emphasized his record of refusing contributions from corporate political action committees.
El-Sayed was endorsed by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt.; U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-NY; and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.
Stevens conceded the race on Aug. 5. In a press release, she congratulated El-Sayed and offered her full support.
“I want to congratulate Abdul El-Sayed on winning the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate,” Stevens said. “He is a doctor, a community health official, a Rhodes Scholar and a dedicated Michigander. I am proud to offer my support as he takes on Mike Rogers in the general election.”
El-Sayed will face former Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers in November’s general election to succeed retiring Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich.
Summer News Editor Zahra Kagal can be reached at zkagal@umich.edu.

sources.news_title: Michigan’s primary reckoning for the Democrats
sources.text:
No congressional candidate in Democratic history ever had as much outside money dumped on them in one primary as Abdul El-Sayed. But El-Sayed has now survived the onslaught in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary. Barely. The Bernie Sanders-endorsed champion of Medicare for All defeated Rep. Haley Stevens by about a 1-point margin on Tuesday, according to the Associated Press.
The dynamics of the election in Michigan were not new. Like in other recent primaries spanning from Manhattan to California’s Central Valley, a populist outsider ran against an establishment Democrat backed by millions of dollars of super PAC money—much of it from AIPAC allies that aim to keep critics of Israel out of Congress. What sets El-Sayed’s victory apart are the stakes and the scale of the effort to defeat him.
Democrats need to keep the Michigan seat that Sen. Gary Peters is retiring from if they hope to take back the Senate. To do that, they now have to defeat former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers in a swing state that has gone for Donald Trump twice, and where Rogers barely lost to Sen. Elissa Slotkin in 2024. It is far from certain that El-Sayed will prevail in November—just as there were no guarantees that Stevens would have won.
After a polarizing primary, El-Sayed has just three months to consolidate Democratic support and make his case to independent voters. El-Sayed began that work in an election-night speech before the race was called. “However much we might disagree with our Democratic opponent, there is so much more that unites us than divides us,” he told supporters. “Tomorrow, we begin to mend fences.” In a Wednesday speech after the race was called, El-Sayed said he had a “great conversation” with Stevens, and called his former opponent “one of the most committed public servants that you’ll ever meet.”
El-Sayed’s margin of victory was much smaller than expected heading into Tuesday: Polls tracked by the New York Times showed El-Sayed leading by double digits in eight surveys in a row. Instead, the results closely resembled Michighan’s 2016 presidential primary, when Sanders defeated Hillary Clinton by 1.4 points. As of Wednesday morning, El-Sayed is leading Stevens by an even smaller margin.
Stevens, who was endorsed by Peters and Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, was the favorite of much of the Democratic establishment including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer. But the results on Tuesday were yet another reminder this primary season that much of the Democratic base wants to go in a different direction than party leadership.
The general election will provide a rare chance to help answer a question that is often litigated online but rarely tested offline: Can progressive populists win a swing state like Michigan? A loss by El-Sayed, on the other hand, would likely lead to many warnings from moderate Democrats about what kind of candidate the party should nominate for president in 2028. Republicans have not won a US Senate election in Michigan in more than three decades; the seat El-Sayed is running for has been held by Democrats since 1979—five years before the 41-year-old candidate was born.
El-Sayed’s victory was not the only win for the left wing of the Democratic party in Michigan on Tuesday. In Michigan’s 7th congressional district, which is centered around Lansing, Will Lawrence pulled off a shocking win. The 7th district is a tossup seat held by Republican Rep. Tom Barrett that Democrats hope to flip in November. To do that, Democratic primary voters had two traditionally safe picks: Bridget Brink, who resigned as the US Ambassador to Ukraine soon after Trump returned to office, and Matt Maasdam, a former Navy SEAL who carried the so-called nuclear football for Barack Obama.
Brink and Maaasdam ended up roughly tied with each getting about 28 percent of votes on Tuesday. That may have allowed Lawrence, a millennial founder of the Sunrise Movement who capitalized on local opposition to AI data centers, to prevail with only about 43 percent of the vote. Many Democratic strategists like David Axelrod believe the seat will now be harder to flip in November.
In the Detroit area, Rep. Shri Thanedar narrowly lost his primary to state Rep. Donavan McKinney, who was endorsed by Sanders, El-Sayed, and the Democratic Socialists of America. Thanedar was a notably weak incumbent who has irritated fellow Democrats in Congress. As a largely self-funding Indian American multimillionaire, he was also an unusual fit in a district where more than 40 percent of residents are Black and more than 40 percent of children live in poverty.
The race between El-Sayed and Stevens was one of the most closely watched primaries this year, but it did not attract record spending because super PACs wanted Democrats to control the Senate. About half of the roughly $60 million spent by outside groups came from the AIPAC-backed United Democracy Project, which has worked to elect pro-Israel members of both parties. The Michigan race was UDP’s top priority; the group spent twice as much as it ever had in a single race. (Overall, super PACS favored Stevens by a more than 10-to-1 margin.)
The total amount put into the race by pro-Israel groups may be even higher: A recently formed dark money group called the Center for Democratic Priorities spent a reported $6.5 million backing Stevens, whose views on Israel are captured by her claim that the country “comes to me in my dreams.” As I reported last week, little is known about the Center for Democratic Priorities beyond the fact that its low-profile director apparently served in a similar role for an AIPAC-backed super PAC in Michigan in 2024.
El-Sayed, a doctor and public health expert who served as the health director for Wayne County, is an unapologetic critic of Israel who has accused the nation of committing genocide in Gaza. If elected, he could quickly become Israel’s most vocal opponent in the Senate—as well as one of its most charismatic members. He would also be the first Muslim senator in US history and one of the youngest members of the chamber. (El-Sayed is younger than all but two sitting senators.)
El-Sayed’s victory—along with those of House candidates like Daniel Biss earlier this year in Illinois—is a clear sign to people running for Congress across the country that pro-Israel spending can be successfully resisted. As El-Sayed told my colleague Najib Aminy before the primary, “ If I prove that you can win statewide, taking on AIPAC and winning, that is catastrophic because of what it says about the future of the party. It is existential to oppose it. I think this race is going to change a lot of minds, and it’s going to scramble a lot of expectations.”
On the campaign trail, El-Sayed was highly effective at depicting AIPAC and the corporations spending against him as villains trying to buy the Senate race. He returned to that theme repeatedly in ads, speeches, and his campaign’s call and response slogan: “Money out of politics. Money in your pocket. Medicare for All.” The tens of millions of dollars in television ads super PACs spent against him presumably cost him the support of some voters, but it also gave him one of his most powerful talking points.
In Illinois this March, AIPAC-backed groups spent about $7 million trying to defeat Biss, the mayor of Evanston. (Biss, who is Jewish, is the descendant of Holocaust survivors and has noted that some of his relatives live in Israel.) Like El-Sayed, Biss capitalized on the spending by AIPAC, which has supported many election deniers and Trump supporters. He won narrowly, while Kat Abughazaleh—who is further left than Biss—came in second. (Abughazaleh is a former Mother Jones contributor.) AIPAC’s pick, Laura Fine, came in third with only 20 percent of the vote. After he won, Biss wrote an op-ed for The Nation under the headline: “I Was AIPAC’s Number 1 Target—and I Beat Them. Here’s How to Do It.”
Still, AIPAC has not yet suffered a total defeat in Michigan. Two-thirds of the money UDP spent in the primary went to attacking El-Sayed—who it misleadingly accused in one ad of “sexist attacks” against women—rather than promoting Stevens. That spending, along with whatever UDP and its allies may put in for the general election, could make it easier for Rogers to defeat El-Sayed in November. If that happens, AIPAC will almost certainly try to take some of the credit.
But for now El-Sayed can claim victory. In his Wednesday speech, El-Sayed pointed out that he and his supporters had taken on a “machine” and record-breaking outside spending. “You’re not supposed to be able to beat that,” he said. “What we showed is that the power of our many is greater than the power of their money.”

sources.news_title: El-Sayed Won Narrowly but Cori Bush Lost Badly in Missouri
sources.text:
Abdul El-Sayed's victory over moderate Rep. Haley Stevens is taking up all the oxygen in the room today but you don't have to look very far for evidence that last night was not the resounding win the far left had been hoping for. Start with El-Sayed himself. Going into election day his win was considered a given and some were seeing a potential double-digit blowout, but that didn't happen.
Coming into Election Day, Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary was widely expected. A blowout seemed possible. Instead, his victory margin will likely be less than two percentage points...
El-Sayed did not deliver a resounding defeat to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, Governor Gretchen Whitmer, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, and other parts of the center-left Democratic establishment who backed Stevens, as his supporters hoped. The election returns suggest that El-Sayed struggled with rural voters, in particular. Looking forward to the general election, that data has to worry Democrats, who tend to lose elections to Republicans because they are blown out in small towns.
That was written sometime early this morning by Perry Bacon. If you actually look at the vote total for El-Sayed, it's currently a lot closer than 2 points. With greater than 95 percent of votes in, El-Sayed is at 48.48 percent and Stevens is at 47.51 percent. So it's less than a 1 percent gap, or about 15,000 votes out of more than 1.5 million cast.
A win is a win and El-Sayed can correctly claim that he was heavily outspent in the most expensive Senate primary in history. Still, this was the opposite of a blowout. If anything he barely eked out a victory. If the results had been reversed would progressive think their views had been discredited by a 1 percent loss? I don't think so.
Democrats now also have to wonder if El-Sayed can deliver in the general. El-Sayed is predicting a seven-point victory, but Sabato's Crystal Ball thinks it's likely he'll underperform a more moderate Democrat.
Either Stevens or El-Sayed would have had work to do to bring the party together, and either could have faced problems with key voting blocs. For instance, El-Sayed did quite well in heavily Arab-American pockets of the Detroit area, while Stevens appears to have done well in some significantly Jewish pockets elsewhere in greater Detroit, reflecting, among other things, their different positions on the conflict between the Israelis and the Palestinians. It’s easy to envision El-Sayed losing ground amidst usually-Democratic Jewish voters: We saw a similar dynamic a few months ago in a special House election in New Jersey, when progressive Israel critic Rep. Analilia Mejia (D, NJ-11) performed fine overall but definitely underperformed among Jewish voters in her district, per a New Jersey Globe analysis. We may take a deeper look at the Michigan Senate primary in a future issue once the results are more firmly settled.
This November, we suspect El-Sayed ultimately will underperform what a more generic Democrat would have gotten, although of course there is no such thing as a “generic Democrat.” However, underperforming does not necessarily mean losing. Democrats just need to hope the broader environment helps paper over their problems in this race.
Could he win? Definitely. But predicting another blowout after last night's squeaker seems like a bad bet.
Meanwhile in Missouri, former Squad and current DSA member Cori Bush attempted to return to Congress and got squashed by Wesley Bell, a pro-Israel moderate.
Representative Wesley Bell of Missouri, a moderate pro-Israel Democrat, fended off a primary challenge from a former congresswoman and democratic socialist on Tuesday, according to The Associated Press, in a loss for the surging socialist movement.
Former Representative Cori Bush, Mr. Bell’s predecessor in the St. Louis district, had hoped to add to the high-profile victories that socialists have notched over Democratic incumbents this year in New York City and Denver.
But Mr. Bell, a former prosecuting attorney and city councilman, held on...
The loss was a setback for democratic socialists...
So it was a very mixed bag for both factions of the Democrat Party last night but I'm not sure that's coming across in most of the coverage of El-Sayed's win.

sources.news_title: A Michigan victory for the Left
Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan's Democratic Senate primary, U.S. media outlets project
Michigan Senate Race's Winners and Losers: AIPAC, CAIR, Whitmer
sources.text:
The DC Brief
Twice A Week
Making sense of what matters most in Washington.
Abdul El-Sayed, a rabble-rousing populist and former public health official, just barely eked out a primary victory Tuesday in Michigan over a centrist rival who was the pick of Washington Democrats to keep a must-hold Senate seat. It was a bad night for the Democratic Establishment, who see the outcome as a major setback to their party's dreams of clawing back control of the Upper Chamber for the final two years of President Donald Trump’s presidency.
But El-Sayed’s squeaker win was not what he or his allies were forecasting as recently as Tuesday morning. For weeks, most polling indicated Michiganders were strongly trending toward El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim Senator if he prevails in November over former Rep. Mike Rogers. Even still, this outcome was not something many foresaw as recently as last year. El-Sayed managed to captured the broad, bipartisan frustration that established leaders are not hearing voters’ concerns.
Strategists are still looking at the data but some top-line folks clearly came out winners—and others losers.
WINNER: El-Sayed
Even if he fell short of expectations, the podcasting populist still had the primary outcome he was counting on. El-Sayed has been planning this moment for a while. He ran for Governor in 2018, another wave year for Democrats, but lost his primary to the current Governor, Gretchen Whitmer.
As TIME’s Nik Popli reported from Michigan earlier this summer, El-Sayed is using his do-over to run against both parties at the same time. He blasted the wealthy, lashed the corporations, and decried the whole system as rigged. In many ways, he was channeling a lefty version of Trump.
El-Sayed, whose surprising rise prompted state senator Mallory McMorrow to suspend her campaign before voting began, is on the cusp of being the latest avatar for the brand of progressive and populist politics promoted by supporters like Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez or Sen. Bernie Sanders. That instant credibility may boost El-Sayed nationally, but risks turning off voters in Michigan, which is precisely what Rep. Haley Stevens warned of during her unsuccessful primary against El-Sayed.
LOSER: Stevens
She had almost every on-paper advantage: a seat in the House, proximity to donors and advocacy groups, a policy wonk’s eye, and an affable every-woman folksiness. But CVs don’t always translate to votes.
Stevens, a former campaign aide to Hillary Clinton and Obama, couldn’t translate her natural political instinct as an operative to convincing a statewide electorate that she deserved their votes. Sometimes, her comments seemed to wander. Her mind moved faster than her lips. And her critics—in not-so-subtly-gendered language—mocked her accent.
Her defeat Tuesday cuts short her time in public office. At least for now.
WINNERS: Populists
The frustrations with the status quo helped El-Sayed, for sure. But it also reflects the true sentiment of how Americans are feeling right now. According to Gallup polling, just 23% of Americans are satisfied with how things are going. With that level of angst, it’s little wonder that Michiganders opted to go with someone calling for remaking the whole system over an incrementalist and pragmatist who pitched herself as someone who can fix the system from the inside.
But, again, this result in Michigan may be a complicating factor as Democrats try to figure out their next leaders. The 2028 presidential primary is already shaping up as yet another soul-searching moment for Democrats, pitting the disparate ideological camps and competing personalities against each other. But winning primaries, even in swing states, doesn’t necessarily mean much when it comes to assembling a broader coalition. As one Democratic strategist told me before polls closed on Tuesday, the night “gives 2028-ers the wrong idea about everything.”
LOSER: AIPAC
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee became an unlikely flashpoint in Michigan. The pro-Israel group has been spending big for several cycles to support allies of Israel and counter increasingly anti-Israel sentiments in the Democratic Party. El-Sayed’s views there left little doubt which side AIPAC would be supporting.
The group spent a record $30 million to help Stevens, an outlay that fed El-Sayed’s characterization of his opponent as little more than a mouthpiece for her deep-pocketed supporters.
While the group is nominally focused on promoting the relationship between the United States and Israel, its advertising focus seldom mentions Israel. In fact, a New York Times analysis of AIPAC’s ads since April of 2022 found 109 ads. Just six mention Israel.
WINNER: CAIR
Michigan is home to one of the nation’s largest and most politically engaged Muslim communities. And one of its most important civic engagement groups, the Council on American-Islamic Relations, or CAIR, pulled a last-minute flex in the final hours of the race.
On the eve of Tuesday’s primary, CAIR began a robocall effort that reached more than 13,000 Muslim Michigan households, where roughly 29,000 mail-in ballot recipients are registered. Another 19,000 low-propensity Muslim voters got calls.
Given El-Sayed’s narrow win, that push looks even more impactful, allowing the country’s largest Muslim civil rights groups to more firmly showcase its power in Michigan, as it finds itself targeted on multiple fronts in some red states.
LOSERS: Establishment Democrats
Stevens was the undisputed choice of the Democratic Establishment. She was a swing state Democrat who previously won on the same ballot as Trump. She had been through the vetting, could raise money, and seemed a practical choice to hold the seat of retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters.
But Washington insiders’ efforts to help Stevens actually worked against her in a year when Democratic voters were more aligned with El-Sayed’s contempt for the Establishment. That anger found a vessel in El-Sayed and a target in Stevens. Even though Democratic leaders didn't get their way, that doesn't mean they're giving up on Michigan. Quickly after El-Sayed's primary victory became clear, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair, released a statement of support. “We look forward to working with Abdul and Democrats across Michigan to win this seat in November," they said.
ACTING LIKE WINNERS: Republicans
Senate Republicans have been rightly nervous about holding their narrow majority. El-Sayed’s nomination takes away some of that stress. While Michigan is expected to be a close race, Republicans were a lot more eager to run against El-Sayed than Stevens. Republicans are ready with plenty of fodder from El-Sayed’s past comments; his unrelenting criticism of Israel will be wielded to sway Michigan’s Jewish voters to either back Rogers or sit the race out.
LOSER: Whitmer
For the longest time, the state’s popular Governor insisted she was not getting involved in the primary. She had defeated El-Sayed to win the nomination in 2018 and has led a diverse state party through some tough family fights, especially when it came to the 2024 presidential race. Whitmer, who is term-limited and will leave office after November’s elections, is often mentioned as a 2028 contender. She has, with varying levels of intensity, said she is not chasing the nomination, but clearly isn’t ready to end her political career.
So it left a lot of watchers surprised when, on July 24, Whitmer endorsed Stevens. It was a move that another Michigan Democrat and oft-mentioned 2028 contender, Sen. Elissa Slotkin, did not make. Whitmer quickly became one of Stevens’ better surrogates, making the argument in a clearer way than the candidate herself did.
As the folks in Whitmer’s lane look around, they may be questioning if there is a lane for their likes heading into 2028, or if a principled stand for pragmatism is truly a non-starter.

sources.news_title: Abdul El-Sayed Wins Michigan Senate Primary as LGBTQ+ Candidates Make Historic Gains
sources.text:
Abdul El-Sayed Wins Michigan Senate Primary as LGBTQ+ Candidates Make Historic Gains
Physician's narrow victory sets up competitive fall race; Joanna Whaley poised to become Michigan's first trans state representative
Dr. Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan's closely watched U.S. Senate Democratic primary Tuesday with 49% of the vote, narrowly edging out moderate U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens' 47% in a race that became a proxy battle between the party's progressive and establishment wings. El-Sayed, backed by U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Rashida Tlaib, will face Republican former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers in November as the Democratic nominee to fill the seat vacated by retiring Sen. Gary Peters.
The Senate primary captured national attention as a test of progressive power within the Democratic Party. Stevens, who received backing from national Democratic leadership and AIPAC as well as a last-minute endorsement from Gov. Whitmer, mounted a spirited challenge that left the race close enough that several major news outlets continued reporting it as "too close to call" as ballots were still being counted Wednesday morning.
"I want the community to know that I intend to be a lion for rights. When somebody's coming for you, I intend to stand in the cut to protect you," El-Sayed told Pride Source ahead of the primary, promising unequivocal support for LGBTQ+ rights even when unpopular. His public health background informs his commitment to protecting trans health specifically. "The Trump administration has tried to weaponize government against LGBTQ+ folks in a space that I know really well, which is health. My hope is to use my specific expertise in the Senate to make sure that I'm undoing a lot of the worst things that the Trump administration has done when it comes to targeting LGBTQ+ health."
In the governor's race, Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson dominated the Democratic primary with 83%of the vote, setting up a general election matchup against Republican U.S. Rep. John James, who edged businessman Perry Johnson to win the GOP primary with 50% of the vote. Speaking to Pride Source ahead of the primary, Benson emphasized her record protecting LGBTQ+ rights at the state level. "To me, this is about building a state where every person feels safe, seen, supported and welcome. That's the Michigan I believe in, and that's the Michigan I'm fighting for," she told Pride Source.
In Michigan's U.S. House District 11, State Sen. Jeremy Moss won his Democratic primary with 49.2% of the vote, positioning him to likely succeed Stevens in a heavily Democratic seat covering the Oakland County communities of Auburn Hills, Ferndale, Pontiac, Royal Oak, Troy, West Bloomfield Township and Wixom. Moss, Michigan's first openly gay state senator, has been a key voice on LGBTQ+ rights in the state legislature.
Perhaps the night's most significant result for LGBTQ+ representation came at the state level, where Joanna Whaley, a trans woman from Allen Park, won the House District 2 Democratic primary with 66% of the vote, defeating former state lawmaker Frank Liberati. The Downriver district includes Lincoln Park, Melvindale and Southgate. If she prevails in November's general election in the safely Democratic district, Whaley will become Michigan's first openly transgender state House member. "To all the volunteers and supporters, let's take this energy into the general election and bring focused leadership to our community," Whaley wrote after her victory.
Liberati had filed a legal challenge in May alleging Whaley violated campaign law by not listing her deadname on her affidavit, but Wayne County Clerk Cathy M. Garrett rejected the complaint. Whaley said the attack only strengthened her campaign. "Every time Frank tries to come after me, our campaign just gets stronger," she told Pride Source earlier this year. "I'm just here trying to talk about getting our utility bills down and getting single-payer health care in the state of Michigan."
Seven LGBTQ+ candidates win state office races
Tuesday's primary delivered victories for seven of 12 featured LGBTQ+ candidates running for state office, suggesting growing political power for the community even as several challengers in competitive races fell short.
Jason Hoskins decisively won the Democratic primary for State Senate District 7, covering Oakland County communities including Southfield, with 28,886 votes, 57% of the total. Hoskins, an incumbent state representative and the first LGBTQ+ person of color elected to Michigan's state legislature, enters the general election favored to expand LGBTQ+ representation at the upper chamber level.
Sitting LGBTQ+ state representatives capitalized on name recognition and constituent service records. Mike McFall won House District 14, a Detroit-area seat, with 71% of the vote. Laurie Pohutsky, Michigan's first openly queer female lawmaker, dominated her House District 17 primary in Oakland County with 99.26%of the vote. Emily Dievendorf, the state's first openly nonbinary state representative, ran unopposed in House District 77, covering Lansing and surrounding Ingham County areas, and won with 1,222 votes.
Chris Gilmer-Hill claimed 49% in House District 8's Democratic primary in Macomb County, edging out incumbent Helena Scott (43%) and two other candidates. Jenn Cornell advanced her political career, securing 56% (5,110 votes) in Ann Arbor's City Council Ward 5 race against challenger Greg Monroe. Elisabeth Dery secured 41% in Oakland County's three-way Probate Court Judge race, outpacing Jessica Ann Hallmark (38%) and Sheila Calvary Worthy-Williams (21%) to become the Democratic nominee for the bench.
Other LGBTQ+ candidates fell short in Tuesday's primary. Amanda Treppa, a bisexual candidate running for State Senate District 10 with backing from Equality Michigan Action Network and Planned Parenthood Advocates of Michigan, did not advance despite endorsements from outgoing State Sen. Mallory McMorrow. Brendan Johnson, running for State Senate District 9 in Oakland County, also failed to win his race. J. Aaron "Lola" Bailey, a trans candidate and democratic socialist in House District 92, lost to Hanna Demerath. Toni Mua's campaign for House District 9 in Detroit similarly came up short.
The August primary reshuffled Michigan's political deck. November will determine which candidates advance to the state House, Senate and Congress, and whether LGBTQ+ political power continues its upward trajectory. Follow our coverage to keep up on LGBTQ+ candidates and issues impacting this race, and check vote411.org for your sample ballot and voting information.

sources.news_title: Abdul El-Sayed, Progressive Senate Candidate, Defeats Centrist Haley Stevens In Michigan Democratic Primary
sources.text:
One of the most high-profile primary races of the 2026 midterm cycle played out in Michigan, with a progressive Democratic Senate candidate defeating a centrist, establishment-backed Democratic opponent. Now, attention turns to the general election, in which Democrats have to be concerned about healing intraparty divisions in order to compete with the GOP for a pivotal Senate seat.
Progressive public health expert defeats establishment candidate despite outside spending
Early Wednesday morning, NBC News projected Abdul El-Sayed as the winner of Michigan’s Democratic primary for the state’s open U.S. Senate seat, defeating Democrat Rep. Haley Stevens. The race was one of the most highly-publicized primary elections in the country, with tens of millions of dollars pouring into the race. The election was presented as a contest between the progressive El-Sayed, a physician and epidemiologist who previously served as a public health official and unsuccessfully ran for governor of Michigan in 2018, against the centrist Stevens, who has represented Michigan’s 11th District since 2019. El-Sayed’s victory is significant given that Stevens had the backing of a number of established Democratic figures, including Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, outgoing Democratic Sen. Gary Peters and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-New York). Stevens and her allies also enjoyed a nearly 9-to-1 advertising spending advantage over El-Sayed, with nearly $65 million spent in advertising for Stevens against El-Sayed.
Divisions over domestic and foreign policies
El-Sayed leaned on his progressive policies and backers. The doctor and former public health chief for Detroit promoted domestic policies including “Medicare for All.” El-Sayed’s progressive campaign comes as other left-leaning candidates, many associated with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), have won key Democratic primaries across the country. El-Sayed is not a member of the DSA and was not formally endorsed by the organization, but popular DSA figures, including Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, campaigned for him heavily. El-Sayed has also been highly critical of Israel, accusing the country of committing genocide in Gaza, and he accused Stevens of being too close to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), the influential pro-Israel lobbying group that spent tens of millions of dollars to support Stevens in the race. The criticisms of AIPAC and Israel’s war in Gaza resonated in Michigan, which has large Arab and Muslim populations; support for the war is thought to have hurt Vice President Kamala Harris in Michigan during the 2024 presidential race.
Task ahead: unifying Democrats, defeating Republicans
With the primary concluded, attention turns to November’s general election. The Michigan seat is seen as one that Democrats must hold as part of their difficult but possible quest to retake control of the Senate from Republicans. El-Sayed will now face Trump-backed Republican Mike Rogers, a former U.S. congressman who won Tuesday’s Republican primary unopposed. Stevens’ campaign had presented her as the more competitive candidate for the general election, and Republicans fed into that narrative by indicating that they preferred to face El-Sayed in November. President Trump told Fox News, “Based on the polls, he’ll do much better against Abdul than he’s going to do against the congresswoman.” El-Sayed and his supporters, meanwhile, have argued that the progressive message was resonating more with voters than the establishment. However, given the divisive nature of the primary race and the personal attacks made by each candidate’s camp against one another, unifying Democrats around El-Sayed may prove challenging. The newly minted Democratic nominee acknowledged the task ahead for him, telling CBS Mornings Wednesday that “there’s a lot of healing to do after a hard-fought primary like this.”
Democrats are facing twin challenges heading into November: attempting to unify the progressive and centrist wings within the party while also seeking to outcompete Republicans in key congressional races. El-Sayed now faces those tasks in Michigan, and his performance between now and November will be a major test of the progressive surge within the Democratic Party and how much the left-leaning appeal will resonate with voters.

sources.news_title: What El-Sayed’s Michigan Win Reveals About Black Voters and Democrats
sources.text:
Abdul El-Sayed is projected to win Michigan’s Democratic primary for a U.S. Senate seat, concluding a bruising contest that became a national proxy battle over where the party is headed and how Black voters might shape that future.
While many observers framed the race around whether El-Sayed could break through with Black Michiganders — who account for about 20% of the state’s Democratic primary electorate — Kermit Williams said what he saw on the ground was more complex.
Williams, the political director of the Oakland Forward Action Fund, told Capital B that he noticed a clear generational divide throughout the campaign. Many older Black Michiganders, he said, embraced U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens’ message of experience, while younger and more progressive Black Michiganders were fueled by El-Sayed’s calls for deep reforms.
“I think that older and more established Black voters believe in incremental change,” said Williams, who spent Election Day conducting election protection efforts at polling stations. “And when you start talking about younger Black voters, they want to see a whole new system. I think that El-Sayed has kind of tapped into that energy.”
With the primary decided, attention is shifting to what the results mean. That focus will include how Black Michiganders voted, whether Democrats can unite their base, and what lies ahead for El-Sayed in November. That contest will have national implications. Senate control runs through the swing state, so reconciling tensions within their diverse coalition and winning the seat is vital if Democrats hope to secure a majority in the upper chamber and push back against the Trump administration’s policies.
A former Detroit public health official, El-Sayed offered a progressive platform, calling for policies such as Medicare for All. Stevens presented herself as a pragmatic Democrat, elevating her congressional record, her support for manufacturing jobs, and her belief that she could win in the general election.
El-Sayed is seen as further testing the resonance of progressive messaging after wins by Mayor Zohran Mamdani and others over the past year. He isn’t a member of the Democratic Socialists of America.
What did the outcome reveal about Black Michiganders’ behavior?
The race underscored that they’re not monolithic.
For weeks, national conversations asked whether El-Sayed could make inroads with Black Michiganders, often treating them as a single constituency. But Williams said that the contest was more like a debate among Black Democratic voters about what kind of party they want.
“I think that it really seemed like a microcosm of the Hillary Clinton versus Bernie Sanders debate,” he said, referring to the 2016 primary matchup that similarly pitted an establishment candidate against a progressive challenger. “You had one candidate who proved herself as an elected official, and then you had another candidate who was moving with bold ideas.”
His observation aligned with what some Black Michiganders said in the runup to the election.
“[Stevens] was on the team that helped save our state when Obama was president. She was right there on the forefront,” Kathie House Vinson, a retired college administrator based in Detroit, told CNN, referring to how Stevens previously served as chief of staff to President Barack Obama’s task force on the auto industry.
“I think in my heart of hearts that [El-Sayed] is a good candidate,” she added, “but Haley has the track record, and I know what she’s done for me.”
El-Sayed enjoyed support from progressive leaders such as U.S. Reps. Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts, Summer Lee of Pennsylvania, and Maxwell Frost of Florida. Stevens was backed by much of the Democratic establishment, including U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina, the kingmaker credited with saving former President Joe Biden’s 2020 White House bid.
Like Williams, Vincent Hutchings, a political scientist at the University of Michigan, also questioned some of the narratives around Black voter behavior. He pushed back against the notion that Black Michiganders formed a single political bloc in the primary, suggesting instead that there was an electorate with an array of ideological priorities and strategic considerations.
“It’s a mistake to think, ‘Oh, well, looks like there’s a divide in the Democratic Party between the ‘progressive forces’ and the ‘establishment forces,’ and it looks like Black voters are on the side of the quote-unquote ‘establishment,’” he told The New Republic.
“That’s an easy story to tell. I get why people tell it,” Hutchings added. “It seems to map onto reality, but only until you scratch a little beneath the surface.”
Can El-Sayed reunite Black Michiganders post-primary?
Williams believes that it’s possible — with some work.
Over the course of the campaign, he said, outside groups and national figures turned the race into a symbolic fight over the party’s future direction. Now, he argued, local Democrats must bridge these schisms.
“What I’ve been working on is trying to figure out how we pull people together after Tuesday,” Williams said. “There have been some divides in this election, and I feel like there are lots of people outside of Michigan who have weighed in on the race and made it more national than local.”
He argued that Democrats share a common objective, regardless of where they landed in the primary, and that they must keep their eye on the ball.
“Ultimately, it comes down to people turning out in November in order for us to have a senator who supports where we stand on issues,” Williams said.
Black Michiganders will be essential to El-Sayed’s effort to win in November, according to Christopher Towler, a political scientist at California State University, Sacramento, and the director of the Black Voter Project.
“You need to really focus on protecting the Black community from [President Donald] Trump and MAGA Republicans and the GOP’s agenda, which has become more and more anti-Black and focused on rolling back the racial progress that this country has made since the civil rights era,” he told The New Republic.
He added that Black voters are often skeptical of major policy promises and suggested that what matters most is broadcasting a message about stopping the GOP, “and then we can start to talk about what type of policy we can provide.”
Both candidates expressed confidence that they can generate enough momentum to win.
Who will El-Sayed face in the general election?
Competing against El-Sayed in the general election will be Republican Mike Rogers. It will be one of the most closely watched races in the country: If Democrats hope to gain control of the Senate, they likely must net the seat.
Rogers served as the U.S. representative for Michigan’s 8th Congressional District 2001 to 2015 and was the Republican nominee in 2024 for Michigan’s U.S. Senate election. He has received Trump’s endorsement and has campaigned around “bringing manufacturing jobs back home” and “setting our kids up for success by prioritizing education not indoctrination,” among other things.
The general election will be held Nov. 3.

sources.news_title: Democratic primaries hand wins to leftist, center factions
sources.text:
Democratic primaries hand wins to leftist, center factions
Both moderate and progressive Democrats won in Michigan, Virginia, Missouri, Kansas and Washington
What happened
The Democratic Party’s moderate and progressive wings each won key primaries in Michigan, Virginia, Missouri, Kansas and Washington state on Tuesday. In the highest-profile showdown between the two factions, progressive candidate Dr. Abdul El-Sayed narrowly won the Senate primary in Michigan, The Associated Press projected, beating establishment-backed Rep. Haley Stevens.
Voters in Kansas defeated a Republican ballot measure that would have turned state Supreme Court appointments into partisan races — a “referendum designed to overturn Kansas’ constitutional right to abortion,” Politico said. In Missouri, voters overwhelmingly rejected a GOP-led amendment that would have made it harder to pass voter-approved ballot measures.
Who said what
The winners in the Democrats’ moderate faction include Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (Wash.), who fended off a leftist challenger; former Rep. Elaine Luria (Va.) and Richmond-area prosecutor Shannon Taylor, who won swing-district primaries; and Rep. Wesley Bell (Mo.), who prevailed in his rematch against democratic socialist former Rep. Cori Bush. Progressive climate activist William Lawrence won a three-way primary against two moderates in Michigan and will face Rep. Tom Barrett (R) in a “competitive contest that will test whether left-wing populism is viable in swing districts,” The New York Times said.
The Week

sources.news_title: Abdul El-Sayed squeaks out win in hotly contested Democratic US Senate primary in Michigan
sources.text:
Abdul El-Sayed squeaks out win in hotly contested Democratic US Senate primary in Michigan
Former Wayne County Health Director Abdul El-Sayed speaks at an election night watch party in Detroit, Mich., on Aug. 4, 2026. The Democratic primary for U.S. Senate was too close to call at the time he spoke. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)
DETROIT – After a grueling primary that saw attacks from Republicans and establishment Democrats alike, Abdul El-Sayed has won in his race to be the party’s nominee to face Republican former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers in the November general election.
Unofficial election results show that El-Sayed was on track to win the race over contender and U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham). The Associated Press called the race for El-Sayed at 9:58 a.m. Wednesday.
El-Sayed, holding his election night victory party in Detroit, addressed his supporters at about 1 a.m. and said it was too close to call at that point.
“Know that the billionaires, corporations, and the special interests-they weren’t going to give up light. We all knew they were going to spend their money,” El-Sayed said. “We didn’t know they were going to spend $70 million of their money. We didn’t know that they were going to outspend us $11 to $1. And yet we’re still standing.”
State Sen. Mallory McMorrow (D-Royal Oak), who had dropped out of the race in early July, endorsed El-Sayed based on NBC News making the call just before 2 a.m.
“I’m proud to give Abdul my full endorsement and support as we head to November together as a unified party,” McMorrow said in a release. “Take it from me — this was a brutal primary. But whatever differences there were between the candidates in this race, those differences are nothing compared to the contrast in November. Donald Trump and Mike Rogers are banking on all of us being too bruised, too proud, and too hurt to come back together to beat them. Let’s prove them wrong.”
Shortly after the AP called the race for El-Sayed, Stevens issued a statement of congratulations and support for the general election fight ahead.
“I want to congratulate Abdul El-Sayed on winning the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate. He is a doctor, a community health official, a Rhodes Scholar, and a dedicated Michigander. I am proud to offer my support as he takes on Mike Rogers in the general election,” Stevens said. “This was a thorough and rigorous campaign that brought out the full span of views within the Democratic Party – and that is why we have primaries. I am proud to have put up my hand to serve, and prouder to continue to work together to make sure this Senate seat remains blue, that we flip the United States Senate and continue the work for Michigan.”
El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, would be the first Muslim U.S. senator if elected in November.
The win sets up a showdown with Rogers, who ran uncontested in the Republican primary. Rogers has been able to gather resources, mainly cash, while the Democrats battled it out wire-to-wire.
Rogers — who lost his 2024 race against current U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Holly) — has $4.41 million cash on hand according to pre-primary FEC filings.
Meanwhile, between April 1 and June 30, El-Sayed raised $4.57 million and spent $4.37 million, leaving him with $2.7 million cash on hand.
El-Sayed has carved out a lane that had pundits calling him both a Barack Obama-type figure for the Democrats and Michigan’s less-socialist Zohran Mamadani. El-Sayed routinely disavowed the democratic socialist label that followed some of his key policy planks, saying he was a capitalist who sees its inherent flaws and wants to fix them.
He did so by centering his campaign on Medicare for All, new leadership in the U.S. Senate, overtures on anti-corporate election interference and on upending decades of U.S. foreign policy — namely, military and diplomatic aid to Israel. While Stevens focused on kitchen table issues like affordability, resistance to the administration of President Donald Trump and rebuilding the might of Michigan’s manufacturing, El-Sayed captured the growing disdain within the Democratic Party for corporate money in politics and the U.S. relationship with Israel. El-Sayed was the first candidate in the race to declare his belief that Israel had committed genocidal actions in its ongoing war with Hamas in Gaza.
As Stevens played to the middle, El-Sayed banked on Michigan’s Democrats joining his new coalition, which included young college-aged or college-educated progressives, union members, climate and anti-fascist activists, and women who were quickly becoming the core of the resistance movement against Trump and the actions of his administration.
Until just the last few weeks before Tuesday’s primary, El-Sayed had been framed as the race’s underdog. Although progressives had shown some strength this year with wins in New York for Mamdani and others, a great many pundits and election observers questioned whether the growing wave of progressive populism could find a root in Michigan, often called the purplest of Midwestern swing states.
El-Sayed had some name recognition from his 2018 Democratic gubernatorial bid, which he lost decisively to current Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, and his time as a progressive celebrity working in the Bernie Sanders sphere of influencers and podcasters. That attracted people like Sanders to his campaign effort, but also more controversial figures like streamer and commentator Hasan Piker.
Whitmer, who had given Stevens a late endorsement, was quick to offer congratulations to all of the Democratic nominees following El-Sayed’s win.
“Congratulations to Jocelyn Benson, Abdul El-Sayed, and every Democrat who won up and down the ballot. They’ve got my support as we fight like hell, together, to win in November,” Whitmer said in a press release. “There was a lot of passion and energy in these primaries, and that’s a good thing—Democrats are ready to beat Republicans across the state. We’re all united by our shared goal: getting things done for the people of Michigan. We know there’s so much on the line this November—health care, costs, our fundamental freedoms. That’s why it’s time to come together, get to work, and win in November.”
For many Dearborn voters that Michigan Advance spoke with Tuesday, there was great enthusiasm to give a progressive like El-Sayed a chance.
Jalen Black, a security guard, said he was most excited to cast his ballot for El-Sayed after voting for him in 2018. Black said El-Sayed’s politics are the closest to his, pointing to his stance against Israel’s actions in Gaza, progressive policies on housing and healthcare, and focus on getting money out of politics.
Black, 27, told the Advance outside of the Dearborn Administrative Center after casting his ballot, that he thought the Democratic Party was “largely out of touch” with people.
“I think it’s mostly pandering at this point,” Black said.
Black said that politicians and the media have been Islamophobic and “weirdly antagonistic” towards Dearborn, referencing the response to the Uncommitted movement in 2024.
“Instead of actually making the attempt to understand Dearborn,” Black said, they were just “pointing the finger and making it seem like they’re irrational”
Gabriella Dias, a video editor, was also casting her ballot at the Dearborn Administrative Center late Tuesday afternoon. She said she was most excited about the Senate race.
“I think it’s an important thing as human beings to care about each other, and I think the first step is in local politics,” Dias, 24, said.
Dias said her generation isn’t politically involved enough, so she has been trying to get her friends to vote. She said she’s “disillusioned” the with American political system and was glad to see a candidate like El-Sayed.
“I think a lot of people like miss the opportunity to be civically involved because they think it’s very complicated. But I just think it’s an important thing to do, and I think it’s morally right to do so.”
Aside from Stevens, who was framed as the race’s frontrunner and establishment favorite from the minute she entered the race, El-Sayed also faced McMorrow, who was trying her best through the race to carve out her own name ID and set herself apart from Stevens and El-Sayed.
That proved difficult for McMorrow, who at times played progressive by attaching herself to issues that El-Sayed championed, including an aversion to corporate campaign donations, including from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee,which Stevens openly accepted, while also supporting Israel’s right to exist as the Jewish homeland in the Middle East.
McMorrow dropped out in July leaving the race to just Stevens and El-Sayed. The battle to the finish line that ensued was intense and at times politically bruising. Stevens attacked El-Sayed on everything from his commitment to transparency and his treatment of women throughout his political career. El-Sayed in turn hit Stevens on her corporate campaign cash and her acceptance of help from AIPAC — which spent more than $40 million on the race to boost her.
The race was coming down to the wire until last week when several polls began to indicate El-Sayed was moving ahead.
El-Sayed ultimately claimed victory Wednesday morning, advancing the progressives in a key state, and one that mimicked other Democratic socialist upsets seen across the nation in the 2026 cycle. He will now have to turn his attention not just to Rogers in the general election, but also to mending ties with Stevens’ supporters, as Democratic unity will be essential if the party wants to hold the seat being left vacant by the retiring U.S. Sen. Gary Peters (D-Bloomfield Township).
Minnah Arshad contributed to this story.

sources.news_title: Left-wing populist wins in Michigan as Democrats reject party establishment
sources.text:
Left-wing populist wins in Michigan as Democrats reject party establishment
Washington: Democrats in the midwestern state of Michigan have chosen Abdul El-Sayed, a left-wing Muslim health administrator, to be their candidate for the US Senate in a result with seismic consequences for the midterm elections and US politics.
They rejected Haley Stevens, a four-term Democratic congresswoman heavily backed by the party establishment, despite outside groups spending more than $US60 million ($84.5 million) for her in the most expensive Democratic Senate primary ever.
His victory comes at a time when Republicans, led by US President Donald Trump, are painting Democrats nationwide as being overtaken by communists who want to destroy America, end capitalism and adopt a range of policies that sit outside the mainstream.
El-Sayed, who was backed by progressive hero Bernie Sanders and democratic socialist Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, will be the Democratic candidate for a seat which the party must hold if it is to win control of the Senate in November.
The 41-year-old campaigned on a platform of taking private finance out of politics, putting money in the pockets of regular Michiganders, and universal healthcare. He promised higher taxes on the wealthy and ending US military aid and arms sales to Israel.
The contest was tighter than many recent polls predicted, with El-Sayed winning 48.5 per cent to 47.5, or about 15,000 votes. CNN and the Associated Press called the race for him just before 10am on Wednesday (midnight AEST), when 99 per cent of the counting had been completed.
Both candidates called for unity. Stevens congratulated her opponent on winning a “thorough and rigorous campaign”, and pledged her support in the battle to come.
Speaking in Detroit, El-Sayed said his campaign “took on a machine” and won. “What we showed is that the power of our many is greater than the power of their money,” he said. “My hope is that our democracy will never be the same.”
Michigan, a swing state that voted for Trump in 2016 and 2024, last sent a Republican to the US Senate in the 1990s. But Republican candidate Mike Rogers, a former congressman, has brand recognition and only lost narrowly last time.
Most experts say El-Sayed’s win makes it harder for Democrats to hold the seat, while strategists were soul-searching about the party’s direction and whether it was moving too far to the left.
Adrian Hemond, chief executive of Grassroots Midwest, a bipartisan Michigan-based public affairs group, told this masthead last week: “If he wins the primary and then loses the general election in the fall, it’s disastrous for national progressives.”
El-Sayed is the first Muslim to win the Democratic nomination for the US Senate (though not the first Republican), and would be the first Muslim to enter the US Senate if he wins in November.
Unlike Ocasio-Cortez or Zohran Mamdani in New York, he is not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America. But he has attended their events in the past, and the DSA supported his campaign. “His policy platform is socialist,” Hemond said.
El Sayed’s victory represents a heavy defeat for the Democratic elite. Stevens had endorsements from Michigan’s Democratic governor Gretchen Whitmer, multiple senators and representatives, mayors and former officeholders.
Sanders, appearing on CNN as the votes were still counted, said he couldn’t recall anything like it.
“Abdul El-Sayed is taking on the entire Michigan Democratic establishment,” Sanders said. “He’s taking on the entire national Democratic establishment. He has been outspent 10 to one.”
The $US60 million in outside funding supporting Stevens’ campaign included more than $US30 million from pro-Israel lobby groups, which became an important focus of the campaign.
Polls show the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, which funds pro-Israel candidates via super PACs, is a toxic entity among Democrats, especially younger ones - as is support for Israel more broadly.
Stevens remained a staunch supporter of the Jewish state and once told a Hanukkah event: “Israel comes to me in my dreams.”
El-Sayed ended up comfortably winning Kent County, which takes in the city of Grand Rapids. He also easily won the state capital, Lansing, and Ann Arbor, home to the University of Michigan.
Stevens won Detroit, largely thanks to its majority population of African Americans, who are less likely to support left-wing candidates than white Democrats.
Trump weighed in Wednesday morning claiming, without evidence, that Wayne Country - which takes in Detroit - was one of the most corrupt voting areas in the US.
“Great news for the Republican Party,” he said. “El-Sayed, a communist loser who hates Jews and Israel, is the projected winner … Now, the Dumocrats crazy policies will only get worse!”

sources.news_title: Stevens concedes and endorses El-Sayed, as GOP attacks his candidacy as ‘dangerous’
sources.text:
Stevens concedes and endorses El-Sayed, as GOP attacks his candidacy as ‘dangerous’
The Republican Jewish Coalition said that Michigan’s 100,000 Jewish voters could make the difference in the battleground race if they choose to back GOP nominee Mike Rogers
Sarah Rice/Bloomberg via Getty Images
Democrats are quickly coalescing behind Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed after the far-left candidate narrowly clinched victory in Michigan’s Democratic primary on Wednesday morning, while Republicans quickly pounced on El-Sayed’s extremist history and ties.
Rep. Haley Stevens (D-MI), who came within a percentage point of defeating El-Sayed, promptly congratulated him on his victory and offered her support.
“I want to congratulate Abdul El-Sayed on winning the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate. He is a doctor, a community health official, a Rhodes Scholar, and a dedicated Michigander. I am proud to offer my support as he takes on Mike Rogers in the general election,” Stevens said. “This was a thorough and rigorous campaign that brought out the full span of views within the Democratic Party — and that is why we have primaries.”
She emphasized the need for Democrats to come together in support of El-Sayed, saying, “We must elect Democrats up and down the ballot. We need to flip some important House seats. We need to re-elect my friends Hillary Scholten and Kristen McDonald Rivet. We need to win this Senate seat, because Elissa Slotkin deserves a partner like Abdul in the U.S. Senate.”
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) also offered support for El-Sayed in a statement.
“Abdul El-Sayed has run an energetic campaign that inspired thousands of Michiganders across the state, with a clear focus on lowering costs and standing up for working families,” the pair said. “Democrats are united by a common purpose: putting a check on Donald Trump by defeating his Republican enablers and taking back the Senate. We look forward to working with Abdul and Democrats across Michigan to win this seat in November.”
Retiring Sen. Gary Peters (D-MI), who had initially planned to stay out of the race but ultimately endorsed Stevens, said that the party must come together behind El-Sayed to block Rogers.
“Both candidates ran strong campaigns focused on improving the lives of all Michiganders. But now it’s time to come together as a party and rally around our nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, to make sure Mike Rogers never sees the floor of the U.S. Senate,” Peters said. “I’ve repeatedly said that I will support our nominee because the most important election is in November.”
Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-MI), who declined to endorse El-Sayed in the primary, offered her support while also saying little about El-Sayed personally and focusing on the need to keep the seat in Democratic hands.
“Congratulations to @AbdulElSayed for winning the Democratic nomination for Senate. It’s been a long primary, but now it’s time to gear up to beat Mike Rogers (again) and win up and down the ticket,” Slotkin said. “There is nothing more important than the mission of the next 90 days: uniting, keeping this seat blue, flipping the House and Senate, and providing a real check on President Trump.”
Meanwhile, Republicans have quickly pounced on El-Sayed, highlighting his extreme history.
“Abdul isn’t just another liberal. He’s an extremist. He wants to empty prisons and put murderers and sex offenders back on our streets. He pledged his support to the Muslim Brotherhood and campaigns with people who refuse to condemn terrorism,” Republican nominee former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-MI) said. “I spent years hunting terrorists and bringing Osama bin Laden to justice. Never in a million years did I think that I would be running against someone who believes America deserved 9/11.” His comment was apparently a reference to El-Sayed’s ties to far-left streamer Hasan Piker, who championed El-Sayed in the primary.
Matt Brooks, CEO of the Republican Jewish Coalition, declared in a statement that El-Sayed is the “most antisemitic U.S. Senate candidate in America” and called on Jewish Democrats, who he said could prove “decisive” in the November general election, to back Rogers.
“Abdul El-Sayed is a direct threat to Michigan’s Jewish community,” Brooks said. “El-Sayed has called the government of the Jewish state as ‘evil’ as Hamas, ‘struggled’ to say that Israel has a right to exist as a Jewish state, and empathized with a terrorist who tried to murder Jewish schoolchildren at Temple Israel in the Detroit suburbs — and yet, Michigan Democrats just picked him as their nominee for the United States Senate.”
The Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC aligned with Senate GOP leadership, announced a six-figure digital ad campaign describing El-Sayed as “dangerous.”
