sources.news_title: Abdul El-Sayed Triumphs Over Haley Stevens in $60M Loss for AIPAC, Corporations
sources.text:
Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.
Former public health official Abdul El-Sayed has achieved a dominant win in Michigan’s Democratic primary for U.S. Senate on Tuesday, winning by a narrow margin over Rep. Haley Stevens in a ground-shaking triumph over the $60 million spent by AIPAC and corporations to oppose him.
With over 95 percent of the vote counted, El-Sayed had 48.5 percent of the vote, compared to Stevens’s 47.5 percent. Mallory McMorrow, who dropped out of the race, received 4 percent of the vote. AP called the race on Wednesday morning.
The race represents the latest major win for the progressive wing of the Democratic Party, which is increasingly defining itself through viewpoints like ending military aid to Israel, opposing data center construction, and abolishing ICE — all stances that El-Sayed has taken.
El-Sayed will face off in the general election against Republican Mike Rogers, who ran uncontested in his primary. Rogers is a former FBI agent and House representative who has the backing of President Donald Trump.
El-Sayed delivered a late night speech when he was leading Stevens by several points but the race had not yet been called. In his remarks, he struck a triumphant tone, praising his supporters for helping to beat the odds and focusing on uniting Democrats for the race ahead. He criticized Rogers for his ties to Big Pharma and his relationship with Trump.
“However we might feel about the campaign we’ve just come through, I want you to understand that it pales in comparison to the cynicism, it pales in comparison to the corporatism, in comparison to the lies that Mike Rogers and Donald Trump are going to tell,” he said. “There is so much more that unites us, however much we might disagree with our Democratic opponent.”
Stevens conceded on Wednesday, issuing a statement congratulating El-Sayed and saying that she would back him in the race.
“Donald Trump and Mike Rogers want us to come out of this primary tired and divided, so their billionaire backers can come in and let multimillionaire Mike Rogers walk away with this Senate seat,” she said. “I’m not going to let that happen.”
El-Sayed centered his platform on getting money out of politics and backing Medicare for All. Through his campaign, he has balanced his policy wonkishness on the latter issue with what supporters saw as a charismatic personality that has elevated him to star status on the national level. His supporters were enthusiastic and high in number, with about 10,000 volunteers knocking on doors and making calls for the former Wayne County health director in this campaign.
“We all knew they were going to spend their money. We didn’t know they were going to spend $70 million of their money. We didn’t know that they were going to outspend us $11 to $1,” said El-Sayed. “And yet we’re still standing.”
While the primary result is a win for progressives within the party, it also marks a loss of seismic proportions for the establishment wing and the lobbyists who back them.
AIPAC, through an affiliated super PAC, poured over $30 million into backing Stevens and opposing El-Sayed — a record amount of spending for the pro-Israel group in a single race.
This was a formula that worked for Stevens in the past; Stevens originally won her House seat with $4.2 million in backing from AIPAC, which was targeting former Rep. Andy Levin for his support of a two-state solution in Israel and Palestine.
But this support comes as AIPAC and support for Israel has become poisonous among large swaths of the electorate, three years into Israel’s genocide in Gaza and nearly six months into a historically unpopular U.S.-Israeli assault on Iran. Polls have repeatedly found that Democratic voters and many independents say that the U.S. should decrease or end aid to Israel, as voters grow increasingly weary of the U.S.’s backing of the apartheid state.
Support for Israel has become a central issue in many primaries, and Stevens is one of Congress’s loudest backers of Israel. Her campaign in particular was plagued by a speech she once gave in which she said: “Israel comes to me in my dreams.” Last week, she additionally faced criticism for a bigoted comment in which she accused El-Sayed of wanting to “blame all of your problems on Jewish Americans,” seemingly in reference to the Muslim candidate’s opposition to funding Israel.
Stevens also got major infusions from corporate-backed PACs, which poured over $30 million into supporting her campaign. Her campaign’s corporate ties ran deep, as reports found ties between her consultants and tech and AI firms like Palantir.
Meanwhile, Stevens had the backing of establishment figures like Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-New York), who quietly lined up behind her. Some Democratic Stevens backers, like Rep. Hillary Scholten (D-Michigan), have even suggested that they won’t back El-Sayed in the general election.
Democratic Michigan voters also expressed support for another progressive candidate on Tuesday in the MI-07 district, which encompasses Lansing.
Voters have chosen progressive activist William Lawrence, a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), in the district’s Democratic primary. Lawrence has also carved a space for himself as progressive figure, condemning Israel for committing a genocide and endorsing progressive priorities like Medicare for All.
Lawrence decisively won with 44 percent of the vote, 15 points over the next candidate. The district is currently represented by a Republican, Rep. Tom Barrett, but is the former seat of Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin.

Leftist El-Sayed narrowly wins high-profile Michigan Democratic Senate primary
Progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed narrowly won Michigan's Democratic US Senate primary, US media projected, handing the party's left wing a significant victory in a pivotal battleground state. The upset over establishment-backed Haley Stevens is expected to sharpen debate over the Democrats' direction on economic populism, healthcare and support for Israel ahead of November's midterm elections.

Abdul El-Sayed has won Michigan’s Democratic nomination for the US Senate, narrowly defeating US Rep. Haley Stevens in a victory for the party’s progressive wing in a battleground state.
The real test of El-Sayed’s and progressives’ strength will now come in a November matchup against Mike Rogers, a former congressman who ran unopposed for the Republican nomination. The seat is pivotal to Democrats’ chances of flipping the Senate and El-Sayed will face the challenge of uniting a divided Democratic base after a bruising primary.
The race remained tight throughout Tuesday night, with a winner not declared until Wednesday morning. In his final remarks at a primary night party before the race was called, El-Sayed said “tomorrow we begin to mend fences.”
Stevens called El-Sayed to concede Wednesday, and she issued a statement saying she would back El-Sayed’s candidacy.

“I am proud to offer my support as he takes on Mike Rogers in the general election,” she said.
Stevens added, “This was a thorough and rigorous campaign that brought out the full span of views within the Democratic Party – and that is why we have primaries.”
El-Sayed’s win represents a significant shift for the Democratic Party; in 2018 he lost the gubernatorial primary to now-Gov. Gretchen Whitmer by 21 percentage points.
El-Sayed, a former health official, campaigned on “Medicare for All,” halting military aid to Israel and campaign finance reform. He had support from progressive leaders including Sen. Bernie Sanders and US Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who framed the race as a grassroots-focused movement and a broader fight against the establishment and big-money spending.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, another progressive leader who endorsed El-Sayed, said the race “should be a wake-up call to the Washington Democratic establishment".
“He was running against a lot of Washington insiders as well as parts of the Michigan Democratic establishment. And he won,” said Van Hollen. “That's an incredible story.”
“Congratulations to him,” said Sen. Gary Peters, the Michigan Democrat whose retirement spurred the contentious primary to replace him. Peters had endorsed Stevens.
Now comes the more difficult challenge for Democrats: uniting the party to defeat Rogers, for whom Republicans have already reserved large sums of money ahead of the general election. Democrats consider the seat a must-win if they are to flip control of the Senate this year.
Early Tuesday evening, El-Sayed’s supporters in Detroit’s Majestic Theatre cheered at the first batches of votes, before mellowing. Hours later Stevens’ previously subdued partygoers roared as she narrowed the margin.
Read moreMichigan Democratic primary seen as latest test for party's progressive wing
“Whatever happens tonight,” El-Sayed told a thinned but still energetic crowd, “we have a responsibility to ensure that we unite, unite to make sure that Mike Rogers never sees the inside of the US Senate.”
El-Sayed, a former Wayne County health director, campaigned on “Medicare for All,” campaign finance reform and ending military aid to Israel.

sources.news_title: El-Sayed Pulls It Off. Now Comes the Hard Part.
sources.text:
Abdul El-Sayed, a public-health official who lost in a primary landslide when he ran for governor of Michigan eight years ago, eked out a victory over Representative Haley Stevens on Tuesday night in one of the most closely watched, bitterly contested and expensive Democratic Senate primaries in the country.
He overcame more than $60 million in super-PAC spending against him, most of it from AIPAC, the deep-pocked pro-Israel group that’s spending in this midterm cycle has backfired against its chosen candidates as much as it has helped. In this campaign, El-Sayed wore the spending barrage against him as a badge of pride.
“As I reflect on the last 15 months, I reflect on people coming together, believing that we really could have a politics bigger than what they said we could have,” he said at an election-eve rally at a cocktail bar and café in Detroit’s wealthy Boston–Edison Historic District. “A politics bigger than a record amount of spending to try and pick a U.S. senator that represents the interests of corporations or special interests rather than the interests of Michiganders.”
For progressive Democrats, the general election between El-Sayed and Mike Rogers, a former representative who lost the 2024 Senate contest to Elissa Slotkin by less than half a percentage point, is set to be a proof-of-concept contest. Win, and they have shown that being as left-wing as El-Sayed is — he once called for defunding the police (a position he now disavows) and favors Medicare for All — isn’t a hindrance. Lose, and Democrats chances of retaking the Senate drop dramatically and with it the appetite among Democrats for a lefty candidate in the upcoming presidential primary, whether it be Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Ro Khanna, or anyone else.
“This is a put-your-chips-all-in moment,” said Adam Green, the head of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee, a left-wing group that was one of the constellation of progressive outfits that worked on behalf of El-Sayed. “If Abdul wins in November, it would send a signal to scared but well-meaning electability voters that a shake-up-the-system economic fighter can win in a battleground state.”
Green’s group decided to back El-Sayed over another progressive candidate in the race last summer. Donald Trump was laying waste to much of the infrastructure of the federal government, and Green was searching for an antidote, someone who would be Trump but in reverse, who would discard the niceties of Washington in order to build, not tear down. El-Sayed in Michigan will be a test case that an economic populist can win in a state that Trump carried twice.
The left has been on a remarkable winning streak this primary season. In New York City, three candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America and Mayor Zohran Mamdani defeated longtime incumbents and candidates packed by the party’s Establishment. In Maine, an oysterman ran the two-term incumbent governor out of the Senate race. A leftist insurgent defeated a 15-term member of Congress in Colorado, and in Washington, D.C., a democratic socialist won the mayoral primary after defeating a candidate favored by the city’s business leaders by 20 points.
But those results could be dismissed as small and localized results in deep-blue enclaves; no presidential candidate has carried Michigan by more than three points since 2012. With Trump’s approval rating tanking — he is 20 points underwater in Michigan — Democrats will need some voters who backed Trump in 2024 to support El-Sayed this time around. The conventional wisdom has always held that the best way to peel those disapproving Trump voters away is by offering a milquetoast Democrat that can give those voters a place to register their dislike of Trump without forcing them to vote for a full suite of liberal priorities.
The El-Sayed campaign had a different theory of the case. Its belief has always been that charisma and political talent is the key to winning elections and that El-Sayed, with his ability communicating across social and traditional media, is more capable of getting voters to the polls.
“The party’s voters are ready to move on from corporate Establishment Democrats that represent the priorities of billionaire donors over the needs of everyday people,” said Usamah Andrabi, a spokesperson for Justice Democrats, which has made it its mission over the past decade to elect more left-wing candidates to Congress. “Block by block we have been showing Democratic voters that they can deserve more from their representatives.”
Meanwhile, Republicans are thrilled at the prospect of running against El-Sayed in the general election.
“He’s a communist,” said one Republican Senate strategist. “The ads write themselves.”

El-Sayed’s Victory in Michigan Was Much Closer Than Anyone Predicted. What Does That Mean for What Comes Next?
sources.text:
Sign up for the Slatest to get the most insightful analysis, criticism, and advice out there, delivered to your inbox daily.
Abdul El-Sayed, a public health official, narrowly defeated four-term Rep. Haley Stevens in the Michigan Democratic Senate primary. The vote proved too close to call on Tuesday evening, but by Wednesday morning, El-Sayed had claimed the win, and Stevens had phoned him to concede. The race was called by about 10 a.m.
It’s a watershed moment in Democratic politics. No other recent instance of a left-wing insurgent defeating the Democratic establishment candidate in a swing-state Senate primary comes to mind. Stevens and her camp threw everything they had into the race. She enjoyed the support of both the Washington and Michigan Democratic establishments. Super PACs spent tens of millions of dollars, dwarfing the money spent on El-Sayed’s behalf, attempting to get Stevens across the finish line. But El-Sayed ably weaponized these resources against Stevens, making her financial superiority the core of his argument against her.
And yet the victory comes with more of a whimper, given expectations heading into the night. Despite public and private polling showing double-digit leads for El-Sayed heading into the night, he defeated Stevens by just 1 percentage point. Stevens put up strong numbers in rural parts of the state to supplement her leads in metro Detroit, though that wasn’t quite enough to offset the margins El-Sayed posted in Grand Rapids and Ann Arbor. The closeness of the race only underscores one of El-Sayed’s challenges going ahead: reuniting a fractured party after a bitter primary campaign. This was not a resounding verdict.
The most watched Senate primary in the country now becomes the most watched Senate election in the country, as El-Sayed will face former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers in November. The matchup gives the progressive movement that Sen. Bernie Sanders ignited 10 years ago a chance to try its case: that left-wing populism is just as, if not more, “electable” in a marquee toss-up election than the cautious moderation offered by the Democratic establishment.
The stakes are high not just for the people of Michigan, or for the candidate who wins control of the Senate in the midterms. What happens in this state could color the Democratic presidential primary in 2028 too.
The Michigan primary was a three-way race for most of its duration. State Sen. Mallory McMorrow, a rising star in the party with a history of viral speeches, positioned herself as a middle-ground option between Stevens’ institutional candidacy and El-Sayed’s fiery progressivism. It’s a strategy that often works better on paper than in reality. Finding the perfect position appeasing those on either side of an issue is exhausting work and prone to error. Eventually, Stevens consolidated establishment and centrist support, while El-Sayed consolidated progressives. McMorrow was squeezed out and quit the race in early July.
That created a true left–vs.–center battle in the final month of the race, as Stevens worked to close El-Sayed’s polling lead. Stevens’ supportive super PACs—most notably the United Democracy Project, a group backed by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee—opened the spigots with both pro-Stevens and anti-El-Sayed television ads. El-Sayed, whose campaign wasn’t poor but couldn’t keep up with Stevens’, countered that the candidate was bought and paid for.
The contest turned deeply nasty in the closing weeks. El-Sayed at one point had to direct his supporters not to mock Stevens in gross personal terms online. But El-Sayed, who does not lack confidence, didn’t always keep his tongue in check. He described Stevens as “a suit with a large AIPAC bank account” who can’t “string together two coherent sentences.” He called her the “least capable candidate in America.” Stevens wasn’t as personally hostile toward El-Sayed—his (attempted) destruction was largely outsourced to super PACs—but that last comment set her off. “Everyone in America understands you want to blame all of your problems on Jewish Americans,” Stevens posted in response to El-Sayed’s provocation.
That post was one of many Stevens tells in the campaign’s final weeks demonstrating that she was the one trying to play catch-up. Neither Michigan Sen. Gary Peters nor Gov. Gretchen Whitmer—the latter Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s first attempted recruit for the Senate race—would have endorsed in the race unless they felt they had to. Stevens’ campaign, meanwhile, went all in on portraying El-Sayed as unelectable. El-Sayed, in the final week of the campaign, began to turn his attention to Mike Rogers.
El-Sayed is eager to face Rogers, predicting, with characteristic moxie, that in the future, if “you say ‘Mike Rogers,’ it’ll be like: ‘Remember when Abdul just completely demolished that man’s political future?’ ” Well, it’s important to maintain a positive attitude. But Rogers and his allies will be taking on El-Sayed with a nine-figure assault, addressed to a more moderate electorate and without concern for maintaining a baseline level of cordiality.
Much of the Democratic Party’s future depends on whether El-Sayed’s impressive speaking ability and quickness on his feet allow him to withstand the Rogers team’s onslaught. If a blue wave materializes in November but a Michigan Senate seat flips red—and helps the Senate stay Republican—the Democratic establishment might find it much easier to get its preferred candidates nominated the next time. But if El-Sayed can defeat Rogers, the appetite for new kinds of candidates will only spread further.
We’re not just talking about Senate races either. El-Sayed’s ability to defeat the “unelectable” tag under such a bright spotlight could substantially affect whom Democrats nominate for president in 2028. Progressive leaders, eager to put one of their own atop the ticket after the Biden debacle and Harris loss in 2024, don’t just know this—they’re counting on it. In both 2016 and 2020, “electability” was a fatal blow to Sanders’ presidential campaigns, and any successor trying to fill his “lane” in 2028 would have to contend with the same issue. What an asset it would be for that candidate to be able to argue, They said the same thing in the biggest Senate race of 2026, and he won. And what a liability it would be if that candidate couldn’t.

sources.news_title: The Electability of Abdul El-Sayed
sources.text:
In late July, when Michigan’s governor, Gretchen Whitmer, endorsed Haley Stevens in the state’s Democratic Senate primary, it was unclear what the move meant. Was Whitmer’s intervention an indication of the Democratic establishment’s confidence that Stevens, a centrist congresswoman who’d struggled to gain traction for much of the campaign, was now, just eleven days before the vote, on a path to victory, and just needed a final push to get over the finish line? Or was it a sign that the establishment was panicked that Stevens’s opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, a liberal former public-health official, was in the lead—and that the only way to prevent him from winning was a desperate, last-minute endorsement from the most popular Democrat in the state, who’d previously pledged to remain neutral? After last night, it’s clear that the latter was the case—and that the Hail Mary failed.
El-Sayed’s win over Stevens in Michigan, while not the blowout the final polls suggested it would be, is nonetheless the insurgent left’s most important victory of 2026—a year that has already featured many successful challenges to the Party’s establishment. So it’s fitting that El-Sayed is also the most politically talented of the group. He has the charisma of Graham Platner, the populist oysterman who won Maine’s Democratic Senate primary before withdrawing from the race after being accused of sexual assault, which he denied, but none of Platner’s skeletons: El-Sayed, a devout Muslim, does not drink, and he and his wife married when they were both in college. As a Rhodes Scholar with an M.D. and a Ph.D., El-Sayed is even more academically credentialled than Darializa Avila Chevalier, a Columbia grad and a doctoral student who unseated a five-term congressman in New York—plus, unlike Avila Chevalier, he’s a gifted orator who can think on his feet and doesn’t wilt under tough questioning. And, though some of El-Sayed’s detractors dismissed his campaign as an internet phenomenon—“I think there’s an extent to which Abdul is certainly winning in the online contest, but Haley is strongly winning with actual voters,” the Michigan congresswoman Hillary Scholten, who endorsed Stevens, said last week—El-Sayed ran an impressive real-life grassroots operation, with nearly five hundred campaign events in more than a hundred different towns and cities, that helped him overcome Stevens’s nine-to-one TV-spending advantage.
As much as El-Sayed’s win is a testament to his talents, it’s also an indictment of the Democratic establishment. Stevens was elected to Congress in 2018, but her Senate campaign was centered on the work she did in 2009, as a twenty-five-year-old factotum on the Obama Administration team that orchestrated the rescue of the U.S. auto industry. Television ads backing Stevens featured Obama almost as much as they did the candidate herself, even though Obama did not endorse Stevens’s bid. When Stevens visited the Greater Emmanuel Institutional Church of God in Christ, a Black Pentecostal church on Detroit’s west side, on a Sunday in May, the church’s pastor introduced her as “the former chief of staff, I think, for President Barack Obama.” Stevens did not correct him. “I will be honored to continue to do the work that I did alongside the great President Barack Obama,” she told the congregation.
Stevens, who benefitted from about sixty million dollars in spending from outside groups, more than half of which reportedly came from the pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC, had much less to say, at the church and in her campaign, about her four terms in Congress. Although she, like pretty much every Democrat these days, described herself as a “fighter” against President Donald Trump, it remained unclear to Michigan Democrats what, exactly, her fighting had got them. El-Sayed, by contrast, spoke openly about his fight against the Democratic establishment and about how he hoped his victory in the state he called “the carotid artery of American politics” would propel a progressive candidate to capture the Party’s Presidential nomination in 2028.
The challenge now for El-Sayed is how to take that fight to the Republicans. Until last night, all of the progressive victories this year came in deep-blue congressional districts or cities, where the Democratic primary is the whole ballgame. But Michigan is a purple state—Trump won there in 2016 and 2024—and El-Sayed will have more than token Republican opposition in the general election in November. Mike Rogers, the G.O.P. nominee, is a former seven-term congressman who, two years ago, came within twenty thousand votes of winning the U.S. Senate race in Michigan. Indeed, the biggest reason that so many establishment Democrats, in both Michigan and Washington, have been so worried about El-Sayed winning the primary is that they believe a candidate as liberal as El-Sayed—who supports Medicare for All and the abolition of ICE, and who calls Israel’s war in Gaza a genocide—cannot win a general election. The bitter nature of the primary contest in its final weeks—with El-Sayed attacking Stevens as “a suit with a large AIPAC bank account” who’s unable “to string together two coherent sentences,” and Stevens accusing El-Sayed of wanting to “blame all of your problems on Jewish Americans”—has only intensified that concern. AIPAC will likely spend heavily on Rogers’s behalf, perhaps even more than it spent on Stevens’s. In the Democratic primary, AIPAC’s support for Stevens turned out to be a boon for El-Sayed—such is the lobbying group’s toxicity among Democratic voters these days—but he’s unlikely to enjoy a similar dynamic in the general election this November.
But El-Sayed is operating with a different theory of electability. He believes that, for every older Michigander whose vote he loses because of his decision to campaign with the leftist streamer Hasan Piker, who has said he didn’t “have an issue” with Hezbollah and that “America deserved 9/11,” he’ll gain more support from younger Michiganders who didn’t previously vote but turned out because they heard about El-Sayed on Piker’s live stream. He believes that his bro-y campaign style, which struck some voters as sexist when employed against Stevens, will hold greater appeal when he turns it against Rogers, whom he recently dubbed a “beta character.” “You know what I’m gonna do to that man?” he boasted to Semafor’s David Weigel last month. “By the time I’m done, his best friends are gonna look at him and think what I think, say what I say. I’m gonna define him into eternity.”
Most of all, El-Sayed believes that, in 2026, it’s no longer good politics to be identified with Washington or to play it safe. When I spoke with him in Michigan in late May, he reflected on how the political climate has changed since his first campaign, in 2018, when he unsuccessfully ran for governor. “When Trump won the first time, it felt like the record had skipped, and this time around everyone understands that it’s baked into the infrastructure of American politics,” he said. “I think we’re learning that the Michigan electorate is actually sick and tired of having two options that look virtually the same. I think they want an option that is going to take on the inherited wisdom of the establishments—both of them.” On Tuesday night, Michigan’s Democrats backed El-Sayed in his gamble that an aggressive, combative, and at times divisive approach to politics will work in a swing state. “If perfectly inoffensive was what wins Michigan,” El-Sayed told me, “Donald Trump would never have won Michigan.” ♦

El-Sayed will face Republican Mike Rogers, a former congressman, in November in a race that will help determine control of the Senate. His first challenge will be unifying Democratic factions after a bitter primary that offered divergent visions for a party desperate for a path back to power.

“In the words of Muhammad Ali, we shook up the world,” he said.
Progressives have been gaining strength this year
The Associated Press declared El-Sayed the winner having confirmed that — after Wednesday morning updates in election returns in Wayne and Oakland counties, two of the state’s largest in the Detroit area — there were simply not enough votes left to count that would allow Stevens to catch up and overtake him as the leader.
El-Sayed’s victory was ultimately so narrow that it wasn’t assured until almost all ballots cast statewide were counted. At the time the AP declared him the winner, El-Sayed led Stevens by 14,893 votes — a margin of just under 1 percentage point — out of more than 1.5 million ballots counted.
His win, however slim, represents a significant shift for the Democratic Party; in 2018 he lost the gubernatorial primary to now-Gov. Gretchen Whitmer by 21 percentage points.
The former health official campaigned on “Medicare for All,” halting military aid to Israel and campaign finance reform. He had support from progressive leaders including Sen. Bernie Sanders and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who framed the race as a grassroots-focused movement and a broader fight against the establishment and big-money spending.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, another progressive leader, said El-Sayed’s victory “should be a wake-up call to the Washington Democratic establishment.”
Now comes the more difficult challenge for Democrats: uniting the party to defeat Rogers, for whom Republicans have already reserved large sums of money ahead of the general election.
“We have got to work together to take this country back,” Curtis Hertel, the chair of Michigan Democratic Party, said.
Michigan is a must-win Senate race for Democrats
The race will help decide which party controls the chamber in the last two years of Trump’s term. Those stakes added heat to the rivalry, with moderates arguing that El-Sayed would have a harder time than Stevens against a Republican in the general election.
Stevens, a four-term congresswoman, won election to Congress in 2018 after serving as chief of staff to President Barack Obama’s auto task force, which helped oversee the federal rescue of General Motors and Chrysler. Her campaign focused on manufacturing and the economy, and she stressed her past victories in tough races as proof she would be best positioned to beat Rogers.
El-Sayed cast himself as the anti-establishment candidate and argued that Democrats need to reject corporate influence and embrace a more progressive agenda.
While the candidate has said he is not a democratic socialist, he found support from some of the group’s members. That included Melat Kiros, who recently beat a longtime incumbent in a Democratic primary for a Denver-based House seat and was at El-Sayed’s watch party. Also there was Hasan Piker, a progressive and controversial influencer online.
The candidates’ differences were clear to some voters.
Kenneth Woodside, 87, of West Bloomfield, said he voted for El-Sayed because “the nation is ready for someone who wants to take some more action rather than on the road we are now, which is on the road to an oligarchy and authoritarianism.”
Nessa Fuller, 51, of Birmingham, said she voted for Stevens because she will “fight to get the right things done, and she’ll work with other people, which is really important to me.”
Outside influences spent millions on the Senate race
National groups poured unprecedented sums into the race, making it one of the country’s biggest tests of outside spending.
Outside groups backing Stevens spent more than $50 million, including more than $30 million from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, amounting to the largest investment ever from the organization that supports pro-Israel candidates.
“We took on a machine,” El-Sayed said.
Support for Israel is contentious within the Democratic Party and the Michigan primary reflected that divide: El-Sayed called for ending military aid to Israel, while Stevens maintained strong support for the relationship.
AIPAC issued a statement Wednesday saying it would oppose El-Sayed and “his radical anti-Israel agenda” in November’s election.
McKinney wins Detroit US House primary
In a heavily Democratic district representing Detroit, the 13th, state Rep. Donavan McKinney defeated Rep. Shri Thanedar. McKinney argued that the city should once again have a Black representative in Congress.
After Thanedar won election in 2022, Detroit had no Black representation in Congress for the first time since the early 1950s.
Associated Press reporters Nathan Ellgren in Washington and Jesse Bedayn in Detroit contributed.

sources.news_title: Left-wing political outsider Abdul El-Sayed wins Democratic Senate primary in Michigan
sources.text:
Left-wing political outsider wins Democratic Senate primary in Michigan
Left-wing political outsider Abdul El-Sayed is projected to win Michigan's Democratic Senate primary, a race that exposed bitter divisions within the party over its future direction.
The former public health official is on track to narrowly beat moderate Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens, according to CBS News, the BBC's US partner.
"In the words of Mohammad Ali, 'We shook up the world,'" El-Sayed said, quoting the famed boxer's declaration after his underdog defeat of Sonny Liston in 1964.
He will face Republican and Trump ally Mike Rogers, in November's midterm elections. If elected, El-Sayed would become the first Muslim to serve in the US senate.
The final result was much closer than El-Sayed's camp had expected, with fewer than 15,000 votes - a margin of just under 1 percentage point out of more than 1.5 million ballots counted - separating him from Stevens as of late Wednesday morning.
"The movement to get money out of politics, put money in your pocket, and pass Medicare for All is a big movement," El-Sayed said on Wednesday, echoing a familiar refrain he had used on the campaign trail.
"I want to congratulate Abdul El-Sayed on winning the Democratic nomination for US Senate," Stevens said in a statement. "He is a doctor, a community health official, a Rhodes Scholar, and a dedicated Michigander. I am proud to offer my support as he takes on Mike Rogers in the general election."
The November midterm elections will determine the balance of power in Washington for the last two years of President Donald Trump's time in office.
Trump declared the Michigan Senate result "Great news for the Republican Party".
In his post on Truth Social, Trump referred to the Democratic Party as the "Dumocrats", and claimed their "crazy policies will only get worse!"
After a bruising and sometimes bitter campaign, El-Sayed hinted at bridge-building when he addressed supporters on Tuesday night, before the outcome was known.
"Whatever happens tonight, we have a responsibility to ensure that we unite, unite to make sure that [Republican] Mike Rogers never sees the inside of the US Senate."
El-Sayed, who was endorsed by left-wing politicians including Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders and New York City congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, has voiced support for progressive causes like universal healthcare and abolishing US Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Stevens, 43, took a more moderate approach, pitching herself as the middle-of-the-road candidate who would appeal to voters unsure of which party to back in November. She made a promise to save manufacturing jobs in Michigan, should she be elected.
Stevens earned the endorsement of Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer, as well as outgoing Senator Gary Peters.
One of the biggest areas where the candidates disagreed was their stance on Israel.
El-Sayed spoke out against US involvement in the Middle East, including aid to Israel. Stevens, meanwhile, is staunchly pro-Israel and has said she supports upholding US aid to Israel without conditions.
El-Sayed's candidacy drew both support and opposition from Michigan's Jewish community due to his stance on the US-Israel relationship.
He has rejected allegations of anti-Semitism, which Trump renewed in his Truth Social post on Wednesday.
"I stand in solidarity with my Jewish sisters and brothers," El-Sayed said on Wednesday. "We can condemn anti-Semitism and at the same time, we can be talking about how we bring people together, and we can be talking about everybody's pain."
The Senate seat is currently held by a retiring Democrat. The last time the Midwestern state elected a Republican senator was in 1994.
In presidential elections Michigan is one of the crucial swing states. It voted for Democrat Joe Biden in 2020 but went for Trump in 2024.
A handful of other US states too held their primaries for statewide and national offices on Tuesday night, setting up partisan battles in November.
In Kansas, Democratic State Senator Cindy Holsher and Trump-backed Republican legislator Ty Masterson advanced in the governor's race.
In Ohio, Congressman Wesley Bell defeated former Congresswoman Cory Bush in a Democratic primary defined by the candidates' diverging stances on the US-Israel relationship.
Missouri voters also rejected a Republican-backed amendment that would have made it significantly harder to change the state's constitution, by raising the bar for passing citizen-led ballot initiatives.

sources.news_title: The meaning of Abdul El-Sayed’s triumph
sources.text:
Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan’s Senate Democratic primary isn’t just a triumph for the progressive Left, though it certainly is that. It must be understood, more broadly, as a rebuke to the Democratic establishment. Long delayed, the establishment’s reckoning has now fully arrived. Democratic elites — the incumbent politicos, corporate donors, the NGO-industrial complex, and aligned media — are on the back foot for the first time in decades. Even two years ago, the idea of candidates like El-Sayed and New York’s Zohran Mamdani winning Democratic primaries with large electorates was almost inconceivable.
El-Sayed, a former public-health official, managed it, clinching (as of this writing) 48.5% of ballots, against 47.5% for his centrist opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens. The narrow margin might prompt Democratic-establishment crowing about El-Sayed’s chances in the general. But consider that AIPAC and other outside groups poured some $60 million into Stevens’s campaign, with more than half of that amount coming from the political action committee of AIPAC, the pro-Israel lobby — making this the most expensive Democratic primary ever. Outside groups backing El-Sayed, by contrast, only managed fewer than $5 million.
Sixty million bucks couldn’t buy a Democratic primary. We have, in every sense, entered a new era.
Stevens was the sort of candidate who, not long ago, breezed to the nomination in a statewide contest. When Mallory McMorrow, the third Democrat in the running, dropped out, it was assumed Stevens could consolidate the anti-El-Sayed vote. This was how centrists almost always beat the Left, after all. In 2020, Bernie Sanders was doomed when Pete Buttigieg, Amy Klobuchar, and Beto O’Rourke dropped out of the primary, endorsing Joe Biden. Even when Leftists were strong, they were factional candidates, doomed to electoral ceilings. Sanders couldn’t get more votes than Biden or Hillary Clinton. The Left had to content itself with small-scale victories, like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez knocking off Joe Crowley in a single New York House district.
But now we have a Left surge of a kind not seen since the late 1960s and early ’70s. Back then, Left-leaning Democrats won primaries on the strength of their full-throated opposition to the Vietnam War. Just so, today it’s Israel-critical Democrats who are being rewarded for aligning the party with popular sentiment. And popular sentiment is clear: the Jewish state is now viewed unfavorably by nearly all major demographic groups (save for Republicans over age 50).
El-Sayed, like Mamdani, is a fierce critic of Israel. Both shattered taboos around what could be said about the Jewish state. AIPAC knew what was at stake, hence its unprecedented spending. The state’s Democratic establishment, led by outgoing Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and outgoing Sen. Gary Peters, likewise lent its backing to Stevens. Before the mid-2020s, that sort of endorsement power alone would have just about ended any statewide primary.
Progressives, of course, can’t claim total victory. The margin was uncomfortably tight, and El-Sayed must survive the general election come November. But here, too, the deck is stacked. Moderates get to lose elections all the time, but if the Left blows a race to a Republican, the alarm bells are heard ringing all across the country. It’s the same way with governance: a centrist like Eric Adams, the former Gotham mayor, can depart City Hall in utter disgrace. But Mamdani, the democratic socialist, must run the city without a whiff of scandal; the slightest failure on his part (supposedly) indicts the entire American Left.
What makes El-Sayed’s victory over Stevens most intriguing, though, is that progressives will finally be able to test a thesis they’ve long entertained: namely, that their brand of politics — populist on economics but still socially liberal — can win in a battleground state. Progressives, typically, haven’t won primaries where a strong Republican is waiting in the wings. If El-Sayed can win Michigan, one of the most pivotal states in the country, he will be a true national star.
For now, at least, the progressive Left has been able to leave its cultural baggage behind. El-Sayed can’t be credibly called anti-woke, but he might be, like Mamdani, post-woke. Mamdani abandoned his earlier calls to defund the police. He does not, like the Democratic Socialists of America and 2010s progressives, support an open border.
El-Sayed has trod a similar path. With his bulging muscles and willingness to mix it up on the podcast circuit and alternative online channels, he codes as the sort of pol who might be able to solve the Democrats’ problem with woke-weary young men. He possesses a certain machismo that, for Leftists, is a more recent phenomenon. And he speaks forthrightly to the cultural crises of young men, telling UnHerd’s Sohrab Ahmari that Leftists should address the structural causes behind male malaise — issues like online gambling and porn addiction — rather than write off men as “toxic.” Whether this is enough to convince young men to vote Democratic again nationally remains to be seen.
The bigger story, though, is the pro-Palestine current running through the party, and the generational shift well under way that will eventually tug top Democrats away from Israel. Like all small-d democratic groups, they eventually respond to their voters, and this is clearly what their voters want. Social media were rife with videos mocking Stevens for her over-the-top devotion to the Jewish state — “Israel comes to me in my dreams” — and the AIPAC largesse floating her campaign.
There was her voice, too, almost a peculiar parody of the Michigander accent — I’ve spent a great amount of time in the state and never heard anyone speak that way — that had many online critics pulling up old clips of Chris Farley. Were these attacks sexist? Maybe. But they came from as many young women as young men. Swaggering El-Sayed was the one they wanted.
The pundit class contends that El-Sayed is a terrible bet in the general election against the Republican nominee, Mike Rogers. Whether they have a point or not, we will find out soon enough. What the Michigan primary proved was that Democratic voters are no longer compelled by that pitch. They once were; the entire premise of Biden’s 2020 campaign was his contention that only he could defeat Trump. Now the electorate is restless. They saw the Democratic failures of 2016 and 2024. They are weary and angry about living, again, under the yoke of Trump. When a Democratic politician or star operative lectures them about electability, they tune out. Wasn’t the failed reality-TV star supposed to be unelectable? Then he won — and won again. Stevens could talk all day and night about how she flipped a Republican seat. Very few people cared.
The harsh reality for the Democratic establishment is that they have, like Republicans in 2016, lost their grip on the party. They have no one but themselves to blame. In 2024, Michigan was the home of the Uncommitted movement: progressives who refused to fall behind Biden and Kamala Harris over the horrors unfolding in Gaza. Why would Stevens, AIPAC’s foot soldier, be the right candidate for 2026 in Michigan of all places, with its sizable Arab and Muslim population?
Now that it has been proved that AIPAC cannot buy a Democratic primary, the group’s influence on Democratic politics, already waning, will collapse sharply. Even if El-Sayed loses in November, there won’t be a lane for Israel hawks in future Democratic primaries, and they will migrate fully to the GOP (where, it must be noted, a warm embrace isn’t certain to greet them).
Organic support for Israel is vanishing, and the vast reserves of cash can’t bring it back. Stevens herself once won a House primary bludgeoning a progressive Jewish Democrat, Andy Levin, whom Israel hawks believed was insufficiently supportive of the Jewish state. Now she is finished. At best, she will be a footnote: one of the very last pure AIPAC Democrats. Like the Rockefeller Republicans of old, she and her cause will fade into history.

sources.news_title: Abdul El-Sayed Beats the Democratic Establishment and AIPAC in Michigan
sources.text:
Despite record amounts of outside spending and attacks from the Democratic establishment, Abdul El-Sayed prevailed in a bitter primary race for the U.S. Senate seat in Michigan.
Voters in the key swing state chose El-Sayed over the establishment’s choice of Rep. Haley Stevens, whose campaign received about $60 million in support from pro-corporate and pro-Israel super PACs, making the race the most expensive Democratic primary ever. El-Sayed won by a margin of around 1 percentage point, according to The Associated Press, which called the race in his favor Wednesday morning.
The victory of El-Sayed, a former public health official endorsed by Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, is the latest sign of the growing influence of the Democratic left. And it’s the most staggering illustration yet of the party establishment’s waning grip on power and the unpopularity of the pro-Israel lobby giant, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, amid shifting American sentiment on Israel and Palestine.
Through its super PAC, the United Democracy Project, AIPAC broke its own single-race spending record by funding $30 million in attack ads against El-Sayed. Ads that dominated airwaves, flooded streaming services, and stuffed mailboxes in the final month of the race misrepresented El-Sayed’s previous comments about Michelle Obama and Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer to allege misogyny, and attempted to paint El-Sayed as a terrorist sympathizer.
El-Sayed’s platform, boosted by an army of 12,000 door-knocking volunteers, centered on policies such as Medicare for All policy, addressing cost of living issues in the state, and removing corporate spending from politics. But it was the two candidates’ stances on Israel and Palestine that came to define the race. El-Sayed condemned Israel’s genocide of Palestinians in Gaza and committed to ending U.S. military aid to Israel. His criticism of Israel also extended to its joint U.S. war on Iran, which he decried as military glut that could be spent instead on healthcare and education in his state.
Stevens opposed any conditioning of military aid to Israel. She has consistently voted in favor of weapons transfers since first assuming office in 2019, including last month when she sided with Republicans against an amendment in a Pentagon budget bill that would have cut military spending for Israel. When AIPAC began pouring money into the Stevens campaign, El-Sayed effectively turned those millions of dollars into a key campaign issue, pointing to Stevens as an illustration of the danger of lobby spending and corporate money in politics.
It’s not the first race in Michigan shaped by AIPAC money. Former Rep. Andy Levin — who was considered the most progressive Jewish member of the House because of his support for Palestinian statehood — lost his seat after redistricting forced a showdown with Stevens in 2022. In that race, Levin was also dramatically outspent by outside money, with AIPAC buying $4 million in ads to attack him and boost Stevens.
El-Sayed’s success, however, shows a major shift in politics since the start of Israel’s most recent war on Gaza. Cutting off military support to Israel has become a mainstream position among Democrats. And AIPAC has since become a politically toxic entity — “a four letter word in Democratic politics,” Levin told The Intercept.
“Most people still don’t vote on Israel and Palestine, they vote on their pocketbooks,” said Levin, who endorsed El-Sayed. “But if you’re not willing to say that Israel perpetrated a genocide in Gaza, Democratic primary voters are like, ‘OK, you’re bought and paid.’ The kind of truth-telling about Israel and Palestine is tied into the truth-telling about the economy, and people wanting real solutions.”
Leftists have claimed victories against establishment picks throughout this year’s midterm primaries, running on similar platforms addressing affordability and support for Palestine. But those wins have so far been in House races, mostly in metropolitan areas where leftist progressive politics have gained a foothold in recent years, such as New York, Pennsylvania, Colorado, New Jersey, and California. In House races in Michigan, leftists also found success with wins for Donavan McKinney, a state representative who defeated the AIPAC-backed incumbent Democratic Rep. Shri Thanedar, and Will Lawrence, a progressive climate activist who beat a pair of moderate Democratic opponents.
Both McKinney and Lawrence, a co-founder of the youth-led Sunrise Movement, had an endorsement from Sanders and a mutual endorsement from El-Sayed. And both ran on a similar platform of lowering the cost of living and opposing war — including Israel’s genocide in Gaza — and for Lawrence, opposing AI data centers. While McKinney is expected to win the general election in a solid blue district, Lawrence now faces a Republican incumbent, Rep. Tom Barrett, in a purple district that had previously been held by Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin.
El-Sayed’s win is the first leftist victory in a Senate race this election cycle.
Unlike other leftist wins so far in the midterms outside of Michigan, El-Sayed faces a difficult challenge in the general election from a formidable Trump-endorsed opponent. Polls have shown El-Sayed neck-and-neck with Republican Mike Rogers, a former congressman and FBI agent who ran unopposed in Tuesday’s primary. In 2024, Rogers ran for Senate and lost to Slotkin by less than 20,000 votes. In Michigan, where voters swung for Trump by about 1 percentage point over Kamala Harris in 2024, the November election is expected to be the most significant midterm test for the left. An El-Sayed win in November is essential to the Democratic effort to regain control of the Senate.
Electability has been among the largest criticisms from Stevens and her supporters against El-Sayed. Conventional establishment thinking maintains that progressive policy is not popular among most Americans. To beat Republicans, the centrists say, Democrats need to run a more moderate candidate who can appeal to more conservative voters. Late last month, the Stevens campaign circulated a quote from Rogers, who called El-Sayed “radical” and claimed “I don’t think he likes America.” Stevens suggested Rogers would prefer to face El-Sayed because of his leftist platform.
Last week, Rep. Hillary Scholten, D-Mich., a Stevens surrogate, said El-Sayed was so polarizing that she could not back him against Rogers in the general election. “I will not stand beside someone who has allowed distinctly anti-American sentiment to enter our public dialogue,” she said, a reference to his campaign events in April where political streamer and commentator Hasan Piker stumped with El-Sayed at university campuses. Despite efforts by the Stevens campaign, AIPAC, and corporate media outlets to play up Piker’s comments faulting U.S. foreign policy for 9/11, there’s little evidence that criticism has resonated with voters.
The National Republican Senatorial Committee released its first attack ad against the “radical” El-Sayed on Wednesday, referring to him by his full name and referring to Piker’s 9/11 comments, a preview of the continued anti-Muslim and anti-Arab tactics that are expected to ratchet up in the general.
The progressive left has long argued that its platform will perform better in front of a broader electorate hungry for political and economic change. Michiganders have paved the way for El-Sayed to try and prove just that. His fate in the general election might reverberate into the 2028 campaign cycle, as the Democratic Party looks to decide what type of candidate to nominate for president.
Soon after NBC News made its call, state Sen. Mallory McMorrow — who dropped out of the U.S. Senate race in July — offered her endorsement to El-Sayed. On Wednesday, Stevens — along with Democratic minority leader Sen. Chuck Schumer and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand — endorsed El-Sayed. Stevens said she had spoken with El-Sayed and was “proud to offer my support as he takes on Mike Rogers in the general election.”
“We’re gonna build a movement that reaches out to everybody — I know not everybody’s gonna agree with me on everything, that’s not how this works. But I know they agree with me on the need to beat Mike Rogers and the need to hold Donald Trump accountable, and the need to provide people healthcare, and the need to address the affordability crisis,” El-Sayed said at the Wednesday press conference, flanked by McMorrow and Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel Jr. “I’m looking forward to unifying together,”
El-Sayed argues the same anti-corporate messaging that has appealed to his progressive base translates to all voters, transcending partisan political framing. A week before Tuesday’s primary, El-Sayed told The Intercept’s Akela Lacy, “Most people don’t walk around asking, ‘Where do I sit on the left–right spectrum?’ Most people are walking around asking, ‘What the hell’s going to happen if I get sick? What’s going to happen if I lose my home or I lose my job?’ … I think those are the things that unite most Michiganders … I’m looking to build a movement that pushes back on the bipartisan consensus that we ought to build a politics that is paid for by corporations.”
Levin said that voters want a candidate who is “authentic,” “brave,” and “speaks truth to power.” He pointed to Michigan’s historic embrace of progressive Democratic politics, such as the nominations of Jesse Jackson’s presidential candidacy in 1988 and Sanders’s in 2016.
It was in Michigan where Democrats in 2024 started the Uncommitted Movement as a protest against the Biden administration’s support of Israel during its genocidal war in Gaza. El-Sayed voted “uncommitted” in that primary. Stevens and her surrogates have attacked his “uncommitted” vote to try and show El-Sayed’s lack of loyalty to the party, despite his immediate endorsement of Harris one day after Biden dropped out of the running.
Levin describes Michigan as the “ultimate swing state,” but cautioned that many political pundits misunderstand what that says about the state’s electorate.
“People act like it means we all must run to the mushy middle. But that’s not what a swing is at all. If a swing just sat in the middle, you would never get on it. It’d be boring. That’s not what it’s about,” Levin said. “We have to realize that ‘swing’ means that people go back and forth. And people in both parties right now — this is national — they are so sick of politics. They are so sick of the money in politics. They are so sick of the rich people and the corporations and the special interests [that] basically do whatever they want in American politics.”
Update: August 5, 2026, 1:22 p.m. ET
This article was updated to include news of Donavan McKinney’s victory, a National Republican Senatorial Committee attack ad, Haley Stevens’s endorsement of Abdul El-Sayed, and remarks from El-Sayed’s victory speech.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

sources.news_title: Abdul El-Sayed Ekes Out Victory In Closer Than Expected Primary
sources.text:
Former public health official Abdul El-Sayed defeated Democratic Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens in the Democratic Senate primary Tuesday, dealing another blow to establishment Democrats and the pro-Israel lobby.
El-Sayed beat Stevens in a 48.5% to 47.5% vote after receiving endorsements from independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, Democratic New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Democratic Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren and other far-left Democrats, results from The Associated Press showed. While establishment Democrats supported Stevens, the pro-Israel lobby spent millions to help Stevens win.
Stevens has served in the House since 2019, flipping her seat from red to blue. In the Senate race, she supported reforming rather than abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement, implementing a public option over Medicare for All and expressing strong support for Israel.
El-Sayed campaigned on supporting Medicare for All, abolishing ICE, codifying abortion into law and permitting so-called “gender-affirming care,” according to his campaign website. He rejected the socialist label, stating that he is a “capitalist” who wanted to regulate monopolies and oligopolies.
“I’m not a socialist. I’m just a capitalist who understands how capitalism works,” El-Sayed said. “I think government ought to be there to regulate monopolies and oligopolies so that everybody can actually participate in the economy without having to be forced to pay more or get paid less.”
Sanders said in a campaign advertisement that the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and further-left candidates are “taking on the establishment.”
“We are taking on the establishment all over this country. All over the country, ordinary people, unionists, young people, people of color [are] getting involved in the political process and they’re saying wait a minute, maybe the Democratic Party should belong to us and not just wealthy campaign contributors. And then in the midst of this comes Dr. Abdul El-Sayed,” Sanders said.
The Michigan Senate primary is a fight as to whether billionaires and their super PACs will continue to control American politics, or whether we can have a government that represents working families.
Tomorrow is Election Day in MI. Let’s elect Abdul El-Sayed. pic.twitter.com/o1auzEzjMU
Stevens received the establishment’s backing, including from Democratic Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, Michigan Sen. Gary Peters, South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn and Delaware Sen. Chris Coons. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer quietly supported Stevens behind the scenes and asked party donors to support her, according to The New York Times. He said in June that Stevens had the “best chance of winning,” to Punchbowl News. (RELATED: Establishment Dems Forced To Cover Left Flank In Vital Swing-State Primary)
Michigan, this is OUR moment. Vote Tuesday, August 4th. pic.twitter.com/2V7iCPR58b
— Dr. Abdul El-Sayed (@AbdulElSayed) August 4, 2026
Former Republican Michigan Rep. Mike Rogers, the presumptive GOP nominee in the race, led El-Sayed by 10 points in a hypothetical matchup, according to a Michigan Education survey from July 28. The poll showed that Rogers was almost tied with Stevens, as Stevens narrowly led him 46% to 45%.
About $80 million had been spent on the Michigan Senate race, making it one of the most expensive races in the U.S., according to CBS News. Around $60 million had been spent on Stevens’ behalf, much of it coming from the pro-Israel lobby.
About 31% of donors who gave at least $200 to Stevens’ Senate campaign also donated to AIPAC since the start of 2025, The Detroit News reported in May. An AIPAC affiliate spent more than $5 million between campaign donations and independent expenditures in 2022, the last time Stevens ran in a House primary.
During a July 28 debate, El-Sayed attacked Stevens for receiving money from the pro-Israel lobby. Stevens doubled down on her support for Israel, arguing that she supported a two-state solution and “long-term peace.”
El-Sayed accused Israel of committing “genocide” in Gaza and criticized U.S. aid to the country. U.S. support for Israel has become a divisive issue within the Democratic Party, as 103 Democratic members of Congress voted for Republican Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie’s amendment to slash $3.3 billion in foreign aid to Israel.

“I am gonna be telling the stories on our behalf. And you better believe I’m gonna be doing it with a little bit of joy, a little bit of enthusiasm, a little bit of energy and a little bit of stick it to ‘em. Because that’s the Michigan way,” Stevens said.
A campaign speech that's got everyone scratching their head.
Democratic Senate candidate Haley Stevens is facing a wave of online mockery after an "awkward" campaign pep talk urging supporters to "stick it to them" went viral, with critics zeroing in on her delivery and style. pic.twitter.com/0JyBJXNNlP
El-Sayed led Stevens by a 15-point margin as of Thursday, according to an Emerson College Polling/WLNS/WOODTV survey.
