Adriano Espaillat in New York’s 13th district in June, while socialist Melat Kiros beat incumbent Democratic Colorado Rep. Diana DeGette, who served 29 years in Congress.

sources.news_title: Abdul El-Sayed projected to win Michigan Democratic Senate primary, defeating Haley Stevens
sources.text:
Abdul El-Sayed projected to win Michigan Democratic Senate primary, defeating Haley Stevens
Washington — Former Michigan health official Abdul El-Sayed defeated Rep. Haley Stevens in the Democratic Senate primary in Michigan, CBS News projects, in a closely watched contest that represented the latest test of the party's divisions.
El-Sayed, 41, ran on a leftist platform and secured the backing of prominent progressives like Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and independent Sen. Bernie Sanders in the primary, which became a distinct choice between diverging factions of the Democratic Party after a third candidate, state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, dropped out of the race last month. Stevens, a 43-year-old who has represented Michigan in the House since 2019, was recruited by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and took a more moderate lane, securing an endorsement from outgoing popular Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer last month.
The pivotal primary contest opened up after Democratic Sen. Gary Peters announced he wouldn't seek reelection, setting up a competitive race in the state.
With the primary victory, El-Sayed is set to take on former Rep. Mike Rogers in November. Rogers ran unopposed in the Republican primary, after narrowly losing to Sen. Elissa Slotkin in the 2024 race for Michigan's other Senate seat, giving him months to home in on his general election pitch while Democrats' primary fight grew increasingly ugly.
Stevens congratulated El-Sayed on Wednesday morning, while offering her support as he prepares to take on Rogers in November.
"Donald Trump and Mike Rogers want us to come out of this primary tired and divided, so their billionaire backers can come in and let multimillionaire Mike Rogers walk away with this Senate seat," Stevens said, while warning of the broader implications for the Senate should the GOP flip the seat. "I'm not going to let that happen."
Addressing supporters and reporters Wednesday morning, El-Sayed called Stevens a "colleague and friend." He said they had a "great conversation" and acknowledged the primary race ended bitterly.
"Whatever differences that we might have had in the primary, they pale in comparison to what unifies us: a recognition that so long as we want to keep our democracy, that democracy better be working for people, and that all of us have to come together to make sure that we never let Mike Rogers see the inside of the U.S. Senate," he said.
Asked by CBS News' Ed O'Keefe about concerns from Jewish voters after El-Sayed responded to March's attack on a Detroit-area synagogue by saying, in part, that "hurt people hurt people," he stood by what he said and reiterated his condemnation of the attack.
"What I mean is that hurt people hurt people, that maybe if we're serious about ending the hurt, we should stop hurting people, that's what I mean," he said. "I condemn the attack. It was a vile, antisemitic attack."
El-Sayed went on to criticize Republicans, who he said were "actively hurting people," and said he stood in solidarity with Jewish people.
"We can condemn antisemitism, and at the same time, we can be talking about how we bring people together, and we can be talking about everybody's pain, and I think anybody who does not want to do that is not serious about actually addressing the hurt that we see across the board," he said.
El-Sayed added that his commitment to Jewish safety is the same as his commitment to his children. "That's the highest commitment I can offer as a father," he said.
The seat in Michigan is considered among the most vulnerable for Democrats this cycle in a state that has flipped between supporting Democrats and Republican presidents in recent elections. National Democrats, who backed Stevens, pitched her as the more electable candidate, citing El-Sayed's more left-leaning views and arguing that they are out of step with the battleground state.
Asked about the dynamic, El-Sayed told O'Keefe ahead of the primary that "it's always funny to me that people want to say that this state votes for moderates when it voted for Donald Trump twice."
"It may just be that the better explanation is not that the state wants moderates, it's that it's so sick and tired of the establishment bought off by corporations on both sides of the political aisle, that it was willing to hold its nose and vote for Donald Trump twice," he added. "Now, what happens if the alternative to the bought-off establishment happens to be instead of a narcissistic, megalomaniacal billionaire, a doctor who rebuilds health departments to eliminate medical debt and put glasses on kids' faces? I'm willing to test that proposition."
El-Sayed's victory comes after a series of primary wins by insurgent Democrats in places like New York City and Colorado in recent months, as progressives and democratic socialists seek changes to the party. The dynamic has been a defining feature of the primary cycle so far. But how it will play in November — especially in battleground states like Michigan — remains to be seen.
El-Sayed, who is not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America but has welcomed its members into his coalition, has run on progressive policies like Medicare for All, and he's been an outspoken critic of Israel's government and the war in Gaza. The issue has been central to the campaign in the Great Lakes State, which is home to the largest concentration of Arabs in the U.S. And he hammered Stevens throughout the campaign for receiving an influx of funding from pro-Israel groups, while receiving criticism himself for campaigning with left-wing podcaster Hasan Piker.
The seat in Michigan is among a handful that Democrats are defending this cycle, while they look to flip seats elsewhere to secure control of the upper chamber. With 53 Republicans in the Senate, Democrats need to flip four seats, while fending off GOP inroads in Michigan and elsewhere to take the majority.
Schumer and Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, the chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, praised El-Sayed in a joint statement following his projected victory for running an "energetic campaign that inspired thousands of Michiganders across the state."
"Democrats are united by a common purpose: putting a check on Donald Trump by defeating his Republican enablers and taking back the Senate," the Democrats said. "We look forward to working with Abdul and Democrats across Michigan to win this seat in November."

sources.news_title: Michigan progressive El-Sayed wins Democratic Senate primary
sources.text:
Abdul El-Sayed has won Michigan’s Democratic U.S. Senate nomination, defeating Rep. Haley Stevens in a major victory for progressives in the key battleground state.
The real test of El-Sayed’s and progressives’ strength will now come in a November matchup against Republican Mike Rogers, a former congressman who ran unopposed for the GOP nomination.
The seat is pivotal to Democrats’ chances of flipping the Senate and El-Sayed will face the challenge of uniting a divided Democratic base after a bruising primary.
The race remained tight throughout Tuesday night, with a winner not declared until early Wednesday. In his final remarks at a primary night party before the race was called, El-Sayed said "tomorrow we begin to mend fences."
El-Sayed’s win represents a significant shift for the Democratic Party. In 2018, he lost the gubernatorial primary to now-Gov. Gretchen Whitmer by 21 percentage points.
A former health official, El-Sayed campaigned on "Medicare for All," halting military aid to Israel and campaign finance reform. He had support from progressive leaders, including Sen. Bernie Sanders and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who framed the race as a grassroots-focused movement and a broader fight against the establishment and big-money spending.
Stevens, a more moderate candidate, was backed by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and tens of millions in outside spending, including the American Israel Public Affairs Committee’s largest outlay ever in a single race.
Now comes the more difficult challenge for Democrats: uniting the party to defeat Rogers, for whom Republicans have already reserved large sums of money ahead of the general election. Democrats consider the seat a must-win if they are to flip control of the Senate this year.

sources.news_title: Abdul El-Sayed’s win tees up the first true swing state test for the Bernie left
sources.text:
Abdul El-Sayed has defeated Haley Stevens in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary — albeit by a significantly smaller margin than preelection polling suggested. He’s beaten back $30 million in AIPAC spending and endorsements from top Democrats, including Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, who backed Stevens. Now he’s moving on to face the GOP nominee, former Rep. Mike Rogers, in a contest crucial to determining Senate control.
Abdul El-Sayed’s win tees up the first true swing-state test for the Bernie left
Left candidates have romped in blue state primaries. A Michigan general election will be a different challenge.
So the next question is: Can El-Sayed beat a Republican?
That will be a cinch, some in his camp claim. “For progressives, getting out of the primary is a far more difficult battle than winning in the general,” left-wing streamer Hasan Piker told CNN last week.
But the reality is that we’ve had very few true tests of how candidates associated with the left flank of the party — and specifically with the Bernie Sanders-backed revolt against the establishment — would fare in competitive swing-state general elections.
Which means that this would be one of the first such tests, and that its outcome will have enormous stakes for the party’s future.
El-Sayed’s views on Israel and his prospective history-making turn as the first-ever Muslim senator have gotten much coverage. But El-Sayed is also a dyed-in-the-wool member of the Sanders faction, having been closely aligned with Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez since his first political campaign in 2018. Both have campaigned for him this cycle.
If El-Sayed defeats Rogers convincingly (he’s personally predicting a 7-point victory as his baseline), he’ll become a megastar and even possibly a presidential contender. He’ll arguably be the first to prove that the Sanders formula — attacking billionaires, corporate influence, and the party establishment, while backing sweeping social welfare spending like Medicare-for-all — can win over voters who once backed President Donald Trump.
“If Abdul El-Sayed beats Stevens I actually think he’s very likely to be the next president,” Nathan J. Robinson, editor-in-chief of the socialist publication Current Affairs, posted on X last month. “If he wins the general, it’s over for centrist Dems.”
Conversely, if El-Sayed — who has trailed Rogers in recent polls — loses, skeptics may conclude that the left can’t appeal to the country’s true swing voters, and that nominating a leftist for president in 2028, or in downballot races, is too big of a risk.
The core disagreement: Will the left’s approach succeed in the general election?
Over the past decade, it has become an article of faith across much of the left that their particular populist approach to economics and foreign policy would be potent in a general election.
They argue that typical Democrats have a more compromised platform and timid style, lacking the populist fire that can win over disaffected Americans. “Bernie would’ve won” in 2016, the saying goes, by using his outsider credibility and ambitious plans to appeal to the working-class voters and independents that went for Trump. Kamala Harris’s defeat, amid intense criticism on the left over her and Joe Biden’s support for Israel, further bolstered their sense that the party establishment just can’t get it done.
Now, left factionalists are pointing to their several high-profile primary victories this year and arguing that energy and enthusiasm are on their side — and would translate to the general election too.
Many mainstream Democrats see this as naive. They believe that while talk of “socialism” and other far-left positions might work fine in deep blue cities and districts, it could well prove toxic in swing states that have voted for Trump. While public opinion on certain issues has moved in the left’s direction, especially Israel, candidates could have a tougher time on issues like crime, where El-Sayed has offered nuanced explanations of his “defund the police” rhetoric from 2020.
“Winning a Democratic primary means close to nothing when it comes to the general election, because these are functionally different voter pools,” Lakshya Jain of the center-left publication The Argument recently wrote.
Some analysts pointed to the primary results as a potential harbinger of general election struggles, with El-Sayed performing poorly against Stevens in the kinds of rural areas that have swung toward Republicans in the Trump era.
Are there past examples of Bernie-aligned candidates making it to tough general elections?
But even though the “Bernie vs. the establishment” battle has been raging on and off for the past decade, there have been very few clean tests about how Bernie-backed candidates would do in swing states.
Sanders never won the presidential nomination, and candidates aligned with him have generally preferred to run in strongly Democratic areas where, if they win the primary, the general election is a fait accompli. The now-expanding “squad” of left-wing House members that began with Reps. Ocasio-Cortez, Ilhan Omar, Rashida Tlaib, and Ayanna Pressley all fit this model.
There have, however, been a few past examples where Sanders-aligned candidates have made it to the general election in tough territory.
One is Andrew Gillum, whose 2018 bid for governor of Florida was backed by Sanders and other progressive groups, including billionaire Tom Steyer’s network. He won the nomination over establishment favorite Gwen Graham — but then went on to lose the general election to Ron DeSantis by a mere four-tenths of a percentage point, ushering in what became the era of Deep Red Florida.
In nominating Gillum, did the left blow a winnable race amid a national Democratic wave? Maybe — but one counterargument is that longtime Sen. Bill Nelson, a thoroughly mainstream Democrat, lost his seat by a similarly tight margin in that same election. Florida may have just been trending redder generally. Gillum’s post-election personal struggles also color views of his candidacy today.
That same cycle, in Nebraska, Kara Eastman upset the establishment favorite to win the nomination for a swing House district. (Sanders hadn’t endorsed her in the primary, but she ran on a platform of Medicare-for-all and free college.) She lost in 2018 — and again in 2020, even though Joe Biden won her district — and has been viewed inside the party as a cautionary tale about blowing a winnable race ever since.
The outcome was happier for Keith Ellison, a close Sanders ally who won his race to be Minnesota’s attorney general in 2018. Yet his margin of victory — about 4 percentage points — wasn’t particularly impressive in a lean blue state in a strongly Democratic year when Tim Walz won the governor’s race by 11. Later, when Ellison ran for reelection in 2022, he eked out a win by less than 1 point while Walz won by 8.
John Fetterman was generally understood to be a “Bernie faction” candidate when he ran for an open US Senate seat in Pennsylvania in 2022. (Sanders stayed neutral in the primary that year, but had backed Fetterman’s earlier lieutenant governor campaign and championed him in the general election.) But he wasn’t exactly running on a bold left platform — he backed off his past Medicare-for-all support and was pro-fracking.
Fetterman ended up winning by 5 points even though it was a favorable cycle for Republicans — but simultaneously, the more centrist Josh Shapiro won the governor’s race by 15. However, Shapiro’s opponent was believed to be weaker and more extreme, and the stroke Fetterman suffered that year complicates efforts to read too much into his performance.
Separate from his electoral performance, Fetterman’s association with the Sanders left ended years ago as his politics moved to the right; lately, there has been talk he might switch parties. This has also fueled arguments from moderates that populist outsider candidates are less reliable than more conventional ones even if they do manage to win.
El-Sayed is running on a bold left platform in a true swing state
Taking this grab bag of outcomes together, one can see why mainstream Democrats might be skeptical that the left has the secret sauce to win swing voters. But each race has had its own unique circumstances and complications.
Furthermore, in this cycle, the electorate could be in a different place — more disenchanted by the establishment and more willing to take a chance on further-left candidates.
Graham Platner was set to be the great hope for the Sanders faction until his Senate campaign was derailed by scandal and he was replaced on the ballot by Troy Jackson — another Sanders-aligned candidate, albeit one with his own long history in state politics. But though Jackson is facing a formidable Republican incumbent, Maine is a blue state that hasn’t backed a GOP presidential candidate since 1988.
Michigan is tougher turf, having voted for Trump in two of the past three presidential elections. The conventional wisdom for how a Democrat can win a race there is to run a cautious campaign, being careful not to alienate potentially winnable Republican and independent voters. A good example is Gary Peters, the departing two-term senator El-Sayed is running to replace, who’s a traditional pro-union Democrat known for keeping a low profile in general.
El-Sayed is not doing that. He supports Medicare-for-all, a billionaire wealth tax, abolishing ICE, and a full arms embargo on Israel. While El-Sayed is not a democratic socialist, he’s very closely tied to Sanders and Ocasio-Cortez — the trio held hands and raised their arms together at a recent rally, in an image Michigan voters may well see in GOP-funded attack ads.
And back in 2020, El-Sayed expressed sympathy with activists calling to “defund the police” and said most major cities spend far too much on police departments, though he’s tried to downplay those views this cycle.
“I’m worried that he’s more passionate about attacking other Dems than Republicans and may not be ready for what’s coming,” Adam Jentleson, president of the center-left Searchlight Institute, posted on X recently.
Now that he’s won the primary, El-Sayed will get the chance to try and show he’s ready — and to test whether his bold left platform will be his greatest asset, or a millstone.

sources.news_title: Abdul El-Sayed Triumphs In Michigan In Major Victory For Progressives
sources.text:
Former public health official Abdul El-Sayed is projected to win the Democratic primary for Michigan’s U.S. Senate seat, defying more than $50 million worth of super PAC spending supporting his opponent to claim one of the biggest victories in the history of the modern progressive movement.
El-Sayed topped moderate Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) and will now face former Rep. Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee, in November in a major test of whether progressives can triumph in the nation’s most critical battleground states.
The Associated Press called the race on Wednesday, with El-Sayed leading Stevens, 48.5% to 47.5%. State Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who officially dropped out of the race last month, nonetheless earned 4% of the vote.
The contest was unexpectedly close. Polls in the weeks leading up to the primary had pointed to a double-digit win for El-Sayed, but Stevens turned in an unexpectedly strong performance in many parts of rural Michigan where progressive candidates have won in the past.
Stevens won by a significant margin in Detroit, but El-Sayed racked up large margins in many of the state’s college towns, held his own in the suburbs, and dominated in Grand Rapids, the state’s second-biggest population center.
Progressives will nonetheless count his narrow victory as a stinging rebuke to the establishment of both parties and proof of both the popularity of a populist economic message and of the unpopularity of unblinking support for Israel within the Democratic Party.
A brash and unapologetic personality, El-Sayed campaigned with the backing of Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and summarized his campaign with a pithy three-part slogan: “Money out of politics, money in your pocket and Medicare for all.” He defined himself in part by his enemies, regularly noting a super PAC with ties to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee spent more than $30 million opposing his candidacy.
Appearing on MSNOW on Tuesday morning, El-Sayed said his campaign was about more than simply changing the Democratic Party, and he reached out to those who had backed Stevens.
“This is not about the future of a party,” he said. “This is about the future of the people of the state of Michigan who deserve to know that their roads are competent, deserve to know where they’ll get their healthcare when they need it, who deserve to know that their kids go to great schools.”
He added: “This is a big movement. And in order for us to build together, we’re going to have to be able to come together around the things that unite us. It’s the feeling that we get when we look our kids in the eye. It’s the feeling that we get when we think about what our country ought to be. And it’s the opportunity we have to take on all that Donald Trump has done to corrupt our country and to corrupt our government.
Stevens, the preferred candidate of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand, proved to be an awkward-at-best fit for the Democratic primary electorate. A longtime ally of AIPAC, she favored unquestioned weapons transfers to Israel, a nation most Democratic voters believe is committing genocide. She welcomed corporate PAC donations and tried to focus her campaign on revitalizing manufacturing in Michigan.
Stevens also attracted the near-unanimous support of the local party establishment, with outgoing Sen. Gary Peters, former Sen. Debbie Stabenow and Gov. Gretchen Whitmer all endorsing her and insisting she gave the party the best chance to win in November.
All of those leaders quickly rallied behind El-Sayed on Wednesday morning.
“Abdul El-Sayed has run an energetic campaign that inspired thousands of Michiganders across the state, with a clear focus on lowering costs and standing up for working families,” Schumer and Gillibrand said in a joint statement. “Democrats are united by a common purpose: putting a check on Donald Trump by defeating his Republican enablers and taking back the Senate. We look forward to working with Abdul and Democrats across Michigan to win this seat in November.
Republicans will welcome an El-Sayed victory, believing he will be the easier candidate to defeat in November. Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC, released a digital ad shortly after his victory attacking him for old statements he made questioning whether police officers needed to carry guns and suggesting he would not have spent state money enforcing federal immigration law.
“From calling to disarm the police to his close ties to extremist figures, Abdul El-Sayed is uniquely dangerous and unqualified,” said Alex Latcham, the group’s executive director.
But the political environment distinctly favors Democrats, and El-Sayed has already declared his intention to attack Rogers harshly.
“He generally has the charisma of a doorknob,” El-Sayed told HuffPost in an interview last month. “He carries all the MAGA baggage, but he also has the aesthetic of the guy at a country club who sneers at you from his Lincoln.”
Compared with some other progressive candidates, El-Sayed boasts traditional credentials. The son of Egyptian immigrants, he was the class speaker at his graduation from the University of Michigan and a Rhodes scholar. He graduated from medical school but decided to become a professor and public health official rather than go through a residency after realizing how many people struggled to afford care.
He left his position as Detroit’s public health officer to run for governor in 2018, losing badly in the Democratic primary to Whitmer. He became a podcaster with Crooked Media, was a prominent surrogate for Sanders’ 2020 presidential bid and then became the lead public health official in Wayne County, Michigan.

sources.text:
Politics
JUST IN: Socialist-Backed Candidate Defeats Dem Rep. In Pivotal Senate Primary
Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan’s bruising Democratic Senate primary Tuesday, defeating Rep. Haley Stevens and handing the party’s progressive wing a major victory in one of the most important battleground states in the country.
The former public health official now advances to a high-stakes November matchup against former Rep. Mike Rogers, who coasted to the Republican nomination without opposition.
The race will help decide which party controls the Senate.
El-Sayed’s win came after Stevens and her allies tried to bury him under a massive outside-spending operation backed by the Democratic establishment.
Gov. Gretchen Whitmer endorsed Stevens late last month, a move widely viewed as an emergency attempt to stop El-Sayed’s rise.
It did not work.
El-Sayed overcame nearly $65 million in outside spending and a party establishment that lined up behind Stevens, who also had the backing of retiring Sen. Gary Peters.
Peters’ decision not to seek a third term opened the seat, creating a top Republican pickup opportunity in a state President Donald Trump won in 2016 and 2024.
Trump endorsed Rogers early, helping clear the GOP field and allowing Republicans to avoid the kind of expensive primary fight Democrats just endured.
Trump weighed in on El-Sayed’s performance during a Tuesday night interview on Fox News, warning that candidates backed by democratic socialists or their allies would be disastrous for the country.
“You go to these cities that are taken over by the socialists and the communists, they’re always filthy, dirty. They’re disgusting,” Trump claimed in the interview. He added, “Aside from crime, aside from all of the other problems — no jobs, no anything, no money — they’re always filthy, disgusting, dirty, and that’s what you’ll get.”
El-Sayed has not been endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America and has told The Wall Street Journal that he is “not technically or practically DSA.”
But he was backed on the trail by two of the left’s biggest names: Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York.
Trump said Tuesday that Rogers would be in a stronger position against El-Sayed than against Stevens.
Trump told Fox News on Tuesday that he thinks Rogers will “do much better against Abdul than he’s going to do against the congresswoman.”
National Republicans had made little secret of their view that El-Sayed would be the easier Democrat to beat in November.
The National Republican Senatorial Committee even produced a digital ad emphasizing El-Sayed’s progressive credentials and Sanders endorsement, a move widely seen as an effort to elevate him in the primary.
El-Sayed campaigned on Medicare for All, fierce opposition to corporate money in politics and sharp criticism of Stevens over her support for aid to Israel.
He also accused Israel of committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, a position that carried particular weight in Michigan, home to large Muslim and Arab American communities.
The Israel issue helped define the race.
AIPAC and affiliated groups spent close to $30 million backing Stevens, the group’s largest investment ever in a single race, according to AP.
Overall, Stevens and her allies spent nearly nine times as much on advertising as El-Sayed and his allied groups did, according to AdImpact.
El-Sayed turned that spending gap into a central part of his message.
“If you need a $60 million crutch, you probably can’t be elected on your own terms,” El-Sayed said at a debate last week in Detroit.
Stevens, a four-term congresswoman, ran as the establishment Democrat with endorsements from Whitmer, Peters and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York.
El-Sayed countered with Sanders, Ocasio-Cortez and the United Auto Workers, a major prize in a state built around the auto industry.
The final stretch grew even uglier after state Sen. Mallory McMorrow dropped out of the race.
POLL: Will You Support Trump And His Candidates In The Midterms?
McMorrow had tried to position herself as a middle lane between Stevens and El-Sayed, but her exit left the race as a direct clash between the party’s establishment and its insurgent left.
After the race was called, McMorrow quickly endorsed El-Sayed and urged Democrats to unite.
“I’m proud to give Abdul my full endorsement and support as we head to November together as a unified party,” McMorrow said in an emailed statement. “Take it from me — this was a brutal primary. But whatever differences there were between the candidates in this race, those differences are nothing compared to the contrast in November.”
Stevens had spent the final days arguing that El-Sayed was too focused on national progressive politics and not enough on Michigan.
Her campaign leaned into that message after audio leaked from a donor call in which El-Sayed said a win in Michigan could echo into 2028 and inspire primary challenges against Democrats such as Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, who has angered the left.
RELATED: CNN Flips, Exposes Top Dem Senate Candidate In Michigan
On that call, El-Sayed characterized such a move as putting “an ogre on a pike,” rhetoric some Democrats believed was aimed at Stevens, though El-Sayed had previously described Fetterman as an “ogre.”
Stevens used the episode at last week’s debate to cast herself as the candidate more connected to ordinary Michigan voters.
“These folks are making fun of the way I sound,” Stevens said at last week’s debate. “But yet, I sound like the people who need help, who are talking to me about what they need.”
El-Sayed stayed on his anti-establishment theme.
“This is about whether or not you deserve a politics of the people, by the people and for the people,” he said at the debate, “or of the corporations, by the billionaires and for the special interests.”
His victory gives the left its biggest Midwest win of the cycle and gives Republicans a general-election contrast they were already eager to draw.
Michigan Democrats had a choice between a four-term congresswoman backed by their governor and a Sanders-AOC-backed progressive who ran against corporate power, Israel aid and the party’s donor class.
They chose El-Sayed.
Now Rogers gets the matchup Donald Trump wanted.

sources.news_title: How Abdul El-Sayed went from political oblivion to progressive breakthrough in Michigan Senate race
sources.text:
How Abdul El-Sayed went from political oblivion to progressive breakthrough in Michigan Senate race
DETROIT — Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official who harnessed Democratic frustration with the party establishment, narrowly defeated Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan’s U.S. Senate primary, setting up a crucial test for progressives in a key battleground state.
El-Sayed will face Republican Mike Rogers, a former congressman, in November in a race that will help determine control of the Senate. His first challenge will be unifying Democratic factions after a bitter primary that offered divergent visions for a party desperate for a path back to power.
The margin was extraordinarily close. El-Sayed walked off the stage at his Tuesday night election party without declaring victory, and the race was not called until early Wednesday, after nearly all ballots statewide had been counted. At the time The Associated Press declared him the winner, El-Sayed led Stevens by 14,893 votes — just under 1 percentage point — out of more than 1.5 million ballots counted, the most in recent state history.
The political significance of the result, however, extends well beyond the slim margin.
“Abdul’s victory was, in my opinion, the most extraordinary victory that I can think of in modern American politics,” said Sen. Bernie Sanders Wednesday, a leader of the progressive movement who was an early supporter of El-Sayed’s candidacy.
El-Sayed, 41, has never held elected office and entered the race seven years after losing Michigan’s Democratic gubernatorial primary by more than 20 percentage points. This time, running on an unapologetically progressive agenda, he overcame more than $60 million in outside spending and an opponent backed by many of Michigan’s top Democrats, including outgoing Sen. Gary Peters, and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer.
“In the words of Muhammad Ali, we shook up the world,” El-Sayed said early Wednesday, standing before The Spirit of Detroit, a landmark bronze statue in the city’s downtown.
El-Sayed went from political wilderness to progressive breakthrough
El-Sayed was joined on Wednesday by state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, a former opponent in the Senate primary, and Curtis Hertel, chair of the Michigan Democratic Party. It was an initial step toward a unified front after a bitter primary, and it reflected El-Sayed’s extraordinary political trajectory in less than a decade.
After losing the 2018 Democratic primary for governor to Gretchen Whitmer, El-Sayed retreated into the political wilderness. He started a podcast, wrote a book and became a regular presence on YouTube and television, slowly building a following while waiting for a political opening he did not know would come.
It arrived when Peters made the surprise announcement that he would not seek reelection, creating an open Senate seat in one of the country’s most competitive states.
El-Sayed launched his campaign in April 2025 with a staff of four. In his victory speech Wednesday, he recalled the small rooms that defined its early months.
“Back in April, I remember talking to a room of five people,” he said. “It was an opportunity for us to share a honest conversation about pain and about purpose. And I’ve been able to have 500 more of those discussions over the past 15 months.”
El-Sayed said he visited 110 cities and hosted more than 500 events. His volunteer network grew alongside the campaign, eventually reaching 12,000 people, according to his campaign.
Julie Brink, a 29-year-old volunteer from the Detroit area, said the campaign still felt like an “underdog” when she joined in February. From there, she said, it was “gaining momentum really consistently.”
“It was a lot of little things along the way,” Brink said. “The field narrowed and Abdul had consistent showing in debates and public appearances where he just cuts through the bullshit all the time.”
The campaign also embraced a media strategy that reflected El-Sayed’s years outside elected office, aggressively pursuing attention across traditional outlets, podcasts and online platforms. Some appearances, including multiple interviews with controversial streamer Hasan Piker, drew swift backlash.
A turning point came when an opponent dropped out
On July 5, McMorrow ended her campaign, leaving a two-person race between El-Sayed and Stevens. Soon after, El-Sayed stood before door-knocking volunteers in a Grand Rapids park and declared that “we have a chance of winning this election.”
“More importantly, we have a chance at winning our politics,” El-Sayed said. “What we’re doing is building a movement of the many against the money.”
In the final days, El-Sayed leaned even further into the strategy that had helped build his campaign. He marched through downtown Detroit alongside social media influencers, then attended a private pool party with content creators, including Piker.
On Election Day, El-Sayed did three interviews with content creators at Detroit’s Eastern Market before doing three more with traditional news organizations, including The Associated Press and MS NOW.
Hours later, the campaign that had once struggled to fill small rooms packed Detroit’s Majestic Theatre for an election night party.
Progressives see a test of their movement
El-Sayed’s victory gave progressives something they have been seeking — evidence that their politics could prevail not just in deep-blue cities and congressional districts, but in a Democratic primary in one of the nation’s premier swing states.
“Abdul El-Sayed is now the tip of the spear for the theory that shake-up-the-system economic fighters can win in swing states,” said Adam Green, co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee, who campaigned alongside El-Sayed in the final days.
The November race against Rogers, Green added, is “put up or shut up time” for the movement.
El-Sayed campaigned on “Medicare for All,” ending military aid to Israel and campaign finance reform. He had support from progressive leaders including Sanders and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who framed the race as both a grassroots movement and a broader fight against the establishment and big-money spending.
Outside groups backing Stevens ultimately spent more than $60 million, including more than $30 million from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee and its affiliates.
“We took on a machine,” El-Sayed said Wednesday.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, another progressive leader who endorsed El-Sayed, said the victory “should be a wake-up call to the Washington Democratic establishment.”
The harder test comes in November
El-Sayed now has three months to prove the movement that carried him through the primary can win a general election. Failure could be a dramatic setback for progressives, who have insisted for years that their approach could be more successful in a political era defined by President Donald Trump.
The Senate Republican campaign arm has already reserved $45 million in Michigan advertising to support Rogers, a number likely to grow as Republicans make clear they prefer their chances against El-Sayed.
AIPAC, which spent more money on Michigan's primary than any other race, also signaled Wednesday that its involvement would not end, saying it would oppose El-Sayed and “his radical anti-Israel agenda” in November.
The narrowness of El-Sayed’s victory also complicates any sweeping conclusions about what the result says about the Democratic Party. Nearly half of Tuesday’s primary voters backed Stevens, who argued throughout the campaign that her more moderate approach and history of winning competitive races made her better positioned to defeat Rogers.
Stevens called El-Sayed early Wednesday to concede the race, with El-Sayed describing it as a “great conversation.” She pledged her support for him, and Michigan Democrats are expected to gather for a unity breakfast Thursday before a public rally Friday.
Hertel, the state Democratic chair, said the primary’s ideological fight was not itself a problem, arguing that voters — rather than party leaders — should determine their direction.
“I don’t think that having a robust discussion is a bad thing,” Hertel said Wednesday. “What I think is important is that we are united afterwards.”
“We will unite together, and we will win this race,” Hertel added, “because we have to.”
—
Associated Press reporter Jacqueline GaNun contributed to this report in Detroit.

Ahead of November’s midterm elections, President Donald Trump is making a rare appearance in Nevada on Wednesday to sell voters on his handling of the economy against a backdrop of high interest rates, a national housing shortage and gasoline made more expensive by the Iran war.
He is seeking to shore up support for Republicans ahead of the November elections, which will determine which party controls Congress.
Abdul El-Sayed has won Michigan’s Democratic U.S. Senate nomination, defeating U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens in a massive victory for the party’s progressive wing in a battleground state. The real test will now come in a November matchup against Republican Mike Rogers for the seat, which is pivotal to Democrats’ chances of flipping the Senate.
The AP declared El-Sayed the winner after confirming Wednesday morning that there were simply not enough votes left to count that would allow Stevens to catch up. El-Sayed’s victory was so narrow that his victory wasn’t assured until almost all statewide ballots were counted. At the time AP declared him the winner, El-Sayed led Stevens by 14,893 votes — a margin of just under 1 percentage point — out of more than 1.5 million ballots counted. See full results.
Here is the latest:
Trump again insists that his White House ballroom is a ‘military complex’
The president told the Las Vegas crowd, “I’m building this big military complex” and that it includes “a lot of different things, and some of the things I can’t even talk about.”
Later, though, he said the project will still be a ballroom.
Trump originally said the ballroom that he demolished the White House’s East Wing to build would be paid for himself and some friendly donors. But costs have ballooned and Senate Republicans eventually tried to advance $1 billion in funding for White House security and military improvements as part of the new complex.
That proposal has since stalled. But Trump continues to say the ballroom will have strategic value, saying it will include things like drone ports.
After insulting Canadians, Trump promotes a mining project in Nevada by a Canadian firm
Trump in his speech brought up the development of one of the world’s largest lithium mines in northern America, the Thacker Pass project.
The U.S. government last year announced it was taking a minority stake in Vancouver-based Lithium Americas, which is jointly developing the mine with General Motors. The U.S. also took a 5% stake in the mine itself.
Trump told the crowd in Las Vegas, more than 500 miles away on the other end of the state, that “Many people in this audience are going to be working there, and you are working there.”
He didn’t mention that the U.S. government was taking a stake in the project, but shortly after that in his speech, he began warning about the dangers of communism.
Trump says US exports are ‘totally on fire in a positive way’
The president is trying to convince Americans that his policies have led the rest of the world to buy American goods, but his claims lack context.
“Just yesterday, it was announced that American exports are totally on fire in a positive way,” Trump said. “They’ve skyrocketed exports to the highest level in American history.”
The U.S. Census Bureau and the Bureau of Economic Analysis said Tuesday that American exports in June fell 0.9% to $314.7 billion. On a three-month moving average, exports are also down.
However, exports have increased 11.7% so far this year, largely because of increased exports of gold, oil and other energy products. Energy prices have increased this year because of the Iran war.

The United States’ decision followed Brazil’s denial of visas last month for two American diplomats who sought to visit ahead of upcoming elections as well as what the U.S. said was Brazil’s stalling on approving Trump’s nominee to be ambassador in Brasilia.

The American Israel Public Affairs Committee, which spent roughly $30 million in a failed effort to defeat El-Sayed in the Democratic primary, says it’s committed to opposing him in the general election.

sources.news_title: El-Sayed narrowly defeats establishment-backed Stevens in Michigan primary
sources.text:
(The Center Square) – Progressive Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan’s Democratic U.S. Senate primary Tuesday night, defeating establishment-backed U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens to become the party's general election nominee.
El-Sayed will face off against Republican and former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers, who ran unopposed, in 90 days.
The race was close throughout Tuesday evening, with NBC calling it for El-Sayed in the early hours of Wednesday morning and Decision Desk HQ doing the same at 8:35 a.m. Eastern. With 96% of the vote in, El-Sayed won with 48.52% of the vote to Stevens' 47.47%.
That is a difference of just 16,000 votes of the more than 1.4 million that were cast.
Michigan state Sen. Mallory McMorrow also appeared on the Democratic primary ballot, receiving 4% of the vote.
El-Sayed's campaign released a statement, applauding his win despite record spending from his opposition.
"Michiganders have spoken,” said Alia Kapasi, El-Sayed's campaign manager. “This was always going to be the many versus the money, and tonight, we have shown that Michiganders want money out of politics, money in their pockets, and Medicare for all. We are building a coalition that is fired up and ready to go beat Mike Rogers.”
Michigan’s U.S. Senate candidates are vying to succeed retiring U.S. Sen. Gary Peters, a Democrat.
Although El-Sayed rejected the label of democratic socialist, he aligned himself with the Democratic Party’s progressive wing.
He has been endorsed by U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-VT, and several members of the progressive congressional group known as “the Squad,” which includes U.S. Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-NY, Rashida Tlaib, D-MI, and Ilhan Omar, D-MN.
While Stevens and El-Sayed shared some progressive positions, El-Sayed embraced a broader slate of left-wing policies, including Medicare for all and a wealth tax on billionaires.
El-Sayed cast himself as the candidate taking on “AIPAC and the establishment.” The American Israel Public Affairs Committee, a pro-Israel lobbying organization, has spent millions backing Stevens’ campaign.
Stevens dismissed several of his policy proposals as “aspirational” during the campaign. She also received the endorsement of the current seat holder, Peters, highlighting her support among Democratic Party leaders. That backing was partly driven by the view that she was the stronger candidate to take on Rogers in the general election.
That wasn’t enough to get her across the finish line though.
The November U.S. Senate race in Michigan is one of the nation's most closely-watched Senate races.
Rogers has received the endorsement of President Donald Trump and recent polling shows Rogers beating El-Sayed by 46.7% to 42.3%. That is according to the average of the last three polls compiled by 270toWin.
In 2024, Michigan’s U.S. Senate race was decided by less than half a percentage point, with U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin narrowly defeating Rogers. While Democrats are divided, on the Republican side, the party leadership and funding has once again rallied around Rogers.
The outcome of Michigan's Senate race will play a role in determining which party controls the 120th Congress.
Of the 100 seats in the U.S. Senate, 33 are up for regular election in 2026, along with two special elections. Democrats currently hold 13 of the seats on the ballot, while Republicans hold 22.

sources.news_title: El-Sayed Holds Narrow Lead Over Stevens in Michigan Democratic Senate Primary
sources.text:
Detroit (AP) — Abdul El-Sayed has won Michigan’s Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate, narrowly defeating U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens in a victory for the party’s progressive wing in a battleground state.
Join our WhatsApp group
Subscribe to our Daily Roundup Email
The real test of El-Sayed’s and progressives’ strength will now come in a November matchup against Mike Rogers, a former congressman who ran unopposed for the Republican nomination. The seat is pivotal to Democrats’ chances of flipping the Senate and El-Sayed will face the challenge of uniting a divided Democratic base after a bruising primary.
The race remained tight throughout Tuesday night, with a winner not declared until Wednesday morning. In his final remarks at a primary night party before the race was called, El-Sayed said “tomorrow we begin to mend fences.”
Stevens called El-Sayed to concede Wednesday, and she issued a statement saying she would back El-Sayed’s candidacy.
“I am proud to offer my support as he takes on Mike Rogers in the general election,” she said.
Stevens added, “This was a thorough and rigorous campaign that brought out the full span of views within the Democratic Party — and that is why we have primaries.”
Progressives have been gaining strength this year
El-Sayed’s win represents a significant shift for the Democratic Party; in 2018 he lost the gubernatorial primary to now-Gov. Gretchen Whitmer by 21 percentage points.
El-Sayed, a former health official, campaigned on “Medicare for All,” halting military aid to Israel and campaign finance reform. He had support from progressive leaders including Sen. Bernie Sanders and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who framed the race as a grassroots-focused movement and a broader fight against the establishment and big-money spending.
Sen. Chris Van Hollen, another progressive leader who endorsed El-Sayed, said the race “should be a wake-up call to the Washington Democratic establishment.”
“He was running against a lot of Washington insiders as well as parts of the Michigan Democratic establishment. And he won,” said Van Hollen. “That’s an incredible story.”
“Congratulations to him,” said Sen. Gary Peters, the Michigan Democrat whose retirement spurred the contentious primary to replace him. Peters had endorsed Stevens.
Now comes the more difficult challenge for Democrats: uniting the party to defeat Rogers, for whom Republicans have already reserved large sums of money ahead of the general election. Democrats consider the seat a must-win if they are to flip control of the Senate this year.
El-Sayed called for unity to defeat Rogers
Early Tuesday evening, El-Sayed’s supporters in Detroit’s Majestic Theatre cheered at the first batches of votes, before mellowing. Hours later Stevens’ previously subdued partygoers roared as she narrowed the margin.
“Whatever happens tonight,” El-Sayed told a thinned but still energetic crowd, “we have a responsibility to ensure that we unite, unite to make sure that Mike Rogers never sees the inside of the U.S. Senate.”
El-Sayed, a former Wayne County health director, campaigned on “Medicare for All,” campaign finance reform and ending military aid to Israel.
Stevens, a four-term congresswoman, focused on manufacturing and the economy. She stressed her past victories in tough races, saying she would be best positioned to beat Rogers.
Stevens benefited from tens of millions of dollars in outside spending, including the largest investment in a race ever from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, which supports pro-Israel candidates.
Michigan is a must-win Senate race for Democrats
The race will help decide which party controls the chamber in the last two years of President Donald Trump’s term. Those stakes have added heat to the rivalry, with moderates arguing that El-Sayed would have a harder time than Stevens against a Republican in the general election.
Stevens won election to Congress in 2018 after serving as chief of staff to President Barack Obama’s auto task force, which helped oversee the federal rescue of General Motors and Chrysler. Her campaign and allied groups have repeatedly highlighted that experience.
El-Sayed cast himself as the anti-establishment candidate and argued that Democrats need to reject corporate influence and embrace a more progressive agenda.
While the candidate has said he is not a democratic socialist, he found support from some of the group’s members. That included Melat Kiros, who recently beat a longtime incumbent in a Democratic primary for a Denver-based House seat and was at El-Sayed’s watch party. Also there was Hasan Piker, a progressive and controversial influencer online.
The candidates’ differences were clear to some voters.
Kenneth Woodside, 87, of West Bloomfield, said he voted for El-Sayed over Stevens because “the nation is ready for someone who wants to take some more action rather than on the road we are now, which is on the road to an oligarchy and authoritarianism.”
Nessa Fuller, 51, of Birmingham, said she voted for Stevens because she will “fight to get the right things done, and she’ll work with other people, which is really important to me.”
Outside influences spent millions on the Senate race
National groups poured unprecedented sums into the race, making it one of the country’s biggest tests of outside spending.
Groups backing Stevens spent more than $50 million, led by more than $30 million from AIPAC and its affiliates.
The spending thrust Israel policy into the center of the race even though the ads never mentioned it. While El-Sayed called for ending military aid to Israel, Stevens maintained strong support for the relationship.
Israel became a contentious issue within the Democratic Party amid a war in Gaza that killed more than 73,000 Palestinians in its retaliatory offensive after about 1,200 people were killed and 251 hostages were taken in attacks by the militant group Hamas.
McKinney wins Detroit US House primary
In a heavily Democratic district representing Detroit, the 13th, state Rep. Donavan McKinney defeated Rep. Shri Thanedar. McKinney argued that the city should once again have a Black representative in Congress.
After Thanedar won election in 2022, Detroit had no Black representation in Congress for the first time since the early 1950s.

sources.news_title: Abdul El-Sayed claims victory in Michigan Democratic primary
sources.text:
Abdul El-Sayed claims victory in Michigan Democratic primary
DETROIT — Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive public health advocate, claimed victory over Michigan’s closely fought Democratic Senate primary on Wednesday.
With more than 95 percent of the votes counted, El-Sayed took to X to celebrate: "We won. I am so proud to be your Democratic nominee for US Senate. Let's win in November."
El-Sayed won the Democratic nomination for the US Senate defeating Congresswoman Haley Stevens.
However, the voting count is still underway as the official results are too close to call. NBC News has declared El-Sayed the winner, but the Associated Press and The New York Times have not yet called the race.
The result represents an enormous blow to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), which backed Stevens, who spent more than $60 million on the campaign mostly with support from pro-Israel groups.
El-Sayed will face former Republican Congressman Mike Rogers in the November 3 general election. The race is considered one of a handful of competitive Senate contests in the November midterms and could determine which party controls the chamber for the rest of President Donald Trump’s term.
If El-Sayed, who is of Egyptian descent, wins in November, he would become the first Muslim senator in US history.
Wednesday’s result in Michigan, a swing state that voted for Trump in 2024, will have major implications for the Democrats’ policies on conflicts in the Middle East.
El-Sayed recognizes Israel’s atrocities in Gaza as a genocide and argues that money spent on conflicts that benefit Israel should be invested in local communities in the US to address healthcare, housing and infrastructure problems.
Maya Berry, executive director of the Arab American Institute, a non-partisan advocacy group that does not endorse candidates, called El-Sayed’s victory a “big deal”.
She said voters “did not buy” the avalanche of ads that did not talk about policies and only launched negative attacks “about an Arab American Muslim man named Abdul”.
“I am thrilled for the rest of the country to learn that Michigan is not going to take it,” Berry told Al Jazeera.
Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel, and AIPAC backed her heavily in 2022 to defeat Andy Levin, a progressive Jewish legislator.
The Michigan election result on Tuesday is the latest election defeat to pro-Israel Democrats as the party’s base – and US public opinion generally – turns against the Middle East ally.
El-Sayed will now look to unite the Democratic base after a bitter primary where Israel and AIPAC’s spending took center stage.
Even before his victory was assured, El-Sayed called on his supporters to “begin to mend fences” within the Democratic Party.
“I’m going to ask all of us as we think about where we go from here, always magnanimity in victory,” he said.
The Democratic candidate went on to warn that the primary contest “pales in comparison to the cynicism” that Rogers and Trump will unleash in the general elections.
Polls had suggested that El-Sayed was set for a comfortable win, but Stevens outperformed expectations across the state and had a strong showing in Detroit, Michigan’s largest city.
As the night went on, Stevens kept closing in on a lead that El-Sayed had built in from early returns. The race remained too close to call for hours after the polls closed.
As soon as that announcement was made, Mallory McMorrow – a state legislator who was in the US Senate race but dropped out weeks before the elections – endorsed El-Sayed.

“If we come through this—when we come through this, inshallah, that we will have taken $70 million on the chin and kept fighting back,” he said.
The victory sets up a November contest against former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers, who secured the Republican nomination Tuesday in the race to replace retiring U.S. Sen. Gary Peters.
El-Sayed campaigned on Medicare for All, removing corporate money from politics and increasing government regulation of major industries. He has also previously advocated for allowing illegal immigrants to obtain Michigan driver’s licenses during his unsuccessful 2018 campaign for governor.
“Time to vote, Michigan,” El-Sayed wrote Tuesday. “For the many. For money out of politics. For money in your pocket. For Medicare for All.”
El-Sayed’s campaign was powered by the Democratic Party’s progressive and socialist wings, earning endorsements from Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Detroit, U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., Marxist political streamer Hasan Piker, and several progressive and socialist organizations.
Sanders framed the primary as a referendum on money and influence inside the Democratic Party.
“The Michigan Senate primary is a fight as to whether billionaires and their super PACs will continue to control American politics, or whether we can have a government that represents working families,” Sanders wrote ahead of the election.
El-Sayed also campaigned alongside self-described Marxist political streamer Hasan Piker, who previously said: “America deserved September 11.”
Piker also broadcast a livestream from El-Sayed’s campaign headquarters on election night as results came in Tuesday night, had previously predicted national Democrats would unite behind El-Sayed if he won the nomination.
“DNC will back Abdul 100%,” Piker said during a recent livestream. “He’s so buttoned up and so well put together. He is an unbelievable asset.”
El-Sayed has repeatedly insisted he is “not a socialist,” describing himself instead as a capitalist who favors aggressive government action against monopolies. His campaign nevertheless received support from Democratic Socialists of America members and activists affiliated with socialist organizations.
Out-of-state progressive activists, left-wing content creators and socialist organizers also traveled to Michigan during the primary’s closing days to canvass for El-Sayed.
Adam Green, co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee, described Michigan as “ground zero in the battle for the future of the Democratic Party and the future of America.”
“If we win big, it changes the face of the party,” Green said at an El-Sayed rally in Grand Rapids.
The primary divided Michigan Democrats, many of whom backed Stevens and raised concerns about El-Sayed’s electability and political associations.
Stevens entered Election Day with endorsements from many of Michigan’s highest-profile Democratic elected officials, including Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, retiring U.S. Sen. Gary Peters, former U.S. Sen. Debbie Stabenow, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, Attorney General Dana Nessel, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and several members of Michigan’s Congress.
Despite that backing from many of the Democratic Party’s most influential elected leaders, primary voters instead nominated El-Sayed.
U.S. Rep. Hillary Scholten, D-Grand Rapids, repeatedly declined to commit to supporting El-Sayed if he won the nomination, saying she “will not stand beside someone who has allowed distinctly anti-American sentiment to enter our public dialogue.”
Scholten criticized El-Sayed’s decision to campaign with Piker and argued he failed to rein in supporters she accused of directing sexist attacks toward Stevens.
State Rep. Helena Scott, D-Detroit, also declined to commit to supporting El-Sayed before the primary. According to journalist Sam Robinson, Scott said, “If Abdul wins, we’re f*cked,” and argued he could not defeat Rogers in November.
U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell, D-Dearborn, offered a different response Tuesday, saying she would support the entire Democratic ticket if El-Sayed won the nomination.
Republicans are expected to focus heavily on El-Sayed’s support for Medicare for All, his past calls to defund police, his ties to socialist activists and his record of comments on immigration, Israel and American history.
The Republican National Committee has argued El-Sayed deleted thousands of social media posts advocating defunding police as he attempted to distance himself from earlier positions.
RNC Research also highlighted previous remarks in which El-Sayed said the United States was “founded on the removal of a whole people” and “founded on the idea that we could compromise on whether or not people as a function of the color of their skin could be enslaved by other people.”
Rogers has already previewed the contrast he intends to draw in the general election.
“There are DSA people in your neighborhood right now knocking on doors,” Rogers said during a recent campaign appearance. “They’re flying in from New York and California and San Francisco.”
Rogers called El-Sayed a Democratic socialist who was attempting to soften his positions before the general election.
“He is going to take this country in the wrong direction,” Rogers said.
Rogers, a former chairman of the House Intelligence Committee, has centered his campaign on affordability, manufacturing, energy, education and public safety. He narrowly lost Michigan’s 2024 Senate election to Democrat Elissa Slotkin and is seeking to become the first Republican elected to represent Michigan in the U.S. Senate since 1994.
The November contest is expected to become one of the country’s most closely watched Senate races as Republicans seek to break more than three decades of Democratic control over Michigan’s two Senate seats.
Michigan GOP Senior Communications Advisor Greg Manz also weighed in on El-Sayed’s primary victory.
“The choice this November is crystal clear: common sense or communist crazy,” Manz said in a statement. “For more than a quarter century, Democrats have controlled Michigan’s two U.S. Senate seats, and the results speak for themselves — 200,000 manufacturing jobs lost, 45th in the nation for education, and the highest energy costs in the Midwest,” he added.
“Sadly, instead of offering solutions, Abdul El-Sayed is doubling down on the same failed, feckless far-left agenda that has held Michigan back,” Manz continued. “Let’s also not forget that Abdul El-Sayed is a terrorist sympathizer who is hellbent on releasing violent criminals from prisons and throwing open our borders so criminal, illegal aliens can flock to Michigan neighborhoods. This November, Michiganders will soundly reject radical, Marxist policies and elect Mike Rogers who will put working families first and protect our freedoms.”

Abdul El-Sayed Wins Michigan Democratic Senate Primary. The Progressive Is Further Shaking Up The Party
The former public health official defeated Rep. Haley Stevens in one of the year's most closely watched Democratic primaries despite being heavily outspent.
Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan's Democratic primary for the U.S. Senate, overcoming a well-funded campaign by Rep. Haley Stevens to secure the nomination in one of the country's most closely watched races ahead of the November midterm elections.
The former Wayne County public health official will now face former Rep. Mike Rogers, who won the Republican nomination unopposed after receiving an early endorsement from President Donald Trump. The Michigan race is expected to be among the most competitive Senate contests this year and could play a key role in determining control of the chamber.
El-Sayed's victory marks a significant win for the Democratic Party's progressive wing in a battleground state. Backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, he defeated Stevens despite her support from much of the Democratic establishment, including Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and retiring Sen. Gary Peters, NBC News says.
The primary became one of the most expensive Democratic Senate contests in recent memory. Stevens and allied outside groups spent tens of millions of dollars on advertising, including support from organizations affiliated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), while El-Sayed ran on a grassroots campaign centered on healthcare, economic inequality and reducing the influence of money in politics.
Throughout the campaign, El-Sayed promoted policies including Medicare for All and criticized continued U.S. military support for Israel, a position that resonated with many voters in Michigan, home to one of the nation's largest Arab American communities, Reuters said. The contest became a broader test of whether progressive candidates could win statewide in a politically divided Midwestern state after similar victories in Democratic primaries elsewhere this year.
Republicans have argued that El-Sayed's progressive platform could make him more vulnerable in the general election. Trump said in a Fox News interview Tuesday that Rogers would fare better against El-Sayed than Stevens, while the National Republican Senatorial Committee had previously highlighted El-Sayed's progressive credentials during the primary campaign, Associated Press reported.
The November race will fill the seat being vacated by Democratic Sen. Gary Peters, who is retiring rather than seeking a third term. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate, making Michigan one of several key battlegrounds that could determine whether Democrats can regain control of the chamber.
Following her defeat, Stevens pledged to support El-Sayed in the general election, while former state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who exited the Democratic primary last month and endorsed El-Sayed, also called for party unity heading into November.

sources.news_title: El-Sayed beats Stevens to take on Rogers in battleground Michigan Senate race
Abdul El-Sayed wins Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate
sources.text:
Abdul El-Sayed wins Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate
Eking out a narrow but significant win for U.S. progressives and making a national name for himself, former health director Abdul El-Sayed won the Democratic nomination to Michigan's open U.S. Senate seat over U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens and her centrist allies in an Aug. 4 primary that was far closer than many expected.
Stevens conceded and congratulated El-Sayed on the morning of Aug. 5 after multiple media outlets called the race. NBC called the race for El-Sayed shortly before 2:30 a.m. on Aug. 5 with most of the vote in and DDHQ called the race shortly before 9 a.m.
El-Sayed had declared himself the winner on X about an hour earlier, writing, "Michigan... We won."
Several other outlets, including the New York Times and CNN, called the race for El-Sayed shortly before 10 a.m., with counts they were using showing him ahead 48.5%-47.5%, or by about 25,000 votes, with 99% of the vote counted. State Sen. Mallory McMorrow, of Royal Oak, who dropped out of the race July 5 but remained on the ballot, had about 4%.
Stevens conceded at about the same time and endorsed El-Sayed. "I am proud to offer my support," she said. “This was a thorough and rigorous campaign that brought out the full span of views within the Democratic Party and that is why we have primaries. I am proud to have put up my hand to serve, and prouder to continue to work together to make sure this Senate seat remains blue."
Now, the never-before-elected former Wayne County and Detroit health director, the son of Egyptian immigrants to the United States, will, barring any challenge to the result, face Republican former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers in the Nov. 3 general election to replace retiring U.S. Sen. Gary Peters.
President Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social website that El-Sayed's victory was, "Great news for the Republican Party," saying it pushes the Democratic Party further to the left.
"(Senate Democratic Leader) Chuck Schumer burned over $60 million propping up Haley Stevens only for Democrats to nominate Abdul El-Sayed, a dangerous threat to the safety and freedoms of every American," said Chris Gustafson, spokesman for the Senate Leadership Fund, a Super PAC that promotes Republicans in the Senate and is launching a six-figure ad campaign against El-Sayed. He added that the organization is "committed to defeating this extremist" and electing Rogers.
Rogers put out a statement on X saying, "The Democrat Party has been lost to the extremists. Full stop."
El-Sayed has voiced support for defunding police in the past but has tempered those remarks in this campaign. But he has taken other progressive positions, such as abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement, saying it has become too tainted and violent under President Donald Trump's administration, and calling for universal government-run health care for every American, that Rogers and Republicans − in turn saddled with an unpopular war with Iran and high energy prices − will try to use against him.
Going into Tuesday's vote tally, El-Sayed was assumed to have a much larger edge based on polling averages and greater on-the-ground energy shown by his supporters. But as the votes were counted, Stevens continued to eat away at his early lead until it was finally too late for her to make up the difference.
No Republican has won a U.S. Senate seat in Michigan since Spencer Abraham in 1994. But Michigan statewide candidates have long tended to be more moderate than El-Sayed and, throughout the campaign, Stevens warned that El-Sayed, while not a democratic socialist, might be seen as too radical to beat Rogers in a state won by President Donald Trump in 2016 and 2024.
Rogers, of White Lake, who was unopposed in the Aug. 4 Republican primary, also lost a narrow U.S. Senate election to then-U.S. Rep. Elissa Slotkin two years ago, underscoring his potential strength.
Before the race was called, both candidates, early on Aug. 5, spoke to supporters, neither claiming victory nor conceding but both saying their backers needed to set aside the acrimony of a harsh primary campaign and unite behind whoever won the nomination to win the general election against the Republicans.
By winning, El-Sayed scored a signature victory for progressives far bigger than others that preceded it, such as Zohran Mamdani's election as New York City's mayor, given that Michigan is a key swing state and has a history of favoring far more centrist candidates for statewide office.
In doing so, he rode a wave of liberal enthusiasm that suggested large blocs of the Democratic Party want to take a more aggressive stance not only against Trump and his Republican allies but in opposition to more corporate- and globalist-friendly policies, demanding government rein in aid to businesses, protect the environment and give more help to poor and working families.
Then there was the question of U.S. support for Israel, which hung over the race from the beginning.
El-Sayed had long opposed military aid to Israel, especially after that country’s counterattacks against Hamas in Gaza, as a growing number of Democrats voiced similar concerns; Stevens, who had the support of the pro-Israel lobby in this and previous elections, has said she believes in a two-state solution for Palestinians but has not called for any meaningful conditions on U.S. aid to Israel, representing a much more Israel-friendly policy embraced by many moderate Democrats.
El-Sayed was also forced to face questions about his positions when he campaigned with an internet influencer, Hasan Piker, who had been accused of making antisemitic statements, which he denied. El-Sayed was also accused – unfairly in some cases – of being disrespectful to women.
El-Sayed, an Ann Arbor public health specialist who trained as a medical doctor, ran as the progressive choice in 2018 for the Democratic gubernatorial nomination, losing to soon-to-become Gov. Gretchen Whitmer.
In this year’s campaign, at crowded rallies, he pushed a message of getting corporate money out of politics, putting more wealth in working people’s pockets, reducing medical debt and supporting “Medicare for All,” meaning a single government health plan covering all Americans.
He also ran with the outward support of leftist firebrands including U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, of Vermont, who 10 years ago scored a progressive win in Michigan, besting Hillary Clinton in the state on her way to the Democratic nomination and a loss to Trump. Other notable progressives, including U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, of New York, and Detroit’s own U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Detroit, also offered key support.
Stevens, on the other hand, was aided by vast sums – more than $60 million – in independent, outside spending on her behalf, much of it by a group linked to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, which supports candidates, including Republicans, who promote U.S. aid to Israel. Much of the other spending came from groups linked to centrist Democrats but with funders linked to corporate givers or undisclosed entirely.
While it wasn't yet known exactly how much the campaigns and their outside allies spent on the Democratic primary, it appeared clear that Stevens' side spent far more, outspending El-Sayed and his allies by a 9-t margin.
The congresswoman leaned on her reputation as a “workhorse” in Congress, touting her experience as a promoter of Michigan manufacturing and a legislator who has helped create jobs in the Michigan economy. Her service, before entering Congress, on then-President Barack Obama’s auto task force, which helped rescue General Motors and what was then Chrysler in 2009-10, was mentioned repeatedly by her campaign, and she relied heavily on significant endorsements, including those by Whitmer, Peters, former Govs. Jennifer Granholm and Jim Blanchard, and former U.S. Sen. Debbie Stabenow.
That support and experience clearly seemed to help her far more than had been expected by some, especially in Detroit and with Black voters and older Democrats. But in the end it was not enough to secure the win.
It was also unclear how much, if at all, she was helped by a third candidate, state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, of Royal Oak, deciding to drop out of the race on July 5th. McMorrow didn’t initially endorse in the race and her name remained on the primary ballot. At the time she got out of the race, however, Stevens’ campaign clearly saw it as an improvement in their fortunes at a time when El-Sayed was showing substantial momentum.
On the day of the election, McMorrow said she would endorse whoever won. After the race was called by NBC, McMorrow almost immediately issued her endorsement for El-Sayed, offering him, "Huge congratulations."
"I’m proud to give Abdul my full endorsement and support as we head to November together as a unified party," McMorrow said. "Take it from me — this was a brutal primary. But whatever differences there were between the candidates in this race, those differences are nothing compared to the contrast in November. Donald Trump and Mike Rogers are banking on all of us being too bruised, too proud and too hurt to come back together to beat them. Let's prove them wrong."
As the race was called for El-Sayed, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, of New York, and Sen. Kristen Gillibrand, of New York, chairman of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, put out a statement supporting him, though they had reportedly supported Stevens in the race.
“Abdul El-Sayed has run an energetic campaign that inspired thousands of Michiganders across the state, with a clear focus on lowering costs and standing up for working families," they said in their statement. “Democrats are united by a common purpose: putting a check on Donald Trump by defeating his Republican enablers and taking back the Senate. We look forward to working with Abdul and Democrats across Michigan to win this seat in November."Free Press staff writer Jalen Williams contributed to this report.Contact Todd Spangler: tspangler@freepress.com. Follow him on X @tsspangler.(This story will be updated.)
