sources.news_title: El-Sayed, Stevens go down to wire in Michigan Democratic Senate primary
El-Sayed wins narrow victory in US Senate primary
sources.text:
El-Sayed wins narrow victory in US Senate primary
Detroit — Abdul El-Sayed defeated Haley Stevens in the most-expensive Democratic U.S. Senate primary contest in U.S. history, with the Associated Press calling the race midmorning Wednesday.
Stevens called El-Sayed to concede the race Wednesday morning, a Stevens spokesperson said.
El-Sayed, 41, will face Republican former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers, 63, of White Lake Township in the November general election.
El-Sayed had about 49% to Stevens' 47%, according to voting results compiled by The Detroit News. The returns showed El-Sayed ahead in Kent County, Macomb County and Washtenaw County (his home county and home to the University of Michigan), and Stevens ahead in Oakland, Wayne, Saginaw and Genesee counties.
A third candidate, state Sen. Mallory McMorrow of Royal Oak, was pulling in about 4% of the vote. She remained on Tuesday’s ballot after dropping out of the race on July 5, but endorsed El-Sayed early Wednesday morning.
El-Sayed declared victory around 7 a.m. Wednesday, saying he was proud to be the state's Democratic nominee: "Let's win in November," he posted on social media.
The fierce contest pitted Stevens, a moderate four-term congresswoman from Birmingham, against El-Sayed, a former public health official and podcaster from Ann Arbor, for the chance to take on Rogers in November.
In a lengthy Wednesday morning statement, Rogers described El-Sayed as an "extremist" bent on raising taxes and reducing imprisonment. He also criticized El-Sayed for campaigning with Hasan Piker, the left-wing social media commentator who once questioned whether the U.S. "deserved" the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks.
The primary battle was widely viewed as a test of whether a progressive Democrat preaching Medicare for All and railing against dark money to young crowds can win “purple” Michigan over the establishment’s pick, who has run a more traditional, blue-collar campaign on building up the state’s manufacturing core and fighting President Donald Trump. Michigan went for Trump in 2024.
The mood was boisterous early in the night at El-Sayed's election night watch party inside the Majestic Theater in Midtown Detroit. Revelers mingled to loud, upbeat music on the concert hall's open floor. A lectern stood center stage in front of them, adorned with a campaign sign reading "MICHIGAN IS NOT FOR SALE."
The crowd of several hundred cheered after the first few tranches of votes were counted and initial tallies — projected onto a screen playing a C-SPAN television feed — showed El-Sayed leading by a comfortable margin. Those cheers became more muted and less frequent as later returns showed a much tighter race than recent polls had shown.
El-Sayed took the stage and addressed supporters shortly after 1 a.m., acknowledging that the race was too close to declare victory.
He began his speech with the call-and-response of his slogan, “Money in your pocket. Money out of politics. Medicare for All,” that has become a hallmark of his campaign events.
The former public health official went on to share a message of building bridges with Stevens supporters — regardless of who wins the primary — and coming together to defeat Republican nominee Mike Rogers.
“We've got 13 weeks to beat Mike Rogers," El-Sayed said. "And however we might feel about the campaign we've just come through, I want you to understand that it pales in comparison to the cynicism, in comparison to the corporatism, in comparison to the lies that Mike Rogers and Donald Trump are going to tell."
He added: “However much we might disagree with our Democratic opponent, there is so much more that unites us than divides us."
At Stevens' watch party in nearby New Center, more than 150 supporters stayed glued to their smartphones and the big-screen TVs posted around the St. Regis Hotel, where loud pop music similarly kept the atmosphere upbeat well past 11 p.m.
Stevens appeared smiling on stage at 12:49 a.m. to a crowd chanting her name.
Joined by former U.S. Sen. Debbie Stabenow of Lansing and U.S Rep Hillary Scholten of Grand Rapids, Stevens waved and thanked supporters, then told them that results would not be known until Wednesday morning or even later and that people should go home and get sleep or coffee.
But the congresswoman told supporters to stay vigilant as they wait for votes to be counted in Detroit, Flint and Muskegon County.
“So we got to get some sleep or get some coffee, and then we got to be ready to go,” Stevens said. “We got to wake up and be ready to go because if we are going to win this thing ― which we are ― we are going to have to get ready and show Mike Rogers what a little stick-it-to-him looks like. “
Senate race got nasty in July
Michigan’s Senate seat is up for grabs because two-term U.S. Sen. Gary Peters, D-Bloomfield Township, is retiring. Republicans haven’t won a Senate race in Michigan since 1994, and Democrats need to win in Michigan if they hope to retake control of the Senate.
El-Sayed had been drawing larger crowds on the campaign trail for weeks and led Stevens in recent public polls. Some Democrats have argued the young energy and well-organized ground game behind El-Sayed's bid could make the difference Tuesday in turning out voters who don't usually cast ballots in an August primary.
The race has been especially nasty and toxic in its closing month, with El-Sayed calling Stevens “the least capable candidate in America” and suggesting she could not “string together two coherent sentences.” He cast her as beholden to corporate dollars and morally bankrupt for her support of U.S. aid for Israel.
“I get real pissed off when they say, ‘You’re unelectable because your name is Abdul.’ Because for me, I push back and say, ‘You don’t know Michigan like I know Michigan,” El-Sayed said at a rally over the weekend. "You don't know what our state needs and deserves like I know what our state needs and deserves."
Stevens has claimed her rival is only running for office to be a “celebrity” senator who wants to sell books, give paid speeches and promote his podcast. She’s also accused him of being an untrustworthy, closeted millionaire hiding his personal finances and blaming the country’s problems on a foreign country, Israel.
“What I have been hearing from Michiganders in these last couple of days, they want to see a proven fighter,” Stevens told reporters Sunday. “Look, I’ve been underestimated before, and also I have stood up for Michigan in really tough moments.”
Peters, who has endorsed Stevens, and other party centrists have warned that selecting the left-wing El-Sayed could jeopardize the seat for Democrats in November.
"It's because of her really common sense, practical problem-solving ability. That's where folks from Michigan are. That's what they like," Peters said after a Sunday rally with Stevens in Madison Heights. "Haley basically represents the kind of people in the Midwest who roll up our sleeves, get to work. It's not about theatrics."
Sen. Bernie Sanders, a Vermont progressive who won Michigan's Democratic presidential primary 10 years ago, has dismissed the concerns about whether El-Sayed could prevail in a general election contest against Rogers.
"Maybe it's time to understand the status quo is not working for working families or the middle class," Sanders told The Detroit News last month. "They want real change, and Abdul is a vehicle for that change. That is why the billionaire super PACs are spending so much money trying to defeat him."
For his part, El-Sayed on Monday predicted he'd defeat Rogers by 7 percentage points, deeming him a "generationally bad candidate.”
The primary contest has featured a record amount of outside spending for a U.S. Senate primary race, about $60 million, with a lop-sided $54 million benefiting Stevens and $5 million benefiting El-Sayed ― a ratio of nearly 11-1.
That total includes over $30.6 million spent by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) ― the most that the group has sunk into a single race since starting their United Democracy Project super PAC in 2022. Their ads boosted the reliably pro-Israel Stevens and attacked El-Sayed, who opposes foreign military aid for Israel and has called its actions in Gaza a genocide.
El-Sayed has said the money spent against him is a “validator” of his message, betting that support for Israel has eroded to such a point in his party that he can criticize U.S. support for it and still be elected.
“If I prove that you can win statewide, taking on AIPAC and winning, that is catastrophic because of what it says about the future of the party,” El-Sayed told Mother Jones last month.
Stevens has largely declined to discuss her support from AIPAC while embracing it. She slammed El-Sayed last week for blaming Jewish Americans "for America's problems."
She has opposed placing conditions on aid for Israel despite concerns about humanitarian aid in Gaza. Stevens has said the goal in the Middle East has to be long-term peace and a two-state solution. "I can say that Israel has a right to peacefully exist alongside the people of Palestine and in Gaza," she said at a debate last month.
Stevens, 43, is in her fourth term representing Oakland County in the U.S. House. She has touted her experience working on the auto rescue team under President Barack Obama and her reputation as a “workhorse” in Congress, helping to pass legislation to boost domestic semiconductor production and the bipartisan infrastructure bill. She has campaigned on controlling costs for working families and standing up to Trump.
El-Sayed, 41, is the physician son of Egyptian immigrants who grew up around Detroit and previously served as the top health official in Wayne County and for the City of Detroit. He has campaigned on single-payer health care, ending the corrupting influence of money in politics and his plan to abolish the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency known as ICE. If elected, he'd be the first Muslim to serve in the Senate.
Voters explain their picks
An hour after the polls had closed, dozens of Stevens’ supporters gathered at the St. Regis Hotel in downtown Detroit, where they ate charcuterie and sipped drinks at a lively party, glancing at TV sets displaying early unofficial results.
Seated on a couch in a hotel gathering space, Daniel Carroll said he voted for Stevens because she is the best chance to defeat the GOP's Rogers in November.
“We need to control the Senate and the House,” Carroll said.
Stevens has experience and will get the job done, he said. “She held public office. He was in the health department, not even statewide. So she has legislative experience. So compared to him, it's a no-brainer.”
Steve France, 61, of St. Clair Shores, said he favored Stevens for Senate, in part because he had not seen negative advertising from her, while he felt other candidates were attacking one another.
“I haven’t seen any negative ads out of her,” France said of Stevens. “Everybody else is, you know, shooting each other in the foot.”
France said he hoped Stevens would do well against the GOP's Rogers in the fall.
“These candidates, right now, are they’ve been working on the same issues for the past 20 years,” he said. “So I’m not expecting anything new. I just don’t want anything radical like what we’re having right now.”
David Dieter, 71, of St. Clair Shores said he was motivated to vote in part because he feels threatened by Trump’s policies and rhetoric as a married gay person.
“Trump is the most evil thing in the world, and he's doing everything possible to destroy our basic belief systems, protecting people like all of us,” he said.
Dieter said he voted for El-Sayed in Tuesday's primary, despite concerns about whether he could win the general election in November.
“I know for a lot of people he's too progressive. He isn't for me," Dieter said. “It’s worth the risk because I think he's more solid, would be more solidly against Trumpism.”
On Stevens, Dieter said that, “even though she has been around a long time, I'm afraid she's going to wimp out under pressure.”
Dieter said electability was a difficult consideration for him and a topic of discussion in his household.
“I figure, even if Stevens wins in the fall, okay," Dieter said. "But I still had to support (El-Sayed) because his time's not over.”
Robert Knevels, a 54-year-old Birmingham resident, said he’d support either Democratic candidate for Senate. But he strongly prefers Stevens, who represents him in the U.S. House.
“I voted for Haley Stevens because I think she has a better chance to beat Mike Rogers in the November election,” he said. “I also want to keep things a little bit more moderate because while I'm a Democrat, I'm not in favor of some of these left-wing policies that the Democrats are doing right now, and so I wanted to make my voice heard here that I like it to be more moderate.”
No matter who wins, Knevels said the most important thing was to beat Rogers in November.
“I’m not going to vote for the other side at all,” he said. “But this is an issue where the Democratic Party has a split in it, and that's rough for me.”
Two El-Sayed voters who cast their votes for him at a polling place in Epicenter of Worship church in south Lansing Tuesday pointed to the progressive Democrat’s stance on healthcare and his chances of beating Rogers in November as important reasons he won their votes.
“I came out to vote for Abdul,” said Stephanie Bergmann, 35, of Lansing. “One less vote for Haley Stevens.”
Bergmann suggested the support Stevens has received from AIPAC will vanish in November, predicting the pro-Israel group would rather see Rogers in office and asserted that is why the group has given Stevens so much support. Because El-Sayed is a better contender against Rogers, Bergmann said.
“I’ve seen her going out and doing her spiels and everything, but I haven’t seen her connect with community as much as Abdul has,” she said. “He seems like more of an approachable person who treats people like people as opposed to pawns to further an agenda.”
El-Sayed’s support for expanded healthcare access earned him a vote from Ali Aljazi, 27, also of Lansing. El-Sayed supports Medicare for All, a single-payer health care system funded by the government and guaranteed to all Americans, and wrote a book on the subject in 2021.
People should be able to access routine and preventative care, Aljazi said, because it could stave off more serious illnesses. Health care is “crazy expensive,” and people can’t control their need to see a doctor, he said.
“If cancer’s early detected, you can get it taken care of, but if you don’t have any coverage, you won’t be going to get it checked out; you won’t have regular checkups, routine visits, and those are key,” he said.
Harrison Township resident Susan Malley, 67, said she voted for Stevens because of “what she believes in,” saying that Stevens is “for the people” and worked under former President Barack Obama, who was her favorite president.
“He did a lot for this country,” Malley said. “He did.”
Malley said the economy is an important issue for her this election. “Our economy sucks,” she said. “It just does.”
Malley, a retiree who voted early, noted that grocery and gas prices are “going up.” She thinks the U.S. shouldn’t be in the Iran war and she doesn’t support Trump.
Harrison Township resident Maddi Sulflow, 27, voted for El-Sayed because of the way he “calls out” corporate funding for other candidates.
“He's highlighting that other candidates, even in his own party, are also accepting money from massive corporations,” she said.
Sulflow, who voted early, said she also likes that El-Sayed “calls out” AIPAC. She said that, if a candidate is accepting AIPAC money, that means they’re “aligned with Israel and what they're doing” to the Palestinians.
“And that's just not something I'm aligned with,” Sulflow said.
Mindi Brouker, 40, of St. Clair Shores, also voted for El-Sayed because of Stevens’ sources of campaign funding.
“I feel like Haley Stevens with all the funds that she’s getting from corporate donors and AIPAC, I’m against,” she said. “So that’s a big reason for me.”
“AIPAC funding, I’m not in support of, and so that’s a big one for me,” Brouker added.
Stevens’ father, Jim, waited excitedly with supporters at the Hotel St. Regis late Tuesday, as people milled around an empty stage, exchanging stories and watching for results. Asked how his daughter was doing, Stevens beamed with pride.
“She knows how to bring people together,” he said. “When she first got elected in Congress, I asked her. I said, ‘What are you going to do your first day?’ She told me, ‘I'm going to go meet every Republican,’ and she probably has.”
Jim Stevens said his daughter knows how to win.
“She has the gift to speak. She has the knowledge,” he said.
El-Sayed is endorsed by progressive icons Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, while Stevens has the backing of big-name Michigan Democrats, including Peters, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and former Sen. Debbie Stabenow of Lansing.
Staff writers Craig Mauger, Candice Williams, Sarah Atwood and Anne Snabes contributed.

sources.news_title: El-Sayed Wins Michigan Democratic Senate Primary, NBC Projects
Live Primary Results: Michigan Senate, House, and Gubernatorial Races
Live updates; Progressive Abdul El-Sayed will win Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, CNN projects
sources.text:
What we covered
• Big win for progressives: Abdul El-Sayed defeated Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan’s marquee Democratic primary for US Senate in a triumph for national progressive leaders. Explore results further and read takeaways here.
• Vows unity: El-Sayed downplayed the narrow margins of his victory, assuring voters the party is unified despite a divisive campaign. He also condemned GOP messaging tactics using his name, saying “I’ll be happy to give you lessons” on pronouncing it.
• A November must-win: El-Sayed will face Republican Mike Rogers in the fall. Democrats almost certainly have to hold the seat being vacated by retiring Sen. Gary Peters to have a chance of winning Senate control.
• Elsewhere in the state: CNN also projects State Rep. Donavan McKinney, a democratic socialist, will defeat Rep. Shri Thanedar to win the Democratic primary in the 13th Congressional District. It marks the latest loss by an incumbent to a democratic socialist challenger this primary season.
Our live coverage of primaries in Michigan and four other states has concluded. Please scroll through the posts below to learn all the developments. You also can explore results further and read takeaways here.
Republican revives House bid after upsetting Trump's pick in Michigan
Republican Tom Smith suspended his campaign for Michigan’s 8th Congressional District last month. But after he remained on the ballot and unexpectedly won the primary Tuesday — beating another Republican backed by President Donald Trump — he is back in.
The House GOP campaign arm signaled support for Smith, who is now Republicans’ standard bearer in a district they have been targeting since the start of the election cycle.
“McDonald Rivet has failed Michiganders and they will send her packing this fall when they elect commonsense conservative Thomas Smith,” Zach Bannon, a spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Committee, said in a statement.
The Trump-endorsed candidate, Amir Hassan, finished a distant second in the primary. In a video posted to Facebook on Wednesday, Hassan acknowledged the surprising loss and said he would “make no excuse” for it.
Catch up after progressive El-Sayed's projected win in Michigan Democratic Senate primary
In a critical race with razor-thin margins, CNN has projected that progressive Abdul El-Sayed will win Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary.
It caps off the latest primary elections in several states and is the latest triumph for national progressive leaders. Michigan is a state Democrats almost certainly must win in November to take control of the Senate.
El-Sayed will face GOP former Rep. Mike Rogers in the fall.
Here’s the latest:
- Victory speech: El-Sayed sought to present a unifying message after a divisive primary campaign. Referring to his former rivals, Rep. Haley Stevens and state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, El-Sayed said that “we cannot wait to come together and win in November.” El-Sayed also called Stevens a committed public servant and said there is more that unites than divides them.
- Democratic reactions: Stevens congratulated El-Sayed on his win and said she was “proud to offer my support.” Democratic leadership also coalesced behind El-Sayed, praising the progressive after making their unofficial backing of Stevens clear during the race. Former Vice President Kamala Harris is raising money for El-Sayed.
- Outgoing senator: Michigan Democratic Sen. Gary Peters said Democrats need to unite behind El-Sayed but emphasized that the progressive Democrat also has to start making inroads with the party “immediately.”
- Eyes toward November: Rogers released a statement on X slamming El-Sayed, claiming his Democratic opponent would make the state less safe and affordable for Michiganders. He also billed El-Sayed as an “extremist.”
- Republican reactions: Republican groups have begun releasing ads targeting El-Sayed. One from the Senate Leadership Fund and National Republican Senatorial Committee paints El-Sayed as “too radical.” President Donald Trump said El-Sayed’s projected victory is “Great news for the Republican Party.”
Abdul El-Sayed called out Republicans, including his GOP opponent Mike Rogers, after the National Republican Senatorial Committee issued a statement attacking the Democrat that referred to him by his full name, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed.
Other projections this morning:
- In another victory for progressives, State Rep. Donavan McKinney, a democratic socialist, is projected to defeat incumbent Rep. Shri Thanedar to win the Democratic primary in Michigan’s 13th Congressional District.
- In an upset, Tom Smith, who suspended his campaign last month, will defeat Trump-backed candidate Amir Hassan in the Republican primary in Michigan’s 8th Congressional District.
CNN’s Aditi Sangal, David Wright, Arlette Saenz, Kaanita Iyer, Aileen Graef, Aaron Blake, Annie Grayer, Abigail Roedersheimer, Richa Sharma and Patrick Svitek contributed reporting.
Bernie Sanders calls El-Sayed's win "extraordinary"
Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders hailed Abdul El-Sayed’s win in the Michigan Democratic primary for Senate as “the most extraordinary victory that I can think of in modern American politics.”
Sanders was one of El-Sayed’s most prominent supporters, visiting Michigan multiple times to campaign with him as he faced off against Rep. Haley Stevens. Sanders also backed two other successful candidates in Tuesday’s primary in Michigan: Donavan McKinney, who defeated Rep. Shri Thanedar, and Will Lawrence, who won the Democratic nomination to challenge Republican Rep. Tom Barrett in his battleground district.
Democrats who opposed El-Sayed in the primary were concerned about his ability to win the general election. Sanders said he was confident El-Sayed would beat Republican nominee Mike Rogers, arguing El-Sayed showed in the primary that he can “expand the voter turnout universe.”
Progressive Will Lawrence dismisses electability concerns in Michigan swing district
Climate activist Will Lawrence dismissed concerns that his progressive views could turn off swing voters in Michigan’s battleground 7th District after he defeated two more moderate candidates in the Democratic primary.
“We’re building this campaign on face to face conversations with voters across the district,” Lawrence told CNN’s Manu Raju on “Inside Politics.” “We’re finding tons of common ground on issues like stopping AI data centers, stopping these stupid wars around the world, and investing in housing and health care that we can actually afford and count on.”
Lawrence noted that he let his Democratic Socialists of America membership lapse last month, saying that while he has a lot of respect for the group, “I felt a need to make it very clear that the platform we’re running on here is the one that has come up based on the conversations we’re having across the 7th District.”
He also addressed controversy that surfaced in the final stretch of his primary campaign, when The Huffington Post in July reported that he’d said on a 2024 podcast that Black political leaders’ support for Democratic leadership “defangs the White left.” He has since apologized for those remarks, but Democrats remain anxious that his history of strident rhetoric could damage the party’s chances of ousting freshman Republican Rep. Tom Barrett.
Speaking Wednesday, Lawrence reiterated that he regretted the 2024 comments, and said that he “look forward to having conversations very soon” with members of the Congressional Black Caucus, hoping to “restore some trust.” And he said that he would vote for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries for Speaker of the House, though they had not yet connected.
Mamdani congratulates El-Sayed but declines to say whether he'll endorse
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani was asked about the comparison some are making between himself and Abdul El-Sayed, who CNN projected will win the Democratic Senate nomination in Michigan.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has been a vocal advocate for change in the Democratic Party, congratulated progressive Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed for his victory in Michigan’s primary election Tuesday.
“He ran a campaign where it was best described by his words of money out of politics, money in your pocket, Medicare for all,” Mamdani said during an event at City Hall in New York Wednesday, praising El-Sayed as the type of candidate he believes could change the party.
Mamdani has said he has spoken with El-Sayed a few times but did not specify if the pair has spoken following this victory.
When asked about the comparison some have made between the two politicians, Mamdani brushed off the sentiment.
He did not say if he would formally endorse El-Sayed in the general election in November. So far, the mayor has focused his endorsements on New York races.
Kamala Harris raises money for El-Sayed
Former Vice President Kamala Harris is raising money for Abdul El-Sayed after he won the Democratic primary for Senate in Michigan.
Harris, a potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidate, urged her supporters to donate to El-Sayed’s campaign in an email Wednesday afternoon. She acknowledged that he was emerging from a contentious primary against Rep. Haley Stevens.
“This was a hard-fought Democratic primary, and Michiganders were lucky to have such inspiring leaders step up in this moment,” Harris said.
A Harris spokesperson made clear before the primary that she would not get involved but noted she was “grateful” to have the support of both Stevens and El-Sayed when she ran for president in 2024.
GOP opponent labels El-Sayed an "extremist" in statement after his win
Michigan GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers released a statement on X slamming Abdul El-Sayed, claiming his Democratic opponent would make the state less safe and affordable for Michiganders.
El-Sayed narrowly defeated Rep. Haley Stevens, a moderate congresswoman from Michigan’s 11th District, while Rogers ran virtually uncontested for his party’s nomination. El-Sayed and Rogers will now face off in November’s general election.
“He wants to empty prisons and put murderers and sex offenders back on our streets. He pledged his support to the Muslim Brotherhood and campaigns with people who refuse to condemn terrorism. And, he advocated for the largest tax hike in American history — costing families already struggling to make ends meet over $3000 more per year,” Rogers continued.
“Never in a million years did I think that I would be running against someone who believes America deserved 9/11,” he added, referring to El-Sayed’s campaigning with Hasan Piker, a popular far-left Twitch streamer who has said he regretted his comment about the September 11 attacks.
Gary Peters congratulates El-Sayed, says he needs to make inroads “immediately” with party
Michigan Democratic Sen. Gary Peters said Democrats need to unite behind Abdul El-Sayed but emphasized that the progressive Democratic nominee also has to start making inroads with the party “immediately.”
Peters said he spoke to El-Sayed today to congratulate him on his victory and relayed that El-Sayed assured him that he will start reaching out across the party.
“We have to come together and understand that whatever differences existed between Haley Stevens and Abdul (El-Sayed), those are very small compared to the difference between Abdul and (GOP nominee) Mike Rogers, and we’re going to make sure that our Democratic Party comes together in Michigan and reach out to independent voters to win the race,” Peters added.
Asked by CNN what El-Sayed’s win means for the direction of the Democratic Party, given Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders’ pick won over Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s preferred candidate, Peters said “Michigan is very diverse. We’ve seen it before.”
On whether El-Sayed’s views on Israel reflect the direction of the Democratic Party, Peters said, “certainly he campaigned on that issue, and the results speak for themselves.”
El-Sayed downplays “intra-family squabbles" and narrow margins in primary race
Abdul El-Sayed downplayed “intra-family squabbles” when asked about the close Democratic race and divisive primary campaign, as he cast the result as a catharsis for state Democrats.
With 99% of the vote counted, El-Sayed led by under 15,000 out of more than 1.5 million votes cast. He hailed the record-breaking turnout in the Senate primary, saying that “when you’ve got 500,000 more voters who came out to be a part of a process to pick a nominee, that means that their voices have been heard.”
And referring to his former rivals, Rep. Haley Stevens and state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, El-Sayed noted that “we’ve had some great conversations about where we go from here, and we cannot wait to come together and win in November.”
El-Sayed vows to keep Jewish Americans safe
Abdul El-Sayed sought to reassure Jewish Americans of his support for them after winning the Democratic primary for Senate in Michigan.
“I want you to know that my commitment to your safety, my commitment to Jewish safety, is the same commitment that I have to the safety of my own daughters,” El-Sayed said, addressing reporters Wednesday morning.
The US relationship with Israel was a flashpoint in El-Sayed’s primary against Rep. Haley Stevens. At one point in the final days, Stevens accused El-Sayed of wanting to “blame all of your problems on Jewish Americans.”
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee spent tens of millions of dollars through its super PAC to defeat El-Sayed. And after his victory, AIPAC said in a statement that its members “remain determined to ensure that voters reject” him.
El-Sayed rebukes Rogers: "Keep the name out your damn mouth"
Abdul El-Sayed rebuked his GOP opponent Mike Rogers and Republicans after the National Republican Senatorial Committee began attacking his campaign and pointedly referred to his full name, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, following his projected victory in the Democratic Senate primary.
Turning to his opponent, El-Sayed continued — echoing New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s memorable zinger against ex-Gov. Andrew Cuomo during their debates last year:
He condemned the messaging tactics, saying that Democrats would remain focused on the issues. “They understand that the only way that they think they can win is to drag us into the mud, to believe the worst about each other, to believe that what divides us is bigger than what unites us,” El-Sayed said.
El-Sayed on his win: “We shook up the world”
Abdul El-Sayed addressed the media Wednesday morning after his projected victory in the Michigan Democratic Senate primary, saying that “in the words of Muhammad Ali, we shook up the world.”
Joined by party leaders, including state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, a former rival who dropped out last month, in a show of unity after a bruising fight against Rep. Haley Stevens, El-Sayed echoed the calls to action for the fall campaign.
State party Chair Curtis Hertel introduced El-Sayed and emphatically praised his campaign. “After last night, a fighter, a true fighter, and that is what people want — Abdul El-Sayed will be our next US senator,” he said.
McMorrow also spoke, affirming her promise to endorse the eventual nominee and joking about the lengthy vote-counting process.
“I had made a commitment earlier that no matter what happened in this race, that I was going to endorse the nominee the minute the race was called, and that I would be at their party,” she said. “Well, Michigan decided maybe we’re not going to the parties last night. So this morning, with all of you, this is the party. This is the start of a celebration of all of us coming together.”
Trump's pick in a Michigan House race will lose to a candidate who dropped out, CNN projects
Wednesday morning featured a rare and pretty remarkable upset in Michigan.
CNN’s Decision Desk now projects that Tom Smith, who suspended his campaign last month, will defeat Trump-backed candidate Amir Hassan in the Republican primary in Michigan’s 8th Congressional District.
Even before he dropped out, the little-known Smith didn’t appear to have run a robust campaign in the first place. His website describes him as a small business owner.
And the upset isn’t just a curiosity; it could actually matter quite a bit in the battle for the House. That’s because Michigan’s 8th District is one of the GOP’s best pickup opportunities. Trump carried the district by two points in 2024, even as Democratic Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet won.
Hassan is a US Navy veteran and former federal law enforcement officer who served as a watch commander in the prison camps at Guantanamo Bay. Trump endorsed him in a social-media post back in June.
He raised more than $700,000 for his campaign. Smith does not appear to have filed a federal campaign finance report.
Trump: El-Sayed winning Democratic primary is “great news” for Republicans
President Donald Trump reacted to progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed’s projected victory in the Michigan Senate Democratic primary, calling it “Great news for the Republican Party.”
“Great news for the Republican Party,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social, adding about the other Democratic candidate, Rep. Haley Stevens, “As usual, the Polls were way off on this one. She was not expected to do nearly as well as she did.”
Vice President JD Vance also mentioned El-Sayed Wednesday morning, painting him as the face of the Democratic Party and a threat to the administration’s accomplishments.
“We don’t want the next administration, whoever you know, God forbid, you’re going to have President El-Sayed in three years. We don’t want him to undo all the incredible work that we’ve been doing,” Vance said during a task force meeting with members of Congress on fraud.
Democrats coalesce behind El-Sayed as Senate nominee
Democratic leadership praised progressive nominee Abdul El-Sayed for winning Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary after making their unofficial backing of his opponent clear during the race.
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Sen. Kristen Gillibrand released a statement praising El-Sayed for “an energetic campaign that inspired thousands of Michiganders,” after the win.
They said that “Democrats are united by a common purpose” of winning in November despite the divisive nominating contest. Senate Majority PAC, a top Democratic super PAC, hailed El-Sayed as a “a real fighter who shows up for working families.”
Outgoing Michigan Sen. Gary Peters, who had endorsed El-Sayed’s rival, Rep. Haley Stevens, also weighed in. “Congratulations to him” Peters told CNN.
Key Republican groups were also responding to El-Sayed’s victory, offering a preview of the intense midterm election race to come. Pointedly referring to his full name – “Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed” – National Republican Senatorial Committee Chair Tim Scott called him “the most radical Democrat Senate nominee ever.”
Progressives get a victory in Michigan as El-Sayed wins nomination
Abdul El-Sayed’s projected victory is a triumph for national progressive leaders including Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. It is a defeat to Sens. Chuck Schumer and Kirsten Gillibrand, the New York senators who respectively lead the Senate Democratic caucus and the Senate Democratic campaign arm. Both Schumer and Gillibrand privately signaled support for Stevens, CNN previously reported.
El-Sayed overcame more than $60 million from outside groups backing his rival. The largest of those groups, United Democracy Project — the super PAC arm of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) — emerged as a flashpoint in the contest, fueling intense debates over campaign finance and US policy toward Israel.
El-Sayed, an outspoken critic of the war in Gaza who has accused Israel of committing genocide in the war, seized on AIPAC’s intervention, amplifying his criticism of Israel and raising questions about Stevens’ integrity. The outside spending also reinforced a broader establishment vs. anti-establishment dynamic that El-Sayed’s camp embraced.
Pairing that with a focus on universal health care, support for labor, and campaign finance reforms, El-Sayed prevailed in the high-stakes primary fight that became a proxy for the national debate over the direction of the Democratic Party.
Both El-Sayed and Stevens were conciliatory in their remarks to supporters after midnight Tuesday, urging party unity and attacking Rogers.
State Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who suspended her primary campaign one month ago, quickly endorsed El-Sayed after promising before polls close to endorse the Democratic winner. In a reflection of how close the matchup between Stevens and El-Sayed ultimately was, the margin in the primary was set to be far smaller than the roughly 60,000 votes McMorrow received because she remained on the ballot Tuesday.
Republicans launch ads targeting El-Sayed
Republican groups have begun releasing ads targeting Abdul El-Sayed, whom CNN’s Decision Desk has projected will win the Michigan Democratic Senate primary.
With El-Sayed now set to face GOP former Rep. Mike Rogers in November, the Senate Leadership Fund and National Republican Senatorial Committee have released videos painting El-Sayed as “radical.”
The video from the NRSC — which came before CNN projected the close Democratic primary race — described El-Sayed as “the most radical Senate candidate in America.”
“Abdul El-Sayed: too radical, too dangerous, wrong for Michigan,” the video says, arguing that El-Sayed wants to hike taxes and has controversial ties.
Similarly, the ad from SLF used clips of El-Sayed’s previous comments on police and immigration to argue he is “dangerously radical.”
“Abdul El-Sayed’s professed agenda threatens the safety and freedom of Michiganders while upending the rule of law,” SLF said in a statement on the release of the ad, sharing that it will pour in $45 million into the race — “the organization’s largest investment ever in Michigan.”
Rep. Haley Stevens congratulates Abdul El-Sayed on Democratic Senate primary win
Rep. Haley Stevens released a statement congratulating rival Abdul El-Sayed on his win in the Michigan Democratic Senate primary, shortly after the race was called by CNN and other networks.
Acknowledging the “rigorous” campaign they waged, Stevens echoed calls across the party for unity heading into the fall.
Stevens has called El-Sayed to concede, according to a source familiar.
“That is why we have primaries,” she said in the statement. “I am proud to have put up my hand to serve, and prouder to continue to work together to make sure this Senate seat remains blue, that we flip the United States Senate and continue the work for Michigan.”
Democratic socialist McKinney will defeat incumbent Michigan Rep. Thanedar, CNN projects
State Rep. Donavan McKinney, a democratic socialist, will defeat Rep. Shri Thanedar to win the Democratic primary in Michigan’s 13th Congressional District, CNN Decision Desk projects.
McKinney’s primary win will almost certainly mean a return of Black congressional representation in Congress to the Detroit-based district. The election of Thanedar, an Indian American immigrant, in 2022 marked the first time since the 1950s that the majority-Black city has not had a Black representative in Congress.
While Thanedar, a former Democratic Socialists of America member himself, supports many progressive priorities, McKinney appealed to voters with an anti-establishment campaign backed by independent Sen. Bernie Sanders and several local Black leaders.
Tuesday’s contest marks the latest incumbent Democrat’s loss to a democratic socialist challenger this primary season, after Darializa Avila Chevalier defeated Rep. Adriano Espaillat in New York and Melat Kiros beat out longtime Rep. Diana DeGette in Colorado.
McKinney, who has focused his platform on support for the Green New Deal, raising taxes on billionaires and corporations, and investing in public schools, will be heavily favored heading into the general election in the Democratic stronghold district.

sources.news_title: Abdul el-Sayed defeats AIPAC-backed rival in Michigan primary, defying millions in lobby spending
sources.text:
Abdul el-Sayed defeats AIPAC-backed rival in Michigan primary, defying millions in lobby spending
The Cradle | August 5, 2026
Abdul el-Sayed, a former public health official, has won Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, defeating AIPAC-backed Representative Haley Stevens in a close race, NBC News reported on 5 August.
Sayed won despite being heavily outfunded, with outside groups pouring close to $65 million into the race to stop him.
More than $30 million of the television advertising behind Stevens came from a group affiliated with the pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC.
Taken together, Stevens and her allies outspent Sayed and the groups supporting him on advertising by a factor of nine to one, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact.
Sayed pointed to the imbalance in his closing argument, saying during a debate, “If you need a $60 million crutch, you probably can’t be elected on your own terms.”
He also went after Stevens’ support for aid to Israel, and stated outright that Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, a position that carries particular weight in Michigan, home to large Muslim and Arab communities.
Sayed made Stevens’ backing from AIPAC and corporate political action committees a central charge against her, attacking both the funds she accepted directly and the advertising her big-spending allies bought on her behalf.
Stevens, a four-term congresswoman, ran with the backing of the Democratic establishment, positioning her campaign squarely within the party leadership alongside Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer.
Governor Gretchen Whitmer endorsed her on 24 July in a late move seen as an attempt to stifle Sayed’s rise. Outgoing Senator Gary Peters, whose seat is at stake, also endorsed her after deciding not to seek a third term.
Despite the cumulative hurdles, Sayed’s victory follows a run of defeats for AIPAC-funded candidates in Democratic primaries this cycle.
On 30 June, Democratic socialist Melat Kiros unseated Diana DeGette in Colorado’s 1st congressional district by nearly 10 percentage points, ending a 30-year congressional career built in part on well over $1.6 million from AIPAC.
A week earlier, in New York, Brad Lander defeated Dan Goldman after attacking his refusal to call the assault on Gaza a genocide or to back restrictions on arms sales to Israel, while Darializa Avila Chevalier unseated Adriano Espaillat in a campaign centered on his acceptance of AIPAC money.
A senior House Democrat called the Colorado result a wake-up call, with support for Israel turning from an asset into a liability. Strategist Jon Paul Lupo told POLITICO that candidates opposing the war on Gaza held a massive political advantage this cycle.
Pew Research Center polling released in April found 60 percent of US citizens now view Israel unfavorably, with very unfavorable sentiment nearly tripling since 2022, while a Gallup poll in February recorded more US citizens sympathizing with Palestinians, at 41 percent, than with Israelis, at 36 percent – the first such result in US history.

sources.text:
Left-wing political outsider Abdul El-Sayed is projected to win the Democratic Senate primary in Michigan, which exposed bitter divisions over the party’s direction. The former public health official is on course to beat moderate four-term Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens, according to CBS News, the BBC’s US partner.
El-Sayed voiced support for left-wing causes like universal healthcare and abolishing US Immigration and Customs Enforcement. He also called for ending unconditional US military aid to Israel.
If officially confirmed as the primary’s winner, he will face Republican and Trump ally Mike Rogers, in November’s midterm elections.
The son of Egyptian immigrants would be the first Muslim US senator if he wins in November.
“We won,” El-Sayed posted on X on Wednesday morning, writing that he was “proud to be your Democratic nominee for US Senate”.
“Money out of politics. Money in your pocket. Medicare for All,” he added, a familiar refrain he had used on the campaign trail.
“I want to congratulate Abdul El-Sayed on winning the Democratic nomination for US Senate,” Stevens said in a statement. “He is a doctor, a community health official, a Rhodes Scholar, and a dedicated Michigander. I am proud to offer my support as he takes on Mike Rogers in the general election.”
The November midterm elections will determine the balance of power in Washington for the last two years of President Donald Trump’s time in office.
Trump declared the Michigan Senate result “Great news for the Republican Party”.
In his post on Truth Social, Trump referred to the Democratic Party as the “Dumocrats”, and claimed their “crazy policies will only get worse!”
After a bruising and sometimes bitter campaign, El-Sayed hinted at bridge-building when he addressed supporters on Tuesday night, before the outcome was known.
“Whatever happens tonight, we have a responsibility to ensure that we unite, unite to make sure that [Republican] Mike Rogers never sees the inside of the US Senate.”
Voters in Michigan, Virginia and Washington state also cast their ballots in Democratic primaries on US House of Representatives candidates on Tuesday.
Both candidates in Michigan have offered a different vision for the state and for the country.
El-Sayed was endorsed by left-wing politicians including Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders and New York City congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
Stevens, 43, took a more moderate approach, pitching herself as the middle-of-the-road candidate who would appeal to voters unsure of which party to back in November. She made a promise to save manufacturing jobs in Michigan, should she be elected.
Stevens earned the endorsement of Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer, as well as outgoing Senator Gary Peters.
One of the biggest areas where the candidates disagreed was their stance on Israel.
El-Sayed spoke out against US involvement in the Middle East, including aid to Israel. Stevens, meanwhile, is staunchly pro-Israel and has said she supports upholding US aid to Israel without conditions.
The senate seat is currently held by a Democrat who is retiring. The last time a Republican senator was elected in this Midwestern state was in 1994.
But in presidential elections it is one of the crucial swing states – Michigan voted for Democrat Joe Biden in 2020 but for Trump in 2024.

sources.news_title: El-Sayed Survives Michigan Primary, Prediction Markets Still Think He Wins In November
sources.text:
Abdul El-Sayed won the Michigan Democratic Senate primary that prediction markets called, but not in the blowout they were selling.
El-Sayed edged out Rep. Haley Stevens on Tuesday in a bruising Democratic Senate race that exposed deep splits in the party and left November looking more like a true toss-up than the near-lock the markets had implied. The Michigan Senate race is one of the most closely watched races of the 2026 midterm election cycle, and the primary turned what prediction markets had treated as a 98% foregone conclusion into another reminder that any election can be close once the votes are in.
The result doesn’t just matter for the future of the Democratic Party. It is a must-hold seat for Democrats in the battle for Senate control, and El-Sayed now has to defend an open Michigan seat against former Republican congressman Mike Rogers in a year when polls already show him trailing.
If Democrats can’t keep retiring Sen. Gary Peters’ seat, their path back to a majority gets brutally narrow, which is why this race will remain one of the central tests of whether the progressive bet pays off in November.
How the primary actually played out
Heading into Tuesday, Kalshi and Polymarket were treating El-Sayed’s nomination as functionally decided. Kalshi had him at 98% on more than $8 million in volume. Polymarket had him at 99% on roughly $1.8 million.
The live returns told a different story. El-Sayed won narrowly, 48.5% to 47.5%, after a long night of counting.
The vote split reflects how hard-fought the race was. El-Sayed built his margin in places like Washtenaw and Kent counties, while Stevens performed better in suburban Oakland, turning the map into a patchwork rather than a simple progressive sweep.
While prediction markets have been solid at predicting outcomes this primary season, they also risk overselling certainty in contests that are still structurally close, like the Michigan Senate race.
Senate control stakes
All of this lands on top of the Senate math, which hasn’t changed. Michigan is a seat Democrats cannot afford to lose. Peters’ retirement created one of the cycle’s few true toss-up races, and whoever won the primary was always going to carry heavy expectations into November.
El-Sayed now faces Rogers, a former congressman who narrowly lost to Sen. Elissa Slotkin in 2024 and comes into this race with name recognition and a tested statewide campaign. A recent polling average on 270toWin has Rogers ahead 46.7% to 42.3% heading toward November.
That’s the kind of data moderate Democrats point to when they warn a progressive nominee might be riskier in a swing state.
Prediction markets, for now, are still more bullish for Democrats than the polls. On Kalshi, El-Sayed is up in two general election contracts: 63% to 40% on $684,000 in volume and 61% to 39% on $552,000.
Polymarket shows similar numbers on just under $200,000. Those prices say Democrats are favored, but they’re nowhere near the near-certainty that surrounded the primary.
Several handicappers and forecast sites continue to rate the race as a toss-up or lean-D at best, reflecting the tension between market optimism and polling reality. If Democrats lose Michigan, it’s hard to see a clean path to 51 seats without an unexpected upset elsewhere.
Progressive wave, with limits
Michigan’s result still matters for the broader intra-party story. El-Sayed’s win adds another progressive notch in a cycle that’s already delivered left-wing candidates wins in places like Colorado and New York.
Michigan is another signal that the Democratic push is heading left, despite expensive campaigns by the more moderate establishment.
But Tuesday also showed where the progressive wave hits resistance. In Missouri’s 1st District, former Rep. Cori Bush failed to complete her comeback, losing again to Rep. Wesley Bell in a rematch defined by clashes over Israel and AIPAC’s role in Democratic primaries. Bell’s decisive win underlined that in some districts, especially where Israel politics are front and center, the progressive lane is still facing steep headwinds, even in a year when left-wing candidates are advancing elsewhere.
That split, with El-Sayed winning narrowly in Michigan and Bush losing big in Missouri, captures the messy reality of the progressive moment: The wave is real, but it’s not universal.
Heading into November
El-Sayed is already talking like the general election is his to win.
He told Politico he’s “going to beat Mike Rogers by 7” in November, framing his campaign as the stronger answer to Rogers and arguing that his progressive agenda is what Michigan voters are looking for. Progressive groups are pushing a similar line, pointing to internal memos that claim El-Sayed is actually better positioned than Stevens against Rogers once the full campaign plays out.
Prediction markets are still on his side, but more cautiously than in the primary. Kalshi and Polymarket both have Democrats favored, yet the odds sit in the 60s. Polls show a genuinely competitive race, with Rogers ahead in some matchups and analysts using words like “toss-up” far more than “lean.”
Michigan remains one of the most important races on the Senate map in the 2026 midterm cycle. It is also one of the clearest tests of how far the progressive bet can go in a state Democrats absolutely have to hold. The markets called the primary right but overshot the margin. Now, November will be the real test of whether they’ve priced the general any more accurately.

sources.news_title: Abdul El-Sayed’s Historic Win Signals Shift in Michigan Politics
sources.text:
Abdul El-Sayed’s recent victory in the Michigan Democratic primary for the U.S. Senate seat marks a significant turning point in the political landscape, showcasing the rising influence of progressive candidates and the diminishing power of the Democratic establishment. Despite facing an onslaught of financial backing for his opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens, El-Sayed emerged victorious by a narrow margin of just one percentage point. El-Sayed, a former public health official with endorsements from prominent figures like Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, ran on a platform that resonated deeply with voters. His key policies included Medicare for All, addressing the rising cost of living, and reducing corporate influence in politics. However, it was his outspoken stance on Israel and Palestine that became a defining issue of the campaign. El-Sayed condemned the actions of Israel in Gaza, advocating for an end to U.S. military aid to Israel, a position that has gained traction among many Democrats disillusioned with traditional party lines.
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) played a pivotal role in the primary, spending $30 million on attack ads against El-Sayed, which dominated the media landscape in the final weeks of the race. These ads misrepresented his comments and attempted to paint him in a negative light. Nonetheless, El-Sayed’s campaign effectively turned this aggressive spending into a focal point, highlighting the dangers of lobbyist influence in politics.
El-Sayed’s success reflects a broader shift in voter sentiment, particularly regarding foreign policy and corporate influence. As former Rep. Andy Levin noted, the electorate is increasingly seeking candidates who are authentic and willing to speak truthfully about contentious issues, including the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. This sentiment is echoed in recent surveys indicating that a significant portion of the Democratic base now supports conditioning military aid to Israel, a stance that was once considered radical.
The implications of El-Sayed’s victory extend beyond Michigan. It signals a potential realignment within the Democratic Party, as leftist candidates continue to challenge establishment figures across the country. In recent primaries, candidates advocating for progressive policies have seen success, particularly in urban areas where voters are more receptive to calls for economic and social reform.
However, the road ahead for El-Sayed is fraught with challenges. He faces a formidable opponent in Republican Mike Rogers, a former congressman and FBI agent, who is expected to mount a strong campaign in the general election. Polls indicate a competitive race, with El-Sayed’s progressive platform being scrutinized for its electability among a broader electorate.
Critics of El-Sayed, including Stevens and her supporters, have raised concerns about his ability to win over moderate voters. They argue that his leftist policies may alienate constituents who lean more conservative. Yet, El-Sayed counters this narrative by asserting that the issues most voters care about—healthcare, job security, and economic stability—transcend partisan divides. He believes that a campaign focused on anti-corporate messaging can resonate with a diverse voter base.
As the general election approaches, El-Sayed’s ability to unify the party and appeal to a wide range of voters will be crucial. His recent endorsements from former opponents and party figures suggest a willingness to rally behind his candidacy, which could bolster his chances against Rogers. The outcome of this race may not only determine the future of El-Sayed’s political career but could also influence the direction of the Democratic Party as it navigates the complexities of modern American politics.
In a state that has historically been a bellwether for national trends, El-Sayed’s campaign represents a microcosm of the broader ideological battles within the Democratic Party. As voters increasingly demand transparency and accountability from their leaders, the success of candidates like El-Sayed may herald a new era of progressive politics in the United States.

DETROIT — Progressive candidate Dr. Abdul El-Sayed narrowly defeated Rep. The Associated Press and multiple news organizations projected El-Sayed as the winner shortly before 10 a.m. Eastern Time on Wednesday. The outspoken progressive campaigned on a platform that included “Medicare for All,” abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), higher taxes, and ending U.S. military aid to Israel.
With 99% of the vote counted, El-Sayed’s lead stood at fewer than 15,000 votes out of more than 1.5 million ballots cast. The razor-thin margin came as a surprise after several polls released during the final week of the campaign showed him holding a comfortable double-digit advantage.
Campaign spending in the contest topped $80 million, making it the costliest Democratic Senate primary in U.S. history, according to AdImpact.
The victory sends El-Sayed, who lost the 2018 Democratic gubernatorial primary to Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, into the general election against former Congressman Mike Rogers. Democrats view the Michigan seat as critical to their effort to regain control of the Senate next year.
The outcome also marks one of the first major electoral successes this cycle for the Democratic Party’s progressive wing outside its traditional liberal strongholds.
Michigan has long been fertile ground for progressive politics. It was the birthplace of the “uncommitted” protest movement against President Joe Biden during the 2024 Democratic presidential primaries and also backed Sen. Bernie Sanders in the state’s 2016 Democratic presidential contest.
If he wins in November, El-Sayed would become the first Muslim ever elected to the U.S. Senate. During his election night gathering in the Detroit area, where large Arab-American and Muslim communities reside, several supporters were seen performing Islamic prayers.
Rogers argued that the bruising Democratic primary would leave his opponent politically weakened heading into the general election.
“Whoever comes out of it is going to have a coalition problem. Remember, voting starts in about five or six weeks. We’re in an election cycle now,” Rogers told The Post hours before El-Sayed’s primary win.
“We’ve been building toward that day. They’ve been fighting each other and moving further and further to the left.”
Tuesday’s primaries also produced victories for several other progressive candidates, including Rep. Rashida Tlaib of Michigan, Michigan state Rep. Donavan McKinney, and Bernie Sanders-backed William Lawrence.
One notable setback for progressives came in Missouri, where Rep. Wesley Bell scored a decisive victory over Cori Bush in a Democratic House primary centered in St. Louis.
The Michigan Senate race evolved into a broader ideological battle between the Democratic establishment and the party’s progressive faction, with each side arguing that its candidate offered the stronger path to victory in November.
Throughout the campaign, El-Sayed advocated eliminating co-pays and deductibles under “Medicare for All,” abolishing ICE, publicly financing elections, imposing an arms embargo on Israel, and freezing property tax assessments for homeowners age 65 and older.
Those positions earned him endorsements from left-wing personalities including streamer Hasan Piker and the Democratic Socialists of America. Although frequently associated with the movement, El-Sayed has said he considers himself a capitalist and is not a member of the DSA.
The race frequently turned personal. El-Sayed argued that Stevens could not “string together two coherent sentences” and suggested she had been influenced by the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), whose affiliated super PAC spent nearly $30 million supporting her campaign.
Stevens, whose Midwestern accent and slogan, “Stick it to ’em,” attracted widespread attention online, sought to frame the race as one centered on Michigan rather than national ideological divisions, insisting, “It’s a Michigan moment for me.”
Should El-Sayed prevail in November, he could create challenges for Senate Democratic leadership. The Michigan Democrat has previously expressed opposition to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer continuing to lead the party.
Schumer endorsed Stevens during the primary, joining other prominent Democrats, including Whitmer and retiring Sen. Gary Peters, who campaigned alongside her in the closing days of the race.
Supporters of Stevens argued she was the stronger general election candidate. A recent EPIC-MRA survey showed Rogers leading El-Sayed 46% to 43%, while Stevens held a narrow 44% to 42% advantage over the Republican.
Rogers narrowly lost Michigan’s Senate race to Sen. Elissa Slotkin in 2024, but El-Sayed has repeatedly dismissed concerns about his electability.
“When they say I’m not electable, they’re not talking about me,” El-Sayed told supporters during a rally in Grand Rapids on Saturday.
“They’re saying that you couldn’t possibly be open-minded enough … to elect somebody with a name like mine who prays like I do in a state like ours.”
El-Sayed also enjoyed the full support of members of the progressive congressional “Squad” during his campaign.
Democrats currently must gain four Senate seats to reclaim the chamber’s majority.
“We have a real shot to take the majority of the United States Senate,” Peters told reporters while campaigning for Stevens on Sunday. “That’s become increasingly likely as every month goes by. But it doesn’t happen if we lose Michigan.

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche’s nomination as attorney general advanced on Tuesday, as the Senate Judiciary Committee gave its approval on a 12-10 party line vote.
But his confirmation is not a sure thing, as the full Senate – where Republicans have a narrow edge – has the final say. One Republican Senator, Susan Collins of Maine, has said she would vote against Blanche, according the The New York Times .
If one more Republican senator votes against him – and assuming no Democrats switch – he won’t be confirmed.
The controversy over Blanche is over his administration of the Justice Department.
Senate Democrats argue that Blanche has meekly complied with direction from President Donald Trump, especially his approval of the “anti-weaponization” fund this might have allowed Jan. 6 rioters to receive financial compensation.
Eight dead, 15 hurt is Russia-Ukraine war
The ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine claimed 11 lives overnight. Another 15 people were wounded, according to United Press International.
The two nations exchanged fire. Ukraine has been focusing on striking Russia’s commercial sector, hitting logistics hub of Wildberries, Russia top online retailer.
Russia, for its part, attacked a hospital in the city of Sumy, resulting in the death of two girls and an elderly woman.
The current phase of conflict between the two nations – both once part of the Soviet Union – began in February 2022 and was widely expected to rule in a quick victory for Russia. But, with help from the U.S. and European allies, the smaller nation has been to forge a stalemate.
Weather: Typical summer weather
Our West Orange County cities will continue to get something unsurprising: typical summer weather for August. Highs in the mid-to-high 80s during the day and overnight temps in the high 60s and low 70s. Wednesday is expected to 84 during the day with a low of 68. Thursday will skip to 86 (69) with Friday the same. Saturday should war slightly to 87 (70). Skies will be cloudy each day except for Friday, when it will be mostly sunny.

sources.news_title: Michigan Senate Race 2026: El-Sayed Projected Winner After Nail-Biter Primary Against Stevens
sources.text:
Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary lived up to every bit of its hype. After a night of see-sawing returns, shrinking leads, and a Wayne County vote count that had both campaigns’ watch parties holding their breath, NBC News has projected Dr. Abdul El-Sayed as the winner over Rep. Haley Stevens.
It was close. It was expensive. And it may end up being the clearest signal yet of where the Democratic Party is headed, or at least where its base wants it to go.
A Race That Came Down to the Wire
Polls closed across Michigan at 8 and 9 p.m. on Tuesday, August 4, but nobody was calling this one early. Early returns had El-Sayed at roughly 49% to Stevens’ 47%, with state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who dropped out of the race back on July 5 but stayed on the ballot, pulling in about 4%.
From there, the count turned into a county-by-county tug of war. El-Sayed built early strength in Kent, Macomb, and Washtenaw counties, his home turf and the seat of the University of Michigan. Stevens held her own in Oakland, Wayne, Saginaw, and Genesee.
Wayne County, home to Detroit, ended up being the story of the night. Stevens started with a majority there, but her lead kept shrinking as Election Day votes from Detroit rolled in, along with results from Dearborn, a city with a large Arab-American population where El-Sayed reportedly won more than three-quarters of the vote. By 1:30 a.m., El-Sayed was holding a narrow but visibly shrinking lead, and both candidates addressed supporters in Detroit without either one claiming victory.
| County | Leading Candidate | Notes | 
|---|---|---|
| Wayne | Stevens (early), narrowing | Detroit and Dearborn returns cut her lead sharply | 
| Oakland | Stevens | Her home base; led by roughly 2 points with 76% counted | 
| Kent | El-Sayed | Grand Rapids area | 
| Macomb | El-Sayed | Suburban Detroit | 
| Washtenaw | El-Sayed | His home county; includes Ann Arbor | 
| Saginaw | Stevens |  | 
| Genesee | Stevens |  | 
Figures reflect partial returns reported on primary night and are not final certified results.
Stevens told her crowd to “get some sleep, or some coffee,” and wait for the final numbers. El-Sayed, watching returns with family and advisers, thanked supporters for a fight he said proved something about grassroots momentum, especially given how heavily he was outspent by outside groups.
Who Are El-Sayed and Stevens?
Abdul El-Sayed is a physician from Ann Arbor who previously served as Detroit’s health director and later ran the Wayne County health department. This wasn’t his first statewide campaign either; he ran for Michigan governor in 2018 and lost the Democratic primary. This time, he ran well to the left, campaigning on Medicare for All and taking aim at billionaire influence in politics.
Haley Stevens is a four-term congresswoman from Birmingham representing a district in Oakland County. She built her campaign around manufacturing, blue-collar jobs, and a more traditional Democratic pitch, positioning herself as the candidate who could actually win in a state Donald Trump carried in 2024.
The two are backed by very different wings of the party. El-Sayed had Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez in his corner. Stevens carried endorsements from outgoing Sen. Gary Peters, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, and former Sen. Debbie Stabenow, essentially the entire Michigan Democratic establishment.
|  | Abdul El-Sayed | Haley Stevens | 
|---|---|---|
| Background | Physician; former Detroit health director; ex-Wayne County health director | Four-term U.S. Representative from Birmingham | 
| Political lane | Progressive | Establishment moderate | 
| Signature policy | Medicare for All; curbing billionaire influence in politics | Manufacturing and blue-collar jobs | 
| Key endorsers | Bernie Sanders, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez | Gary Peters, Chuck Schumer, Gretchen Whitmer, Debbie Stabenow | 
| Stance on Israel | Critical of continued U.S. military support | Firmly pro-Israel | 
| Prior statewide run | 2018 Michigan governor primary (lost) | First statewide run | 
Israel Policy Became the Defining Fault Line
If one issue defined this primary, it was foreign policy, specifically, U.S. support for Israel amid the war in Gaza. El-Sayed made criticism of that support a central plank of his campaign, arguing the money would be better spent at home. “Rather than fund the genocide perpetrated by a foreign government, we’d better build schools right here in Grand Rapids,” he told a crowd at a recent campaign stop.
Stevens, by contrast, ran as the pro-Israel candidate in the race and cast El-Sayed as the choice Republicans were quietly rooting for. “You see the Republicans, they’re propping up my Democratic opponent,” she said on MS NOW, adding that she had no intention of making things easier for the GOP.
That divide showed up in the numbers too. In Oakland County, a suburban Detroit region with a significant Jewish population that Stevens represents in Congress, she was leading by around 2 points with three-quarters of the votes counted. Outside spending tied to the Israel debate, including reported backing from AIPAC-aligned groups, made this the most expensive Democratic Senate primary in U.S. history, according to reporting from the Detroit News.
Beyond Israel, the two candidates also split over how to regulate AI data centers, another flashpoint that separated El-Sayed’s more restrictive, consumer-protection approach from Stevens’ focus on economic growth and job creation.
What Happens Next
The winner inherits a seat that matters enormously to both parties. Sen. Gary Peters is retiring after two terms, and Democrats need to hold Michigan if they want any real shot at retaking the Senate. Republicans haven’t won a Senate race in the state since 1994, but this cycle feels different given how competitive statewide races have become.
Waiting in November is former Rep. Mike Rogers, who ran unopposed in the Republican primary. Rogers came close to beating Stevens in general election polling published before the primary and has already started framing the Democratic nominee, whoever it turned out to be, as too extreme for Michigan voters. A campaign spokesperson didn’t hold back on primary night, saying Rogers was “winning” while Democrats fought what they called a “bloody” internal battle.
Whoever heads into the fall as the Democratic nominee now has to do two things fast: unify a party that just spent months tearing itself apart over Israel policy, AI regulation, and what kind of Democrat can actually win in a purple state, and pivot immediately into a general election fight that both parties are treating as a must-win.
Michigan’s Senate race isn’t just a local story anymore. It’s a preview of the argument Democrats are having with themselves nationally, and in a few months, voters here will decide which side of that argument gets a shot at the general election.

sources.news_title: U.S. Senate race results remain undecided
sources.text:
U.S. Senate race win goes to El-Sayed
- :
- 10 hours ago
- 3 min read
Although the hotly contested Democratic primary contest for the U.S. Senate in Michigan, between Congresswoman Haley Stevens and former Wayne County medical director Abdul El-Sayed, was simply too close to call as of 1:30 a.m. Wednesday morning, Stevens at 10 a.m. Wednesday called El-Sayed to concede the election.
Despite several recent polls showing El-Sayed leading by as much as 15 points, Stevens was only trailing by about one point. El-Sayed had 740,950 (48.48 percent) votes to 726, 057 votes for Stevens.
In another closely watched contest, for the open seat in the 11th district of Congress now held by Haley Stevens, as of about 10:30 p.m., it appeared that current state Senator Jeremy Moss (D-Bloomfield Township), with about 49 percent of votes cast, would be the next member of the U.S. House.
The district includes Birmingham, Bloomfield Township, Bloomfield Hills and the majority of Oakland County.
Moss, who would be the first openly gay member of Congress from Oakland County, raised about $1.4 million in the reports filed in July, and has been in the state Senate since 2019 after time in the state House. In both chambers of the legislature Moss was an important factor in the fight for women’s health care rights, expanded voting rights, gun control and rights for the LGBTQ+ community.
He had the backing of Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson and state Attorney General Dana Nessel, plus others of note. Moss beat candidates Aisha Farooqi, John Paul Torres and Don Ufford, and is expected to be the victor in November in a district that is considered in the Democratic column.
Democrat Jason Hoskins, a current state Representative, appeared to be the winner in the three-person contest for the 7th district of the state Senate which includes Birmingham, Bloomfield Township and Bloomfield Hills.
Several hours after the polls closed, Hoskins had picked up almost 57 percent of the votes cast.
Hoskins, prior the entering the House, has spent a decade as a legislative aide in Lansing.
He beat back challenges from Shadia Martini and Rakesh Ramakrishnan. Hoskins will now face Republican Anthony Paesano in the November general election.
In the Democratic primary for the state House 6th district, which includes most of Birmingham and part of Bloomfield Township, Melanie Macey appeared well on her way to victory with about 65 percent of the vote as of midnight.
Macey defeated Democrats David Lauer and Charlie Gandy-Thompson for the right to face in November Mike Steger who was unopposed in the Republican primary.
As of midnight, incumbent Democrat House member Samantha Steckloff was leading with almost 72 percent of the vote against Brandon Young for the district that includes part of Birmingham and Bloomfield Township
On the Republican primary for the 19th House district, Kevin Hammer was leading with just over 66 percent of the vote against Mitch Swoboda but there was a considerable number of votes still not counted.
In the Republican primary for the 20th House district, which includes a very small part of Bloomfield Township, S. David Sullivan had 59 percent of the vote against Herman Barbe. However, a considerable number of votes have yet to be counted. The winner of this race will face incumbent Democrat House member Noah Arbit.
At 12;30 a.m., the Republican primary contest for the 54th House district, which includes Bloomfield Hills and part of Bloomfield Township, the race was very close. Roman Gaskey had 50.76 percent of the votes and Jeffrey Omtvedt had 49.24 percent. The winner will face Democrat Sarah Pounds in the general election.
As far as ballot issues, a renewal of public safety millage and road millage passed in Bloomfield Township.
On what is being billed as a county-wide enhancement millage for schools, as of 1 a.m. the “no” votes were 121,161 and votes in support were 118,511. The 1.5-mill tax would be collected for the first time this December and would last six years.
An update on close contests will be provided mid-morning on Wednesday.

sources.news_title: Michigan Senate race tightens as El-Sayed leads Stevens in Democratic primary
sources.text:
Progressives in Michigan are expressing concern over the tightening race for the open U.S. Senate seat as the state’s Democratic primary unfolds. With incumbent Gary Peters retiring, the contest between Abdul El-Sayed and Haley Stevens has become a focal point for the party’s internal struggle between progressive and moderate factions. Recent polling indicates El-Sayed, who has the backing of prominent figures like Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, is leading Stevens. However, the margin of victory remains in question, and the primary is of critical importance as Michigan is considered a toss-up state that Democrats need to hold to maintain control of the Senate.
Key Takeaways
- Market data suggests a decrease in confidence that Abdul El-Sayed will secure a decisive 10–15% victory margin in the Michigan Senate Democratic primary, with YES pricing dropping significantly.
- Activity in the Macomb County sub-market indicates reduced confidence in El-Sayed’s ability to secure a win there, with YES probability declining amid concerns about his performance in the broader primary.
- The progressive-moderate divide within the Democratic Party is highlighted by the endorsements from key figures, affecting market perceptions of El-Sayed’s chances in both the statewide and local contests.
What to Watch
Observers should monitor upcoming polling results, particularly from reputable pollsters like Emerson, which could solidify or further disrupt current market expectations. Key endorsements and voter turnout patterns, especially in areas like Macomb County, will be crucial indicators of the primary’s outcome. Any shifts in support from former McMorrow backers or late-breaking developments in the campaigns could significantly influence market pricing and the eventual resolution of these contests.
